nodes.label: Set Fundamentals
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: How a set is written and which standard number sets exist. Everything later depends on reading a set-builder rule correctly.

nodes.label: Definition and Notation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, and $a \in A$ states membership while $a \notin A$ denies it. JEE exploits 'well-defined' by offering vague collections such as 'the best cricketers in India'.

nodes.label: Standard Number Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The usual chain is $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Rational numbers are $\mathbb{Q} = \{p/q : p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \ q \neq 0\}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ covers every complex number.

nodes.label: Roster and Set-Builder Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Roster form lists the elements, set-builder form gives the defining rule. Always expand the rule into a list before you start counting.

nodes.label: Example: Roster Expansion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The builder $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : |x| \le 3\}$ expands to $\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$, so the cardinality is $n(A) = 7$.

nodes.label: Types of Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Classification by size and by comparison. The empty set trap and the equal-versus-equivalent distinction are the two favourites of paper setters.

nodes.label: Empty and Singleton Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The empty set satisfies $n(\phi) = 0$, yet $\{\phi\}$ is a singleton with exactly one element. Options built on this confusion appear almost every year.

nodes.label: Finite, Infinite and Cardinality
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The cardinality $n(A)$ counts distinct elements of a finite set, and $n(\phi) = 0$. Infinite sets such as $\mathbb{R}$ carry no finite count, so count questions always restrict to a finite universe.

nodes.label: Equal vs Equivalent Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Equivalent means $n(A) = n(B)$, while equal means $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ together, giving $A = B$. Equal sets are always equivalent, but equivalent sets need not be equal.

nodes.label: Subsets and Power Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Subset logic and the $2^n$ power-set count drive quick option-based questions where all subsets must be enumerated.

nodes.label: Subset and Proper Subset
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ lies in $B$, and $A \subset B$ adds $A \neq B$. The empty set is a subset of every set, which makes it the default element of any intersection.

nodes.label: Power Set
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $P(A)$ collects all subsets of $A$, so $n(A) = n$ gives $n(P(A)) = 2^n$. The power set is never empty because $\phi \in P(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Power Set of a Two-Element Set
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $A = \{1, 2\}$ we get $P(A) = \{\phi, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}$. Here $A \in P(A)$ is true but $\{A\} \notin P(A)$, a distinction worth memorising.

nodes.label: Disjoint and Comparable Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Two sets are disjoint when $A \cap B = \phi$, and comparable when one contains the other. Disjointness is exactly what lets you drop the intersection term in counting formulas.

nodes.label: Real Intervals
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Closed and open intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, for example $[a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}$. Mixed forms such as $[a, b)$ show up constantly in domain and range answers.

nodes.label: Set Operations and Algebraic Laws
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and complement, together with the laws that regroup them. Every De Morgan question reduces to one of these rules.

nodes.label: Union of Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$ gathers every element of either set. It is commutative and associative, with identity $A \cup \phi = A$.

nodes.label: Intersection of Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$ keeps only common elements, and $A \cap \phi = \phi$. Intersection distributes over union: $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Difference of Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A - B = A \cap B'$ removes from $A$ everything that also lies in $B$. Consequently $A - B = A$ holds exactly when $A \cap B = \phi$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Difference
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \Delta B = (A - B) \cup (B - A)$ is the exclusive part of the union, and $n(A \Delta B) = n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A \cap B)$. It distributes over intersection: $A \cap (B \Delta C) = (A \cap B) \Delta (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Complement and De Morgan Laws
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: De Morgan gives $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$, alongside $A \cup A' = U$ and $A \cap A' = \phi$. Flip the operation and swap the sets.

nodes.label: Example: Complement Counting
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $n(U) = 50$ and $n(A \cap B) = 12$, then $n((A \cap B)') = n(U) - n(A \cap B) = 38$. Complement questions are subtraction from the universe and nothing more.

nodes.label: Commutative, Associative and Idempotent Laws
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \cup B = B \cup A$, $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ and $A \cup A = A$, with mirror laws for intersection. These let you regroup a long union while shading a Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Cardinality and Counting
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Inclusion-exclusion on finite sets. This is where most JEE Main set questions actually live.

nodes.label: Two-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$, and the intersection term disappears for disjoint sets. This is the most used counting identity in the chapter.

nodes.label: Example: Survey Counting
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If 30 students like physics, 25 like chemistry and 10 like both, then $n(P \cup C) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45$ of the surveyed students like at least one.

nodes.label: Three-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(C \cap A) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$. Add singles, subtract pairs, then add back the triple overlap.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly Two Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A) - 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements lying in precisely two of the three sets. The coefficient 3 strips out the triple overlap counted in every pair.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly One Set
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - 2[n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A)] + 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements in exactly one set. Most-attempted region in a three-circle Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Counting Differences
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ and $n(B - A) = n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Use these when only one region is asked, instead of shading the whole diagram.

nodes.label: Cartesian Products
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Ordered pairs and product sets. This is the bridge from sets to relations and functions, so it appears in both chapters.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: cartesian products coordinate inequalities and divisibility relations

nodes.label: Ordered Pairs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(a_1, b_1) = (a_2, b_2)$ holds iff $a_1 = a_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$, so order matters and $(1, 2) \neq (2, 1)$. This single idea is why $(a, b) \neq (b, a)$ in counting questions.

nodes.label: Cartesian Product Definition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}$ and $n(A \times B) = n(A) n(B)$. Also $A \times B = \phi$ exactly when at least one of the sets is empty.

nodes.label: Properties of the Product
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(A \times B) \cap (C \times D) = (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D)$, and $A \subseteq B, C \subseteq D$ implies $A \times C \subseteq B \times D$. Distribution over union, intersection and difference all hold.

nodes.label: Example: Shared Ordered Pairs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $A$ and $B$ have $n$ elements in common, then $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ share exactly $n^2$ ordered pairs, because both coordinates must be shared.

nodes.label: Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A relation is simply a subset of a product set. Domain, range, inverse and composition follow from that reading.

nodes.label: Relation as a Subset
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$, written $aRb$ for $(a, b) \in R$. With $n(A) = m$ and $n(B) = n$ there are $2^{mn}$ possible relations.

nodes.label: Domain, Range and Codomain
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\text{Domain}(R) = \{a \in A : (a, b) \in R\}$ collects the first entries and the range collects the second. Passing to $R^{-1}$ swaps domain and range.

nodes.label: Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Reflexive demands $(a, a) \in R$ for all $a$, symmetric demands $aRb \Rightarrow bRa$, and transitive demands $aRb, bRc \Rightarrow aRc$. One missing pair destroys each property.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: types of relations equivalence relations and closures

nodes.label: Example: Counting Reflexive Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: On an $n$-element set the diagonal pairs are forced, so reflexive relations number $2^{n^2 - n}$. For $n = 3$ that is $2^6 = 64$ out of $2^9 = 512$ total relations.

nodes.label: Inverse and Composition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $R^{-1} = \{(b, a) : (a, b) \in R\}$ and $(S \circ R)^{-1} = R^{-1} \circ S^{-1}$. Composition is not commutative in general, so the order of the arrows matters.

nodes.label: Equivalence Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive at once. Such relations split the set into clean, non-overlapping classes.

nodes.label: Definition of an Equivalence Relation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Standard examples are equality, congruence modulo $n$ and 'born in the same year'.

nodes.label: Equivalence Classes
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $[a] = \{x \in A : (x, a) \in R\}$, and any two classes are either identical or disjoint. The classes partition $A$, so their cardinalities add up to $n(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Classes Modulo 3
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Congruence mod 3 splits $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$ into the three classes $\{-2, 1\}$, $\{-1, 2\}$ and $\{0, 3\}$, which are disjoint and together cover the set.

nodes.label: Combining Equivalence Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $R$ and $S$ are equivalence relations then $R \cap S$ is again an equivalence relation, but $R \cup S$ need not be. The inverse $R^{-1}$ of an equivalence relation is always one.

nodes.label: Functions and Mappings
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: What makes a rule a function, and how domain, codomain and range differ. One missed condition here turns a relation into a function in the answer key.

nodes.label: Definition of a Function
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A function $f: A \to B$ assigns to each $x \in A$ a unique image $f(x) \in B$. Every element of $A$ must be used, and no element may get two images.

nodes.label: Domain, Codomain and Range
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\text{Range}(f) = \{f(x) : x \in A\}$ sits inside the codomain $B$. Range equal to codomain is precisely the onto condition, so this comparison decides surjectivity.

nodes.label: Vertical Line Test
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A curve represents a function exactly when no vertical line cuts it twice. Curves like $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $y^2 = 4ax$ fail it, so they are relations rather than functions.

nodes.label: Equality of Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Two functions are equal only if their domains match, codomains match and rules agree everywhere. $\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ and $x+1$ are unequal because the first is undefined at $x = 1$.

nodes.label: Mapping Classifications
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: One-one, onto, into and bijection, together with the counting formulas built on them. These counting questions are a recurring JEE Main fixture.

nodes.label: One-One (Injective)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$, equivalently every horizontal line cuts the graph at most once. With $n(A) = m$, $n(B) = n$ and $n \ge m$, the count is ${}^{n}P_{m}$.

nodes.label: Many-One Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Distinct elements may share an image, so any function that turns around is many-one. The count is $n^{m} - {}^{n}P_{m}$ when $n \ge m$, and $n^{m}$ otherwise.

nodes.label: Onto (Surjective)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Onto means $\text{Range}(f) = B$, so every codomain element is hit. For finite sets the count is $\sum_{r=0}^{n} (-1)^{r} \binom{n}{r} (n-r)^{m}$, and every odd-degree real polynomial is onto $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.label: Into Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Into means the range sits properly inside the codomain, that is $\text{Range}(f) \subset B$. Count it as $n^{m} - N_{\text{onto}}$, the leftover maps.

nodes.label: Bijective Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A bijection is one-one and onto at once, which is possible only when the two sets have equal size, giving $n!$ such maps. Bijection is exactly the invertibility condition.

nodes.label: Counting All Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Every element of $A$ has $|B|$ choices, so there are $n^{m}$ functions total. This number is the base from which one-one and onto counts are carved out.

nodes.label: Example: Maps Between Small Sets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $|A| = 3$ and $|B| = 5$ the totals are $5^{3} = 125$ functions, ${}^{5}P_{3} = 60$ one-one functions and $125 - 60 = 65$ many-one functions.

nodes.label: Domain and Range Techniques
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Systematic rules for finding where a function lives and what values it takes. The domain-range pair answers most two-mark function questions directly.

nodes.label: Domain Rules
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Exclude zeroes of denominators, require even radicands to satisfy $f(x) \ge 0$, require $f(x) > 0$ for logarithms, and require $|f(x)| \ge 1$ for inverse secant and cosecant.

nodes.label: Combining Domains
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For sums and products take $\text{Domain}(f) = D_{1} \cap D_{2}$, and for quotients also delete the zeroes of the denominator. Never merge domains by addition.

nodes.label: Range by Inversion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Set $y = f(x)$, solve for $x$ in terms of $y$, and keep the $y$ values for which $x$ is real and inside the domain. This is the fastest route for algebraic fractions.

nodes.label: Range by Monotonicity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: On a closed interval a continuous function attains its extremes at critical points or endpoints, so $\text{Range} = [\min f, \max f]$. Use this once the derivative changes sign.

nodes.label: Discriminant Method
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $y = \frac{a_{1}x^{2}+b_{1}x+c_{1}}{a_{2}x^{2}+b_{2}x+c_{2}}$ collect terms as $(a_{2}y - a_{1})x^{2} + (b_{2}y - b_{1})x + (c_{2}y - c_{1}) = 0$ and impose $D \ge 0$, testing the case where the $x^2$ coefficient vanishes separately.

nodes.label: Example: Range of a Rational Function
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $y = \frac{x^{2}-x+1}{x^{2}+x+1}$ the condition $D \ge 0$ reduces to $3y^{2} - 10y + 3 \le 0$, so the range is $[1/3, 3]$.

nodes.label: Standard Function Graphs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The catalogue of shapes JEE assumes you know cold: lines, parabolas, modulus, floor, exponential and logarithmic curves.

nodes.label: Polynomial and Linear Graphs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $f(x) = ax^{2}+bx+c$ has vertex $\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{D}{4a}\right)$ and, for $a > 0$, range $[-D/(4a), \infty)$. The line $y = ax+b$ has slope $a$ and range $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.label: Modulus and Signum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ otherwise, with range $[0, \infty)$; $\text{sgn}(x)$ takes only $-1, 0, 1$. The modulus curve has a corner at the origin, which is why it is not differentiable there.

nodes.label: Greatest Integer and Fractional Part
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $[x] \le x < [x]+1$ and $\{x\} = x - [x] \in [0, 1)$, with $\{x\}$ periodic of period 1. The floor jumps at every integer, so it is discontinuous on $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.label: Example: Hermite's Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Hermite's identity with $n = 2$ reads $[x] + [x + 1/2] = [2x]$ for all real $x$. It converts a sum of two floor terms into a single one in a single step.

nodes.label: Exponential and Logarithmic Graphs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $a^{x}$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$ and passes through $(0, 1)$; $\log_{a} x$ has domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$ and passes through $(1, 0)$. The two are reflections across $y = x$.

nodes.label: Power and Root Graphs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $y = x^{n}$ with even $n$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis with range $[0, \infty)$, while odd $n$ is odd with range $\mathbb{R}$. The square root function $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ has domain $[0, \infty)$.

nodes.label: Composition and Inverses
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: How functions chain and how they are undone. The range-inside-domain test decides whether a composition even exists.

nodes.label: Algebra of Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(f \pm g)(x) = f(x) \pm g(x)$ and $(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)$ all live on $D_{f} \cap D_{g}$, while $\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(x)$ additionally removes zeroes of $g$.

nodes.label: Composite Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$ exists only where $\text{Range}(f) \subseteq \text{Domain}(g)$. Composition is associative but not commutative, so $g \circ f \neq f \circ g$ in general.

nodes.label: Domain of a Composite
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\text{Domain}(g \circ f) = \{x \in D_{f} : f(x) \in D_{g}\}$. It is the inner output, not the inner domain, that gets filtered, the classic source of lost marks.

nodes.label: Inverse Function
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A function is invertible exactly when it is bijective, with $f(x) = y \iff f^{-1}(y) = x$. The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the mirror image of $f$ across the line $y = x$.

nodes.label: Example: Inverse of a Linear Fraction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $f(x) = \frac{2x+3}{x-4}$, solving $y = \frac{2x+3}{x-4}$ gives $f^{-1}(x) = \frac{4x+3}{x-2}$. The domain of $f^{-1}$ is $x \neq 2$, which is the range of $f$.

nodes.label: Reversal Rule for Inverses
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$, and $\text{Domain}(f^{-1}) = \text{Range}(f)$ with $\text{Range}(f^{-1}) = \text{Domain}(f)$. Also $(f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x$.

nodes.label: Periodicity and Symmetry
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Periods, even and odd symmetry, and the algebra that combines them. Trigonometric function questions lean on this pillar constantly.

nodes.label: Periodic Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $f(x+T) = f(x)$ for all $x$ with $T > 0$, and the least such $T$ is the fundamental period. $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ have period $2\pi$, while $\tan x$ and $\cot x$ have period $\pi$.

nodes.label: Transforming the Period
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $f$ has period $T$ then $k f(ax+b)$ has period $\frac{T}{|a|}$. For $a f(x) \pm b g(x)$ the period is $\text{LCM}(T_{1}, T_{2})$ only when $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \in \mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.label: Example: Complementary Pair Trap
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|\sin x| + |\cos x|$ looks like it has period $\pi$, yet shifting by $\pi/2$ swaps the two terms, so $f(x + \pi/2) = f(x)$ and the fundamental period is $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

nodes.label: Even and Odd Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $f(-x) = f(x)$ means even and symmetric about the $y$-axis, while $f(-x) = -f(x)$ means odd and symmetric about the origin. The domain must first be symmetric about $0$, and an odd function defined at $0$ has $f(0) = 0$.

nodes.label: Algebra of Even and Odd Parts
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Even times odd is odd, odd times odd is even, and differentiation flips parity. Every function splits as $f(x) = \frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}$ into even and odd pieces.

nodes.label: Binary Operations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Operations on a set, their laws, identities and inverses, plus the counting theorems JEE loves to ask in one line.

nodes.label: Binary Operation and Closure
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A binary operation maps $S \times S$ into $S$, so closure is built in: $a * b \in S$ always. Addition fails closure on the irrationals since $\sqrt{2} + (-\sqrt{2}) = 0$.

nodes.label: Commutativity, Associativity, Distributivity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $a * b = b * a$ is commutativity, $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$ is associativity, and $a * (b \circ c) = (a * b) \circ (a * c)$ is distributivity. Check each separately, since one need not imply another.

nodes.label: Identity and Inverse
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The identity obeys $a * e = e * a = a$ and is unique; the inverse of $a$ is the $b$ with $a * b = b * a = e$. Then the reversal law gives $(a * b)^{-1} = b^{-1} * a^{-1}$.

nodes.label: Counting Binary Operations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A binary operation is a function on the $n^{2}$ pairs of $S \times S$, giving $n^{n^{2}}$ of them. Commutativity makes the Cayley table symmetric, leaving $n^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}$.

nodes.label: Example: Operations on a Three-Element Set
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $|S| = 3$ the totals are $3^{9} = 19683$ binary operations and $3^{6} = 729$ commutative ones. The gap shows how expensive commutativity is as a constraint.

nodes.label: Fundamentals of Complex Numbers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Definition, equality and the cyclic behaviour of the imaginary unit. Small ideas that decide whether a complex equation yields one real condition or two.

nodes.label: Definition and Components
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z = x + iy$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $i = \sqrt{-1}$, where $\text{Re}(z) = x$ and $\text{Im}(z) = y$ is itself real. $z$ is purely real iff $z = \bar z$, and purely imaginary iff $z = -\bar z$ for $z \neq 0$.

nodes.label: Equality of Complex Numbers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z_{1} = z_{2}$ holds iff $x_{1} = x_{2}$ and $y_{1} = y_{2}$. One complex equality therefore hands you two independent real equations, which is how unknowns get eliminated.

nodes.label: Order Is Not Defined
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Statements like $z_{1} > z_{2}$ are meaningless in $\mathbb{C}$ unless both numbers are real, because order needs a line. Moduli are real, so $|z_{1}| > |z_{2}|$ is always legitimate.

nodes.label: Powers of Iota
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $i^{4n} = 1$, $i^{4n+1} = i$, $i^{4n+2} = -1$ and $i^{4n+3} = -i$ repeat with period 4. Four consecutive powers always cancel: $i^{n} + i^{n+1} + i^{n+2} + i^{n+3} = 0$.

nodes.label: The Square Root Product Trap
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\sqrt{-2}\sqrt{-3} = (i\sqrt{2})(i\sqrt{3}) = -\sqrt{6}$, not $\sqrt{6}$. The rule $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$ needs at least one of $a, b$ to be non-negative.

nodes.label: Algebra of Complex Numbers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Addition, multiplication and division in Cartesian form. Division always runs through the conjugate.

nodes.label: Addition and Multiplication
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z_{1} + z_{2} = (x_{1}+x_{2}) + i(y_{1}+y_{2})$ and $z_{1}z_{2} = (x_{1}x_{2} - y_{1}y_{2}) + i(x_{1}y_{2} + x_{2}y_{1})$. Multiplication rotates and stretches, addition just translates.

nodes.label: Division by the Conjugate
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}} = \frac{z_{1}\bar z_{2}}{|z_{2}|^{2}}$ for $z_{2} \neq 0$, obtained by multiplying numerator and denominator by $\bar z_{2}$. Every complex quotient is rationalised this way.

nodes.label: Multiplicative Inverse
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z^{-1} = \frac{\bar z}{|z|^{2}} = \frac{x - iy}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ for $z \neq 0$, powered by the identity $z \bar z = |z|^{2}$. The inverse exists for every nonzero $z$.

nodes.label: Conjugate of a Complex Number
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Reflection across the real axis, and the tool for extracting real and imaginary parts cleanly.

nodes.label: Basic Conjugate Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z + \bar z = 2\text{Re}(z)$, $z - \bar z = 2i\text{Im}(z)$ and $\overline{\bar z} = z$. Hence $z = \bar z$ characterises real numbers and $z + \bar z = 0$ characterises purely imaginary ones.

nodes.label: Conjugate Across Operations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\overline{z_{1} z_{2}} = \bar z_{1} \bar z_{2}$, $\overline{\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right)} = \frac{\bar z_{1}}{\bar z_{2}}$ and $\overline{z^{n}} = (\bar z)^{n}$. The conjugate distributes over products, quotients and powers.

nodes.label: Geometric Meaning of Conjugation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\bar z$ is the mirror of $z$ across the real axis, so conjugation reverses the argument: $\arg(\bar z) = -\arg(z)$ whenever $z$ is not a negative real number.

nodes.label: Modulus and Inequalities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Length in the complex plane, with multiplicative rules and the two inequalities that bound every locus problem.

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: algebra modulus argument and conjugate properties

nodes.label: Definition of Modulus
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|z| = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ is the distance from the origin, and $|z| = 0$ iff $z = 0$. Also $-|z| \le \text{Re}(z) \le |z|$ bounds each component.

nodes.label: Multiplicative Properties
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|z_{1}z_{2}| = |z_{1}||z_{2}|$, $\left|\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right| = \frac{|z_{1}|}{|z_{2}|}$ and $|z^{n}| = |z|^{n}$. Modulus converts products into products of lengths, which is why it simplifies power questions.

nodes.label: Parallelogram Law
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|z_{1}+z_{2}|^{2} + |z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2} = 2(|z_{1}|^{2} + |z_{2}|^{2})$, the complex form of the parallelogram diagonal identity. Use it when sums and differences of moduli appear together.

nodes.label: Triangle Inequality
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $||z_{1}| - |z_{2}|| \le |z_{1} \pm z_{2}| \le |z_{1}| + |z_{2}|$. Equality in the upper bound needs $\arg(z_{1}) = \arg(z_{2})$, which is the condition most often forgotten.

nodes.label: Example: Modulus on a Circle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $|z - 3 - 4i| = 2$, the centre is at distance $5$ from the origin, so $|z|$ ranges over $[3, 7]$. Extremes always occur along the line through the origin and the centre.

nodes.label: Argand Plane and Argument
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Polar form and angle measurement. Every rotation, locus and geometry question in the complex plane starts here.

nodes.label: Polar and Trigonometric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta = \arg(z)$, the angle from the positive real axis to the vector $\vec{Oz}$.

nodes.label: Principal Argument
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\operatorname{Arg}(z) \in (-\pi, \pi]$ and equals $\pi - \alpha$ in the second quadrant and $-\pi + \alpha$ in the third, where $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|$. The quadrant decides the sign and shift.

nodes.label: Properties of the Argument
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\arg(z_{1}z_{2}) = \arg(z_{1}) + \arg(z_{2})$ and $\arg\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right) = \arg(z_{1}) - \arg(z_{2})$, each valid up to an integer multiple of $2\pi$. Products add angles, quotients subtract them.

nodes.label: Axial and Special Arguments
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Positive reals have $\theta = 0$, negative reals $\theta = \pi$, and $\pm i$ have $\theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$. The argument of $z = 0$ is undefined, so split that case out.

nodes.label: Exponential Form and De Moivre
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Euler's formula and the power rule for arguments. This is the engine behind roots of unity and trigonometric sums.

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: de moivre roots of unity and polynomial equations

nodes.label: Euler's Formula
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, so $z = re^{i\theta}$ and $\bar z = re^{-i\theta}$. It also yields $\cos\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}}{2}$ and $\sin\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta}}{2i}$.

nodes.label: De Moivre's Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^{n} = \cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)$ for every integer $n$. Powers multiply the argument while leaving the modulus's role to $r^{n}$.

nodes.label: Rational Powers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z^{p/q}$ has exactly $q$ distinct values $\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi+p\theta}{q}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{2k\pi+p\theta}{q}\right)$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, q-1$. Never report a single root when $q > 1$.

nodes.label: Roots of Unity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Solutions of $z^{n} = 1$, their algebraic identities and their regular polygon. A JEE favourite because it mixes algebra with geometry.

nodes.label: Cube Roots of Unity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The roots are $1, \omega, \omega^{2}$ with $\omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, satisfying $1 + \omega + \omega^{2} = 0$ and $\omega^{3} = 1$. Also $\bar\omega = \omega^{2}$ and $\frac{1}{\omega} = \omega^{2}$.

nodes.label: Factorisations with Omega
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $a^{2}+ab+b^{2} = (a-\omega b)(a-\omega^{2}b)$ and $a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}-3abc = (a+b+c)(a+b\omega+c\omega^{2})(a+b\omega^{2}+c\omega)$. These turn irreducible quadratics into linear complex factors.

nodes.label: n-th Roots of Unity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha_{k} = e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{n}}$ for $k = 0, \dots, n-1$ form a geometric progression, so $1 + \alpha + \dots + \alpha^{n-1} = 0$ and the product of all roots equals $(-1)^{n-1}$.

nodes.label: Geometry of the Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The $n$ roots are the vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in $|z| = 1$ with one vertex at $1$. Non-real roots always come in conjugate pairs.

nodes.label: Example: Sums of Powers of Omega
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Since $\omega^{3} = 1$ and $1 + \omega + \omega^{2} = 0$, we get $\omega^{5} + \omega^{7} = \omega^{2} + \omega = -1$. Reduce the exponent mod 3 before adding anything.

nodes.label: Geometry in the Complex Plane
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Distance, triangle centres, lines and circles rewritten in complex language. Shorter than coordinate geometry and often the faster route in an exam.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: geometry loci circles and conic transformations

nodes.label: Distance and Section Formulas
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $d = |z_{1} - z_{2}|$, the midpoint is $z = \frac{z_{1}+z_{2}}{2}$ and internal division in ratio $m : n$ gives $z = \frac{mz_{2}+nz_{1}}{m+n}$. These replace the usual coordinate versions.

nodes.label: Triangle Centers and Area
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The centroid is $z_{G} = \frac{z_{1}+z_{2}+z_{3}}{3}$ and the incentre is $z_{I} = \frac{az_{1}+bz_{2}+cz_{3}}{a+b+c}$ with $a = |z_{2}-z_{3}|$ and cyclic partners.

nodes.label: Collinearity Test
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ are collinear iff $\frac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}} \in \mathbb{R}$, equivalently iff $\begin{vmatrix} z_{1} & \bar z_{1} & 1 \\ z_{2} & \bar z_{2} & 1 \\ z_{3} & \bar z_{3} & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$. A real quotient means no rotation.

nodes.label: Line in the Complex Plane
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\bar a z + a\bar z + b = 0$ with $b \in \mathbb{R}$ is a straight line, and its distance from $z_{0}$ equals $\frac{|\bar a z_{0} + a\bar z_{0} + b|}{2|a|}$.

nodes.label: Complex Slope of a Line
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The complex slope is $\mu = \frac{z_{1}-z_{2}}{\bar z_{1}-\bar z_{2}}$, with two lines parallel iff $\mu_{1} = \mu_{2}$ and perpendicular iff $\mu_{1} + \mu_{2} = 0$.

nodes.label: Circle Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|z - z_{0}| = r$ is a circle of centre $z_{0}$, while $z\bar z + \bar a z + a\bar z + b = 0$ has centre $-a$ and radius $\sqrt{|a|^{2} - b}$, which needs $|a|^{2} \ge b$ to exist.

nodes.label: Apollonius Circle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\left|\frac{z-z_{1}}{z-z_{2}}\right| = k$ is a circle when $k \neq 1$ and the perpendicular bisector of $z_{1}z_{2}$ when $k = 1$. This locus appears repeatedly in JEE Main loci questions.

nodes.label: Rotation Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\frac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}} = \left|\frac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}\right| e^{i\alpha}$ states that $z_{3}-z_{1}$ is $z_{2}-z_{1}$ turned through $\alpha$. It is the fastest tool for equilateral and right-angled configurations.

nodes.label: Example: Rotation by a Right Angle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Turning $z_{2}-z_{1}$ by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ gives $\frac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}} = i$, hence $z_{3} = z_{1} + i(z_{2}-z_{1})$. Multiplication by $i$ is exactly a quarter turn.

nodes.label: Square Roots and Logarithms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Extracting roots and logs of complex numbers, both of which are multi-valued and easy to under-report.

nodes.label: Square Root of a Complex Number
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\sqrt{x+iy} = \pm\left(\sqrt{\frac{|z|+x}{2}} + i\,\text{sgn}(y)\sqrt{\frac{|z|-x}{2}}\right)$, so $\sqrt{i} = \pm\frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}}$. Always carry both signs.

nodes.label: Logarithm of a Complex Number
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\log(z) = \ln|z| + i(\arg(z) + 2k\pi)$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, with principal value $\ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$. The infinite family comes from the argument, not from the modulus.

nodes.label: Theory of Equations and Inequations — Introduction
nodes.subject: maths

nodes.label: Polynomials and Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Degree, the fundamental theorem and the equation-versus-identity distinction. Skipping the degree check is the most common way to lose an easy question.

nodes.label: Degree and the Fundamental Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $P(x) = a_{n}x^{n} + \dots + a_{1}x + a_{0}$ with $a_{n} \neq 0$ has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$, so $P(x) = a_{n}(x-\alpha_{1})(x-\alpha_{2})\cdots(x-\alpha_{n})$. Degree counts roots with multiplicity.

nodes.label: Equation vs Polynomial
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $P(x) = 0$ is an equation with finitely many solutions, while $P(x) \equiv 0$ is an identity true for every $x$. If $a = 0$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ the degree drops and the quadratic formula becomes illegal.

nodes.label: Identity Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $P(x) \equiv 0$ holds iff every coefficient is zero, so a quadratic satisfied by three distinct values forces $a = 0$, $b = 0$ and $c = 0$. A degree $n$ identity needs only $n+1$ test values to be proven.

nodes.label: Example: Proving an Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\frac{(x-b)(x-c)}{(a-b)(a-c)} + \frac{(x-c)(x-a)}{(b-c)(b-a)} + \frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(c-a)(c-b)} = 1$ holds at $x = a$, $x = b$ and $x = c$, so by the identity theorem it holds for all real $x$.

nodes.label: Parameterised Leading Coefficient
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $(\lambda-2)x^{2} + 2\lambda x + (\lambda-1) = 0$ first split into $\lambda = 2$, which is linear with one root, and $\lambda \neq 2$, which is quadratic with $D \ge 0$. Testing the discriminant alone misses the linear case.

nodes.label: Roots and Coefficients
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Vieta's relations turn questions about roots into arithmetic on coefficients, with no need to solve the equation.

nodes.label: The Quadratic Formula
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} = \frac{D}{4a^{2}}$, hence $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}$ with $D = b^{2}-4ac$. Everything else in the chapter is built on this line.

nodes.label: Sum and Product of Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}$. Any symmetric condition on the roots can be rewritten using only these two numbers.

nodes.label: Difference of Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{D}}{|a|}$, coming from $(\alpha-\beta)^{2} = (\alpha+\beta)^{2} - 4\alpha\beta$. Use it whenever the distance between roots is asked.

nodes.label: Transformation of Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Roots $\alpha+k$ come from $x = y-k$, roots $k\alpha$ from $x = y/k$, and reciprocal roots from $x = 1/y$. Substitute backwards into the original equation.

nodes.label: Example: Reciprocal Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Replacing $x$ by $1/y$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ and clearing denominators gives $cy^{2}+by+a=0$, whose roots are $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$. The coefficients simply reverse.

nodes.label: Sign Conditions on Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Roots of opposite signs require only $\frac{c}{a} < 0$, which already forces $D > 0$. Both roots positive need $D \ge 0$ together with $-\frac{b}{2a} > 0$ and $\frac{c}{a} > 0$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions and Newton's Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Rewriting power sums of roots in terms of $S = \alpha+\beta$ and $P = \alpha\beta$, and the recurrence that generates them.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions of Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2} = S^{2}-2P$, $\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{S}{P}$ and $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{S^{2}-2P}{P}$. Symmetry is what allows expression purely in $S$ and $P$.

nodes.label: Higher Power Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha^{3}+\beta^{3} = S^{3}-3SP$ and $\alpha^{4}+\beta^{4} = (S^{2}-2P)^{2} - 2P^{2}$. Expand from $S$ and $P$ rather than computing the roots.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: quadratic roots discriminant and newton sums

nodes.label: Newton's Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $S_{n} = p\alpha^{n} + q\beta^{n}$ the recurrence $aS_{n} + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$ holds for every integer $n$. It answers very high powers without ever finding $\alpha$ or $\beta$.

nodes.label: Example: Running the Recurrence
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: With $S_{n} = \alpha^{n}+\beta^{n}$ the recurrence reads $S_{n} = -\frac{b}{a}S_{n-1} - \frac{c}{a}S_{n-2}$, seeded by $S_{0} = 2$ and $S_{1} = -\frac{b}{a}$. Two seeds generate every later term.

nodes.label: Nature of Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: What the discriminant and the coefficient field together say about the roots, including the pairing theorems and their traps.

nodes.label: Real Field Classification
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $D > 0$ gives real distinct roots, $D = 0$ gives the repeated root $-\frac{b}{2a}$, and $D < 0$ gives the conjugate pair $p \pm iq$ with $p = -\frac{b}{2a}$. Geometrically it is two cuts, one touch, or no touch of the $x$-axis.

nodes.label: Rational and Surd Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $D > 0$, a perfect square $D$ gives rational roots and a non-square $D$ gives the surd pair $p \pm \sqrt{q}$. Surds therefore never appear alone.

nodes.label: Integral Root Conditions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Integer roots need $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a = 1$ or $a$ dividing both $b$ and $c$, plus $D$ a perfect square. All three conditions together, not just the last one.

nodes.label: Conjugate Pair Theorems
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Real coefficients force complex roots in pairs $z, \bar z$, and rational coefficients force surd pairs $p+\sqrt{q}, p-\sqrt{q}$. The pairing fails the moment coefficients leave that field.

nodes.label: The Conjugate Root Trap
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $x^{2} - (2+i)x + (1+i) = 0$ has roots $1$ and $1+i$, with no conjugate present, because the coefficients are complex. Always check the field before invoking conjugate pairing.

nodes.label: Graph of a Quadratic
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The parabola, its vertex, sign chart and range. Nearly every inequality question is answered by reading this picture.

nodes.label: Vertex and Axis
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $y = a\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} - \frac{D}{4a}$, so the vertex is $V\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{D}{4a}\right)$ and the axis is $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$.

nodes.label: Sign Chart with Two Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $a > 0$ and roots $\alpha < \beta$, the expression is negative inside $(\alpha, \beta)$ and positive outside it. Reverse every sign when $a < 0$.

nodes.label: Strict Positivity Invariant
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $ax^{2}+bx+c > 0$ for every real $x$ iff $a > 0$ and $D < 0$; it is always negative iff $a < 0$ and $D < 0$. Two conditions, always both required.

nodes.label: Example: Always Positive
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $x^{2}+x+1$ we get $D = 1-4 = -3 < 0$ with $a = 1 > 0$, so the curve floats above the axis and $x^{2}+x+1 > 0$ for all real $x$. It never vanishes.

nodes.label: Range on a Restricted Domain
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: On $[x_{1}, x_{2}]$ compare the endpoint values with the vertex value $-\frac{D}{4a}$ if $x_{v} = -\frac{b}{2a}$ lies inside the interval. Otherwise the function is monotone there and endpoints suffice.

nodes.label: Intercepts
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The $y$-intercept is $(0, c)$ and the $x$-intercepts are $\left(\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}, 0\right)$. When $D < 0$ the parabola meets neither axis except at $c$.

nodes.label: Location of Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The canonical conditions for placing roots relative to a point or an interval. Each regime combines the discriminant, the vertex and one sign test.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: location of roots quadratic expressions and inequations

nodes.label: Both Roots Beyond a Point k
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha, \beta > k$ needs $D \ge 0$, $-\frac{b}{2a} > k$ and $af(k) > 0$; for $\alpha, \beta < k$ the middle condition flips to $-\frac{b}{2a} < k$. Three conditions intersected.

nodes.label: k Between the Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha < k < \beta$ is captured by the single condition $af(k) < 0$, which automatically forces $D > 0$. This is the shortest condition in the whole topic.

nodes.label: Both Roots Inside an Interval
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Roots inside $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ need $D \ge 0$, $k_{1} < -\frac{b}{2a} < k_{2}$, $af(k_{1}) > 0$ and $af(k_{2}) > 0$. Real roots, the vertex and both endpoints are all constrained.

nodes.label: Exactly One Root in an Interval
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Exactly one root in the open interval $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ is simply $f(k_{1}) \cdot f(k_{2}) < 0$, since the curve must cross zero between the endpoints. Handle endpoints that are roots separately.

nodes.label: Interval Between the Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\alpha < k_{1} < k_{2} < \beta$ needs $af(k_{1}) < 0$ and $af(k_{2}) < 0$, and either one already implies $D > 0$. The interval then sits in the negative well of an upward parabola.

nodes.label: Common Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Two quadratics sharing roots, decided either by an eliminant or by proportionality of coefficients.

nodes.label: Both Roots Common
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Both roots are shared iff the coefficient triples are proportional: $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$. The two equations then describe the same parabola scaled.

nodes.label: Subtraction Gives a Candidate
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Subtracting $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ and $x^{2}+cx+d=0$ yields the candidate $x = \frac{d-b}{a-c}$, which must be substituted back. If $a = c$ and $b \neq d$ there is no common root at all.

nodes.label: Complex Common Root Trap
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If the first equation has real coefficients and $D_{1} < 0$, a shared complex root forces the conjugate to be shared too, so both roots are common and $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$.

nodes.label: Range of Rational Functions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Finding the range of a ratio of quadratics by reversing the problem into a discriminant condition on the numerator.

nodes.label: Discriminant Inversion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Cross-multiplying $y = \frac{a_{1}x^{2}+b_{1}x+c_{1}}{a_{2}x^{2}+b_{2}x+c_{2}}$ gives $(ya_{2}-a_{1})x^{2} + (yb_{2}-b_{1})x + (yc_{2}-c_{1}) = 0$, and requiring $D_{x} \ge 0$ yields an inequality in $y$ for the range.

nodes.label: Boundary and Asymptote Check
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The candidate $y = \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}$, where the coefficient of $x^{2}$ dies, must be tested separately by substituting back into the linear equation. It is the horizontal asymptote $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} y$.

nodes.label: Removable Common Factor Trap
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $(x-k)$ cancels from numerator and denominator, the graph has a hole at $x = k$ and the value $\frac{k-\alpha}{k-\beta}$ is never attained. Delete it from the otherwise computed range.

nodes.label: Higher Degree Polynomials
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Generalised Vieta, cubics, roots in progressions and sign counting. The same symmetric-function logic simply scales up.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: common roots cubic and higher degree polynomials

nodes.label: Generalised Vieta Formulas
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For degree $n$, $\sum \alpha_{i} = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_{n}}$, $\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j} = \frac{a_{n-2}}{a_{n}}$ and $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\cdots\alpha_{n} = (-1)^{n}\frac{a_{0}}{a_{n}}$. Signs alternate from the top.

nodes.label: Cubic Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$ the roots obey $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = -\frac{b}{a}$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma = -\frac{d}{a}$.

nodes.label: Roots in AP, GP and HP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For roots in AP assume $t-d, t, t+d$, giving $t = -\frac{b}{3a}$; for GP use $\frac{t}{r}, t, tr$, giving $t^{3} = -\frac{d}{a}$; for HP substitute $x = \frac{1}{y}$ to get roots in AP.

nodes.label: Descartes' Rule of Signs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The number of positive real roots equals the sign changes among non-zero coefficients of $P(x)$, or is less by an even number; for negative roots apply the rule to $P(-x)$.

nodes.label: Turning Points
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $P'(x) = 0$ locates the local extrema, so a degree $n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ turning points. Between two distinct real roots there is always one turning point.

nodes.label: Reducible and Symmetric Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Higher-degree equations that collapse into a quadratic after a smart substitution.

nodes.label: Reciprocal (Palindromic) Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+bx+a=0$ divide by $x^{2}$ and set $u = x + \frac{1}{x}$, using $x^{2} + \frac{1}{x^{2}} = u^{2}-2$. The quartic becomes a quadratic in $u$.

nodes.label: The |u| >= 2 Condition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Solving $x + \frac{1}{x} = u$ gives real $x$ iff $|u| \ge 2$, and for $|u| < 2$ the roots are non-real conjugates. Reject the $u$ values that fail this test.

nodes.label: Equations with a Modulus
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: In $ax^{2}+b|x|+c=0$ substitute $u = |x| \ge 0$ and solve for $u$. Each $u > 0$ yields two roots $x = \pm u$, $u = 0$ yields one, and negative $u$ yields none.

nodes.label: Example: Counting Roots
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $x^{2} - 5|x| + 6 = 0$ the substitution gives $u = 2$ or $u = 3$, so there are four real roots $\pm 2$ and $\pm 3$. Count in $u$ first, then translate back to $x$.

nodes.label: Sequence Fundamentals
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Definitions and core invariants that link a sequence to its partial sums. These identities are the entry point for almost every JEE series problem.

nodes.label: Sequence as a Function
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A sequence assigns each natural number n a unique term: $$a_n = f(n), \ n \in \mathbb{N}$$. Finite and infinite types both appear in sum-of-n problems.

nodes.label: Series and Partial Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A series is the indicated sum of terms, and its partial sum is $$S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k$$. JEE problems often hand you S_n and ask for the sum of specific terms.

nodes.label: Term from Sum Relation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Recover the nth term from the partial sums: $$a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \ (n \ge 2), \ a_1 = S_1$$. The n >= 2 restriction is a classic off-by-one trap.

nodes.label: Mini-Example: S_n Given
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $S_n = 2n^2 + 3n$, then $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} = 4n + 1$ for $n \ge 2$, and $a_1 = S_1 = 5$, which matches $4(1)+1$.

nodes.label: Finite vs Infinite Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Finite series stop at a last term, while infinite series need a convergence check before any sum formula applies. $$S_\infty = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k$$ exists only when terms vanish fast enough.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Progression
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The workhorse of JEE sequences: constant difference between consecutive terms. Most questions reduce to the nth-term or sum formula.

nodes.label: Common Difference
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The difference is constant: $$d = a_{k+1} - a_k$$. A zero d gives a constant sequence, worth spotting in modified progressions.

nodes.label: nth Term of an AP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = a + (n-1)d$$. Asking which term equals X is a direct linear equation in n.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of AP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The sum of the first n terms is $$S_n = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right]$$. It is quadratic in n, so a quadratic S_n signals an AP.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Mean
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The middle term of three terms in AP is their mean: $$b = \frac{a+c}{2}$$. Inserting k AMs between a and b is a standard JEE step.

nodes.label: Equidistant Term Property
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Terms equidistant from the ends sum equally: $$a_k + a_{n+1-k} = a_1 + a_n$$. Use it to shortcut sums of symmetric selected terms.

nodes.label: Example: Sum of an AP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $3, 7, 11, \dots$ ($a=3, d=4$): $S_{20} = \frac{20}{2}[6 + 19\cdot 4] = 820$. JEE wraps this in word problems about arithmetic totals.

nodes.label: Geometric Progression
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Constant ratio between consecutive terms. Infinite GP sums and mean relations are heavily tested.

nodes.label: Common Ratio
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Each term is a fixed multiple of the previous: $$r = \frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}$$. The sign and magnitude of r decide monotonicity and convergence.

nodes.label: nth Term of a GP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = ar^{n-1}$$. Logarithms convert GP problems into AP problems, a standard JEE manipulation.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of GP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For r not equal to 1 the partial sum is $$S_n = a\frac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}$$. The $r = 1$ case collapses to $S_n = na$.

nodes.label: Infinite Geometric Sum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $|r| < 1$ the series converges: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}$$. This single formula powers recurring-decimal and geometric-tail questions.

nodes.label: Geometric Mean
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For three terms in GP, the middle is the geometric mean: $$b^2 = ac$$. Two positive numbers have GM $\sqrt{ac}$, linking to the AM-GM-HM chain.

nodes.label: Harmonic Progression
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Reciprocals form an AP. HP questions are usually disguised AM/GM problems.

nodes.label: HP Definition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A sequence is harmonic when its reciprocals form an AP: $$\frac{1}{a_{k+1}} - \frac{1}{a_k} = \text{constant}$$. Its nth term mirrors the AP structure on reciprocals.

nodes.label: nth Term of an HP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If reciprocals are an AP with first A and difference D, then $$T_n = \frac{1}{A + (n-1)D}$$. Take reciprocals first, then apply AP formulas.

nodes.label: Harmonic Mean
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The harmonic mean of two numbers is $$H = \frac{2ab}{a+b}$$. HM of a and b is the reciprocal of the AM of $1/a$ and $1/b$.

nodes.label: Example: HM of Two Numbers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: HM of 2 and 6 is $H = \frac{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6}{2 + 6} = 3$, and $2, 3, 6$ are in HP since $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{6}$ are in AP.

nodes.label: Means and Inequalities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: AM-GM-HM relations and Cauchy-Schwarz give quick answers to max-min JEE questions.

nodes.label: AM-GM-HM Chain
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For positive reals the three means are ordered: $$AM \ge GM \ge HM$$. Equality holds iff all numbers are equal.

nodes.label: Weighted AM-GM
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Weights turn the inequality into $$w_1 a_1 + w_2 a_2 \ge a_1^{w_1} a_2^{w_2}, \ w_1 + w_2 = 1$$. Handy for optimization under a constraint.

nodes.label: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$(a_1^2 + a_2^2)(b_1^2 + b_2^2) \ge (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2)^2$$ bounds a dot product by the product of norms. Common in sum-bound questions.

nodes.label: Example: Max Product
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $x + y = 10$, AM-GM gives $\sqrt{xy} \le 5$, so the product $xy \le 25$, maximized at $x = y = 5$.

nodes.label: Arithmetico-Geometric Progression
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Product of an AP and a GP term by term. The shift-and-subtract derivation is the key skill.

nodes.label: AGP Term Structure
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Each term multiplies an AP factor by a GP factor: $$T_n = [a + (n-1)d]\, r^{n-1}$$. Recognize the mixed structure before applying formulas.

nodes.label: AGP Finite Sum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Multiply $S_n$ by r and subtract to collapse the series: $$S_n = \frac{a - [a+(n-1)d]r^n}{1-r} + \frac{dr(1 - r^{n-1})}{(1-r)^2}$$. The shift-and-subtract idea is asked conceptually in JEE.

nodes.label: AGP Infinite Sum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $|r| < 1$: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} + \frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$$. The second term is the correction from the arithmetic part.

nodes.label: Example: 2 + 8 + 24 + 64
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $S = 1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 4 + 3\cdot 8 + \dots$ the AGP has $a=1, d=1, r=2$; since $|r|>1$ only finite partial sums exist, found via shift-and-subtract.

nodes.label: Summation Methods
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Difference tables, telescoping, and sigma identities cover non-standard series in JEE.

nodes.label: Method of Differences
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Successive differences reveal the polynomial degree of the nth term: $$\Delta T_n = T_{n+1} - T_n$$. If the first differences are constant, T_n is linear; two rounds give a quadratic.

nodes.label: Telescoping Series
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Write each term as a difference and cancel in between: $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}(V_k - V_{k-1}) = V_n - V_0$$. Partial-fraction splits set this up.

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: special series telescoping sums and inequalities

nodes.label: Example: Telescoping Sum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \sum \left(\frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1}$, a classic telescoping collapse.

nodes.label: Standard Sigma Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^3 = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$$. Memorize all three for direct use.

nodes.label: Counting Principles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The sum and product rules plus complement arguments decide every direct count. Factorials supply the raw material.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: fundamental counting word permutations and dictionary rank
nodes.formula: $$\text{E, G, N, T, T, W, Y}$$

nodes.label: Sum Rule
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Mutually exclusive alternatives add: $$N = m + n$$. Use it for case splits like 'numbers divisible by 2 or 5'.

nodes.label: Product Rule
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Sequential dependent stages multiply: $$N = m \times n \times p$$. Password and license-plate problems are direct applications.

nodes.label: Complement Principle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Count the unwanted arrangements and subtract: $$N_{wanted} = N_{total} - N_{unwanted}$$. Often the only clean route when 'at least one' appears.

nodes.label: Bijection Principle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A one-to-one correspondence transfers a count to a simpler set with the same cardinality. Classic use: mapping subsets to binary strings of length n, giving $2^n$.

nodes.label: Factorial Notation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1, \ 0! = 1$$. Every arrangement count in this chapter is a quotient of factorials.

nodes.label: Permutations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Ordered selections from distinct or repeated objects.

nodes.label: Permutations of Distinct Objects
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The number of ordered r-selections from n distinct objects is $${}^nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$. Arrangement of 5 students in a row is $5!$.

nodes.label: Arrangements with Repetition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: With repetition allowed, each of the r positions has n choices: $$N = n^r$$. This counts strings of length r over an n-letter alphabet.

nodes.label: Example: PIN Codes
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A 4-digit PIN with digits repeatable has $10^4 = 10000$ possibilities, direct product-rule reasoning.

nodes.label: Arrangement Constraints
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Block (tie) method, gap method, and dictionary rank handle restricted arrangements.

nodes.label: Block Method
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Glue the objects that must stay together into one super-object: $$N = k! \times (\text{internal arrangements})$$. For the word MOTHER with vowels together, treat OE as one block.

nodes.label: Gap Method
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Arrange the free objects first, then place restricted ones in the gaps: $$N = (\text{free})! \times {}^{g}P_{r}$$. No two vowels together means vowels go into consonant gaps.

nodes.label: Lexicographic Rank
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Rank a word in dictionary order by counting words starting with smaller letters at each position. Rank of a permutation like 'EAMCET' needs a left-to-right factorial count.

nodes.label: Example: Rank of a Word
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For words from letters A, B, C with all used, words starting with A come first ($2! = 2$ of them); this prefix-counting logic gives the rank.

nodes.label: Combinations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Unordered selections and the identities that simplify them.

nodes.label: Combinations of Distinct Objects
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Selecting r from n without regard to order: $${}^nC_r = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$$. Choosing a 3-member team from 10 players is ${}^{10}C_3 = 120$.

nodes.label: Pascal's Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $${}^nC_r = {}^{n-1}C_{r-1} + {}^{n-1}C_r$$ underlies Pascal's triangle. It justifies term counts in binomial expansions.

nodes.label: Multiset Selection
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Selecting r objects from a set with repetitions allowed: $$N = {}^{n+r-1}C_{r}$$. Choosing 4 fruits from 3 types with repetition allowed gives ${}^{6}C_4 = 15$.

nodes.label: Symmetry of nCr
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $${}^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$$ because choosing r to include equals choosing n - r to exclude. It halves computation when r > n/2.

nodes.label: Circular and Identical Arrangements
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Rotations merge in a circle; alike objects divide out permutations.

nodes.label: Circular Permutations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Fix one object to kill rotational duplicates: $$N = (n-1)!$$. The round-table seating of n people gives $(n-1)!$.

nodes.label: ×6 questions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.pattern: restricted permutations string gap and circular arrangements

nodes.label: Garland (Necklace) Symmetry
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Flipping a garland also duplicates arrangements, so divide by 2: $$N = \frac{(n-1)!}{2}$$. Distinguishing garlands from rings is a classic JEE MCQ twist.

nodes.label: Permutations of Multisets
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: With n_i alike objects of each type i, divide by the repeats: $$N = \frac{n!}{n_1!\, n_2! \cdots n_k!}$$. Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI follow this template.

nodes.label: Division and Distribution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Splitting distinct or identical objects into groups is stars-and-bars territory.

nodes.label: Division into Unequal Groups
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Divide n distinct objects into groups of sizes $p, q, r$: $$N = \frac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!}$$. Group labels matter only when groups are sized differently and destinations differ.

nodes.label: Division into Equal Groups
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For k equal groups of size m, divide further by the group orderings: $$N = \frac{n!}{(m!)^k \, k!}$$. The extra $k!$ kills the interchange of identical groups.

nodes.label: Stars and Bars
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Non-negative integer solutions to $x_1 + \dots + x_k = n$: $$N = {}^{n+k-1}C_{k-1}$$. Distributing identical chocolates to k children maps directly onto this count.

nodes.label: Positive Integer Solutions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Strictly positive solutions to $x_1 + \dots + x_k = n$ need $x_i \ge 1$: $$N = {}^{n-1}C_{k-1}$$. Substitute $y_i = x_i - 1$ and reuse stars and bars.

nodes.label: Advanced Combinatorics
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: PIE, derangements, surjections, and prime-exponent in factorials.

nodes.label: Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Count a union by adding singles, subtracting pairs, adding triples: $$|A \cup B \cup C| = \sum |A_i| - \sum |A_i \cap A_j| + |A \cap B \cap C|$$. 'At least one' counts for properties use it.

nodes.label: Derangements
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Permutations with no fixed point: $$D_n = n! \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$$. The !n notation (subfactorial) counts hat-check disasters and letter swapped envelopes.

nodes.label: Onto Functions (Surjections)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Number of onto maps from an m-set to an n-set: $$N = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k {}^nC_k \, (n-k)^m$$. Applying PIE to 'every element hit' gives this inclusion count.

nodes.label: Legendre's Formula
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Exponent of a prime p in n!: $$E_p(n!) = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^2} \right\rfloor + \cdots$$. It settles trailing-zero and divisibility questions about factorials.

nodes.label: Divisor Count from Factorization
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $N = p_1^{a_1} p_2^{a_2} \cdots$, then the number of divisors is $$\tau(N) = (a_1+1)(a_2+1)\cdots$$. Pairing divisors around $\sqrt{N}$ relates to product problems.

nodes.label: Binomial Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Expansions, term analytics, and coefficient series - a guaranteed JEE Main presence.

nodes.label: General Expansion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$(x + a)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} {}^nC_r x^{n-r} a^r$$. The $(r+1)$th term is ${}^nC_r x^{n-r} a^r$ and there are n + 1 terms total.

nodes.label: Middle Term
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For even n the middle term index is $r = n/2$: $$T_{n/2 + 1} = {}^nC_{n/2} x^{n/2} a^{n/2}$$. For odd n there are two middle terms, $r = (n-1)/2$ and $(n+1)/2$.

nodes.label: Numerically Greatest Term
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Find r from the ratio test on $|T_{r+1}/T_r|$ and the threshold $r \le \frac{(n+1)|a|}{|x| + |a|}$$. JEE traps students who forget the integer-floor boundary.

nodes.label: Binomial for Any Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For any rational alpha with |x| < 1: $$(1+x)^\alpha = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$. Approximation $(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ holds when $|x| \ll 1$.

nodes.label: Multinomial Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum \frac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2! \cdots n_k!} x_1^{n_1} \cdots x_k^{n_k}$$. The number of distinct terms is ${}^{n+k-1}C_{k-1}$.

nodes.label: Trigonometric Ratios and Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Definitions and the fundamental identities that everything else uses.

nodes.label: Six Ratios
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Sine, cosine, tangent and their reciprocals on a right triangle: $$\sin \theta = \frac{opp}{hyp}, \ \cos \theta = \frac{adj}{hyp}, \ \tan \theta = \frac{opp}{adj}$$. The reciprocal pairings $csc = 1/sin$, $sec = 1/cos$, $cot = 1/tan$ complete the set.

nodes.label: Reciprocal Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Cosecant, secant, and cotangent are reciprocals: $$\csc \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta}, \ \sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta}, \ \cot \theta = \frac{1}{\tan \theta}$$. JEE options often hide reciprocal traps among near-identical choices.

nodes.label: Pythagorean Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1, \ 1 + \tan^2 \theta = \sec^2 \theta, \ 1 + \cot^2 \theta = \csc^2 \theta$$. Divide the first identity by $\cos^2$ or $\sin^2$ to get the other two.

nodes.label: Standard Exact Values
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Key angles: $$\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, \ \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, \ \tan 45^\circ = 1$$. A memory table for $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$ is non-negotiable.

nodes.label: Identity Reduction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Simplify compound expressions by rewriting in sine and cosine: e.g. $$\tan \theta + \cot \theta = \frac{\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta}{\sin \theta \cos \theta} = \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}$$. JEE 'prove that' items demand this conversion.

nodes.label: Example: Simplification
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\frac{\sin \theta}{1 - \cos \theta} = \cot(\theta/2)$ follows by multiplying numerator and denominator by $1 + \cos \theta$ and using $1 - \cos^2 = \sin^2$.

nodes.label: Allied Angles and ASTC
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Signs and reductions for angles in all quadrants.

nodes.label: ASTC Rule
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Quadrant signs: all positive in I, sine positive in II, tangent positive in III, cosine positive in IV. 'All Snakes Take Coffee' is the memory hook for which ratios are positive in each quadrant.

nodes.label: Allied Angle Reduction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Reduce any angle to a first-quadrant reference: $$\sin(90^\circ \pm \theta) = \cos \theta, \ \sin(180^\circ \pm \theta) = \mp \sin \theta$$. Sign from ASTC, cofunction swap for odd multiples of 90.

nodes.label: Mini-Example: Reduction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\cos 150^\circ = \cos(180^\circ - 30^\circ) = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Minutes of error in sign sink most JEE one-markers.

nodes.label: Compound Angles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Sum and difference formulas plus product-to-sum conversions.

nodes.label: Addition and Subtraction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B$$ $$\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B$$ $$\tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}$$. Every compound-angle JEE item starts here.

nodes.label: Sum-to-Product (C and D) Formulas
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin \frac{C+D}{2} \cos \frac{C-D}{2}$$ and similarly for $\sin C - \sin D$, $\cos C \pm \cos D$. Factoring sums is how trig series telescoped in JEE.

nodes.label: Product-to-Sum Formulas
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$2\sin A \cos B = \sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)$$ $$2\cos A \cos B = \cos(A+B) + \cos(A-B)$$. Multiplication terms collapse into sums, easing integration-style algebra.

nodes.label: Multiple and Sub-Multiple Angles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Double, triple, and half-angle relations plus special products.

nodes.label: Double Angle Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta, \ \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta, \ \tan 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta}$$. Half-angle forms come from reversing them.

nodes.label: Triple Angle Relations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta, \ \cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$$. Factor these as cubics in $\sin$ or $\cos$ for equations.

nodes.label: Symmetrical Triplet Product
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\cos\theta \cos(60^\circ - \theta)\cos(60^\circ + \theta) = \frac{1}{4}\cos 3\theta$$. A frequently regurgitated JEE identity for max-min on trig products.

nodes.label: Half-Angle Substitutions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin \theta = \frac{2t}{1+t^2}, \ \cos \theta = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}, \ t = \tan(\theta/2)$$. The t-substitution rationalizes trig equations.

nodes.label: Conditional Identities in a Triangle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $A + B + C = \pi$, special relations between the angles appear.

nodes.label: Linear Conditional Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If $A + B + C = \pi$: $$\sin A + \sin B + \sin C = 4\cos\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{B}{2}\cos\frac{C}{2}$$. Sum-to-product on two terms starts the proof.

nodes.label: Tangent Conditional Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: In a triangle: $$\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A \tan B \tan C$$. Also $\tan\frac{A}{2}\tan\frac{B}{2} + \tan\frac{B}{2}\tan\frac{C}{2} + \tan\frac{C}{2}\tan\frac{A}{2} = 1$.

nodes.label: Cosine Conditional Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: In a triangle: $$\cos A + \cos B + \cos C = 1 + 4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}$$. This converts a cosine sum into a product of half-angle sines.

nodes.label: Trigonometric Equations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: General solutions and the linear-equation trick.

nodes.label: Standard General Solutions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sin \theta = \sin \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi + (-1)^n \alpha$$ $$\cos \theta = \cos \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha$$ $$\tan \theta = \tan \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi + \alpha$$. All n are integers.

nodes.label: Linear Equation a cos + b sin = c
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Divide by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and write as $\cos(\theta - \alpha) = c/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ where $\tan \alpha = b/a$. Solvability needs $|c| \le \sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

nodes.label: Cofunction Identities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Complementary angles swap sine and cosine: $$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cos \theta, \ \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cot \theta$$. Used when two angles in a problem sum to $\pi/2$.

nodes.label: Example: General Solution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $\sin 2\theta = \sin \theta$ gives $2\theta = n\pi + (-1)^n \theta$, splitting into $\theta = 2n\pi/3$ or $\theta = \pi + 2n\pi$.

nodes.label: Height and Distance
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Angles of elevation and depression with sine and cosine rules.

nodes.label: Angle of Elevation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight to an object above. With height h and base distance d: $$\tan \alpha = \frac{h}{d}$$. Theodolite problems always start with a right triangle.

nodes.label: Angle of Depression
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight to an object below. By alternate interior angles, depression from A to B equals elevation from B to A.

nodes.label: Example: Tower and Shadow
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A tower casts a shadow of length 20 m at elevation $60^\circ$: $h = 20 \tan 60^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}$ m.

nodes.label: Sine and Cosine Rules in Triangulation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For oblique triangles: $$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$$ and $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$$. Use when the pole leans or the two stations are not level.

nodes.label: Max-Min and Series
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Boundedness of trig expressions and arithmetic-angle series.

nodes.label: Max of a sin + b cos
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta \in [-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}, \ \sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$$. This single bound answers most 'range of expression' questions.

nodes.label: Quadratic Trig Forms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Rewrite $a\sin^2\theta + b\sin\theta\cos\theta + c\cos^2\theta$ using double-angle identities to separate a constant and a single $\sin 2\theta / \cos 2\theta$ term.

nodes.label: Example: Range via Bound
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The range of $f(\theta) = 3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ is $[-5, 5]$ since $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so no solving of the equation is needed.

nodes.label: Sine and Cosine Series in AP
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \sin(a + kd) = \frac{\sin(nd/2)}{\sin(d/2)} \sin\left(a + \frac{(n-1)d}{2}\right)$$. Multiply and divide by $2\sin(d/2)$ to get a telescoping product-to-sum series.

nodes.label: Modern Physics and Dual Nature — Introduction
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Photoelectric Effect
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Light ejects electrons only if each photon carries enough energy. The threshold condition is $$h\nu_0 = \phi$$, where $\phi$ is the work function.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: photoelectric effect work function and stopping potential

nodes.label: Planck Photon Hypothesis
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Light energy is quantized in packets: $$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}$. Higher frequency means more energetic photons, not brighter light.

nodes.label: Photon Energy Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $\lambda = 500\ \text{nm}$: $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \approx 3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \approx 2.48\ \text{eV}$$.

nodes.label: Einstein Photoelectric Equation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$ converts photon energy into electron kinetic energy minus escape cost. It explains threshold frequency and instantaneous emission.

nodes.label: Einstein Equation Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Light of $\lambda = 400\ \text{nm}$ hits a metal with $\phi = 2.0\ \text{eV}$: photon energy $E \approx 3.1\ \text{eV}$, so $K_{max} \approx 1.1\ \text{eV}$.

nodes.label: Stopping Potential
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The reverse voltage that just stops the fastest electrons measures $K_{max}$: $$eV_s = h\nu - \phi$$. A plot of $V_s$ vs $\nu$ is linear with slope $h/e$.

nodes.label: Threshold Frequency and Work Function
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Emission starts only above $$\nu_0 = \frac{\phi}{h}$$. Different metals have different $\phi$, so their thresholds differ.

nodes.label: Saturation Current vs Intensity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Saturation photocurrent is proportional to incident intensity (photon flux), while stopping potential is intensity-independent: $$i_{sat} \propto I, \ V_s \text{ independent of } I$$. More photons means more electrons, not faster electrons.

nodes.label: Radiation Pressure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For absorption, pressure is $$P = \frac{I}{c}$$; for perfect reflection, $$P = \frac{2I}{c}$$. Momentum transfer per photon is $p = E/c$.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: radiation pressure photon flux and momentum transfer

nodes.label: Classical Wave Theory Failures
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Wave theory predicts emission for any frequency given enough intensity and a time lag, both contradicted experimentally. Photons fix this via $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$, independent of intensity.

nodes.label: Photocell I-V Curves
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a vacuum photocell, current rises with collector voltage then saturates: $$i_{sat} = \frac{ne}{t}$$. The stopping voltage intercept gives $h/e$.

nodes.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$.

nodes.label: De Broglie Wavelength
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Every moving particle has an associated wavelength: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$. Macroscopic momenta give negligibly small $\lambda$, hiding wave behavior.

nodes.label: Electron Wavelength
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An electron at $10^6\ \text{m}/\text{s}$ has $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \approx 0.73\ \text{nm}$$, comparable to atomic spacings, hence diffraction.

nodes.label: Electron Accelerated Through V
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: After acceleration through potential $V$, $$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}$$. This sets the resolving scale of electron microscopes.

nodes.label: Davisson-Germer Experiment
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Electrons scattered off nickel showed diffraction peaks at angles matching Bragg's law: $$2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$$. It confirmed matter waves directly.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: de broglie matter waves and davisson germer experiment

nodes.label: Matter Waves in Bohr Orbits
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Allowed orbits fit an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_n = n\lambda = \frac{nh}{mv}$$. This recovers Bohr's angular momentum quantization.

nodes.label: Standing Wave Check
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For the $n=2$ orbit of hydrogen, the circumference fits exactly two de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_2 = 2\lambda, \ \lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$.

nodes.label: Atomic Structure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rutherford's scattering established the nuclear atom. Bohr quantized its stationary states: $$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$$.

nodes.label: Rutherford Scattering
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Alpha particles deflect off a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Distance of closest approach is $$r_{min} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2Ze^2}{K}$$.

nodes.label: Bohr Radius and Orbit Scaling
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$r_n = \frac{n^2}{Z}a_0, \ a_0 = 0.529\ \text{nm}$$. Radii grow as $n^2$, so outer orbits are much larger.

nodes.label: Bohr Energy Levels
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$E_n = -\frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. The negative sign means the electron is bound; ionization is the transition to $E = 0$.

nodes.label: Rydberg Formula and Spectral Series
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$. Lyman ends at $n=1$ (UV), Balmer at $n=2$ (visible), Paschen at $n=3$ (IR).

nodes.label: Balmer H-alpha
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The H-alpha line is $n=3 \to n=2$: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}, \ \lambda \approx 656\ \text{nm}$$.

nodes.label: Ionization Energy and Excitation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Energy to remove an electron from level $n$ is $$E_{ion} = \frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. Excitation energy to the next level is the difference of level energies.

nodes.label: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Quantum mechanics replaces trajectories with wavefunctions. The Schrodinger equation $$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V\psi = E\psi$$ governs it.
