nodes.label: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: $$\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$$. It forbids definite electron orbits inside the atom.

nodes.label: Uncertainty Estimate
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If an electron is confined to a nucleus of size $\Delta x \approx 10^{-14}\ \text{m}$, then $$\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2\Delta x} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{kg m/s}$$, implying kinetic energies of tens of MeV.

nodes.label: Born Probability Interpretation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$|\psi|^2$$ is the probability density: $$P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$$. The wavefunction itself is not directly observable.

nodes.label: Four Quantum Numbers
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $n$ sets shell, $l$ sets subshell shape ($0 \le l \le n-1$), $m_l$ sets orientation ($-l \le m_l \le l$), and $m_s = \pm\frac{1}{2}$ sets spin.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration Rules
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Aufbau fills lowest energy first with the $(n+l)$ rule, Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and Hund maximizes spin multiplicity: $$S = \frac{1}{2}\times(\text{unpaired electrons})$$.

nodes.label: Nitrogen Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Nitrogen ($Z = 7$): $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$. Hund puts all three $2p$ electrons in separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving $S = 3/2$.

nodes.label: X-Rays and Nuclear Physics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: X-rays probe inner-shell transitions, radioactive decay is statistical, and mass defects power nuclei: $$\Delta E = \Delta m\,c^2$$.

nodes.label: Moseley's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Characteristic X-ray frequency follows $$\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)$$. It reorganized the periodic table by atomic number.

nodes.label: Duane-Hunt Cutoff
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The shortest bremsstrahlung wavelength from an X-ray tube is $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$$. Higher tube voltage shifts the cutoff to shorter wavelengths.

nodes.label: Radioactive Decay Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}, \ T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$. Activity is $A = \lambda N$.

nodes.label: Binding Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$B = \left[Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n - M\right]c^2$$. Peak binding energy per nucleon near iron explains fusion and fission energy release.

nodes.label: Compton Scattering
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: X-rays scattered off electrons show a wavelength shift: $$\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$$. It proved photon momentum $p = h/\lambda$.

nodes.label: Half-Life Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A sample with $T_{1/2} = 3$ days drops to $$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/3}$$. After 9 days only $1/8$ remains.

nodes.label: ×12 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: hookes law stress strain and youngs modulus

nodes.label: Laws of Motion and Friction — Introduction
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Newton's Three Laws
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The foundational laws of dynamics: inertia, force-momentum relation, and action-reaction.

nodes.label: First Law: Inertia
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force: $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \iff \vec{a} = 0$$. This defines inertial reference frames.

nodes.label: Second Law: F = ma
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The net force equals the rate of change of momentum: $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$$. For constant mass, $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a}$$.

nodes.label: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum: $$\vec{J} = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec{F}\,dt = \Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$$. The area under an $$F$$-$$t$$ curve gives impulse.

nodes.label: Third Law: Action-Reaction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: $$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$$. The pair acts on two different bodies simultaneously and can never cancel.

nodes.label: Action-Reaction Properties
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Action and reaction act on distinct bodies, are simultaneous, share the same physical nature, and are collinear. They never act on the same body and never cancel each other.

nodes.label: Pseudo Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a non-inertial frame accelerating at $$\vec{a}_0$$, a fictitious force $$\vec{F}_{\text{pseudo}} = -m\vec{a}_0$$ must be introduced. It has no reaction partner and acts through the center of mass.

nodes.label: Apparent Weight in Elevator
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In an elevator accelerating upward at $$a$$: $$N = m(g+a)$$. Accelerating downward: $$N = m(g-a)$$. In free fall: $$N = 0$$ (weightlessness).

nodes.label: Free Fall Weightlessness
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When the elevator cable snaps ($$a = g$$ downward), the normal reaction vanishes: $$N = m(g-g) = 0$$. The passenger experiences apparent weightlessness.

nodes.label: Inertial Reference Frames
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds: an unforced particle maintains constant velocity. The ground frame is approximately inertial for JEE problems.

nodes.label: Constraints and Pulley Systems
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: String constraints, wedge contacts, Atwood machines, and spring dynamics with the sudden cut principle.

nodes.label: String Constraints
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For an ideal massless inextensible string, the virtual work shortcut gives $$\sum \vec{T}_i \cdot \vec{a}_i = 0$$. This relates the accelerations of connected masses.

nodes.label: Movable Pulley
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a movable pulley with acceleration $$a_p$$ and connected masses with accelerations $$a_1$$ and $$a_2$$: $$a_p = \frac{a_1 + a_2}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Ideal String Assumptions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An ideal string is massless and inextensible. It cannot store energy, so the net work done by internal tension forces on the system is zero: $$\sum W_T = 0$$.

nodes.label: Wedge Contact Constraint
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two rigid bodies in contact cannot penetrate each other. The acceleration components perpendicular to the contact surface must match: $$a_{1,\perp} = a_{2,\perp}$$.

nodes.label: Atwood Machine
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two masses $$m_1 > m_2$$ connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. The common acceleration is $$a = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$ and tension is $$T = \frac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$.

nodes.label: Clamp Thrust
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The thrust on the supporting pulley clamp is $$F_{\text{clamp}} = 2T = \frac{4m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$. This is strictly less than the total weight $$(m_1 + m_2)g$$.

nodes.label: Spring Dynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Hooke's law gives the restoring force $$\vec{F}_s = -k\vec{x}$$. The product $$k \cdot L$$ is constant for a given spring, so cutting changes stiffness.

nodes.label: Sudden Cut Principle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When a string is cut, tension drops instantaneously: $$T(0^+) = 0$$. A spring force cannot change instantaneously: $$F_s(0^+) = F_s(0^-)$$.

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Springs
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Series: $$\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$$. Parallel: $$k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$$.

nodes.label: Virtual Work Method
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Since ideal strings cannot store energy, the net work done by internal tensions is zero: $$\sum \vec{T}_i \cdot \vec{v}_i = 0$$. This gives constraint relations between accelerations.

nodes.label: Friction Mechanics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Static and kinetic friction laws, angle of friction, angle of repose, and optimal pulling force.

nodes.label: Static Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Static friction is self-adjusting: $$0 \le f_s \le f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$. It matches the applied tangential force up to the limiting value.

nodes.label: Kinetic Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Once sliding begins, $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ where $$\mu_k \le \mu_s$$. Kinetic friction is nearly independent of sliding speed and contact area.

nodes.label: Direction of Kinetic Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Kinetic friction opposes the relative motion between the two contacted surfaces, not the absolute motion. On a two-block system, friction on the top block can act forward.

nodes.label: Angle of Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The angle of friction is $$\lambda = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$$. The total contact force is $$R = \sqrt{N^2 + f^2}$$ and ranges from $$N$$ to $$N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}$$.

nodes.label: Total Contact Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The resultant contact force $$\vec{R} = \vec{N} + \vec{f}$$ makes angle $$\lambda$$ with the normal when friction is at its limiting value: $$\tan\lambda = \frac{f_{s,\max}}{N} = \mu_s$$.

nodes.label: Angle of Repose
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The maximum incline angle for static equilibrium is $$\theta_r = \tan^{-1}\mu_s = \lambda$$. At this angle, $$mg\sin\theta_r = \mu_s mg\cos\theta_r$$.

nodes.label: Acceleration Down Incline
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $$\theta > \theta_r$$, the body accelerates down: $$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$$. For $$\theta < \theta_r$$, static friction holds it at rest.

nodes.label: Minimum Pulling Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: To pull a block on a rough horizontal surface with force $$F$$ at angle $$\theta$$: $$F = \frac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta}$$. The minimum occurs at $$\theta = \lambda$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Pull Value
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The minimum pulling force is $$F_{\min} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} = mg\sin\lambda$$, achieved when the pull angle equals the angle of friction.

nodes.label: Nature of Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Friction is an electromagnetic contact force that opposes relative sliding or the tendency of relative sliding. It is independent of apparent contact area.

nodes.label: Two-Block Friction Systems
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Friction between two blocks with external force applied to either the top or bottom block. The slipping threshold depends on which block is pulled.

nodes.label: ×9 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: friction inclined planes and two block systems

nodes.label: Force on Top Block
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When force $$F$$ is applied to the top block $$m_1$$ on bottom block $$m_2$$ (smooth floor), the maximum acceleration of $$m_2$$ without slipping is $$a_{B,\max} = \frac{\mu m_1 g}{m_2}$$.

nodes.label: Top Pull Threshold
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The threshold force for slipping is $$F_{\text{th}} = \mu m_1 g\left(1 + \frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)$$. Below this, both blocks move together at $$a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$$.

nodes.label: Force on Bottom Block
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When force $$F$$ is applied to the bottom block $$m_2$$, the top block $$m_1$$ is accelerated only by friction. The maximum acceleration of $$m_1$$ without slipping is $$a_{A,\max} = \mu g$$.

nodes.label: Bottom Pull Threshold
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The threshold force for slipping is $$F_{\text{th}} = \mu(m_1 + m_2)g$$. Below this, both blocks move together; above this, $$m_1$$ slides at constant $$a = \mu g$$.

nodes.label: Slipping Regimes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Below threshold, both blocks move with common acceleration. Above threshold, the pulled block accelerates independently while the other moves at constant friction-limited acceleration.

nodes.label: Friction as Accelerator
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In the bottom-pull case, friction on the top block acts forward, accelerating it in the direction of motion. Friction is not always a retarding force.

nodes.label: Maximum Friction Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The maximum friction force available between two blocks is $$f_{\max} = \mu m_1 g$$ where $$m_1$$ is the top block. This limits the acceleration that friction can transmit.

nodes.label: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Mole counting, concentration and stoichiometry: the bookkeeping every other physical-chemistry chapter assumes.

nodes.label: Mole Counting and Molar Mass
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: One mole is a packet of $N_A$ particles; most JEE basics start here.

nodes.label: Concentration Terms
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: JEE mixes molarity, molality, mole fraction and normality; keep their definitions distinct.

nodes.label: Molarity, Molality, Mole Fraction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$M = n/V_L,\quad m = n/\text{kg solvent},\quad x_A = n_A/(n_A+n_B)$$. Watch solvent vs solution volume in conversions.

nodes.label: Percentage Composition and Empirical Formula
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: From mass percentages to the simplest formula, then to the molecular formula from molar mass.

nodes.label: Stoichiometry and Limiting Reagent
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Balancing gives mole ratios; the reagent that runs out first caps the product.

nodes.label: Atomic Structure
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Models of the atom from Rutherford to the quantum picture; explains line spectra and reactivity trends used across JEE.

nodes.label: ×24 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: dual nature photoelectric effect and uncertainty principle

nodes.label: Rutherford Nuclear Model
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Alpha-scattering showed a tiny dense positive nucleus with most of the atom empty.

nodes.label: Bohr Model and Energy Levels
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Quantised circular orbits give hydrogen's spectral lines; a heavy JEE favourite.

nodes.label: ×14 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: bohrs atomic model energies and spectral series

nodes.label: Bohr Energy Levels
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$E_n = -13.6/n^2\ \text{eV}$$ for hydrogen; transitions emit $$\Delta E = 13.6\left(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2\right)\ \text{eV}$$.

nodes.label: Quantum Numbers
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: n, l, m_l, m_s uniquely label an electron orbital and fix the periodic table's block structure.

nodes.label: Orbitals and Probability Density
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Schrodinger picture: orbitals are 3D probability clouds shaped by l; nodes explain bonding.

nodes.label: ×22 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: quantum mechanics wavefunctions and electronic configurations

nodes.label: de Broglie Wavelength
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\lambda = h/mv = h/p$$. Matter waves set the scale of electron diffraction and orbit stability.

nodes.label: Chemical Bonding
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Kept thin for the physical-chemistry graph: only bonding ideas that recur in equilibria, gases and solids.

nodes.label: Lewis Structures, Octet and Hybridisation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Electron bookkeeping predicts geometry and polarity; hybridisation links geometry to sigma/pi bond counts.

nodes.label: VSEPR Geometry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Electron pairs repel to maximise separation; lone pairs compress bond angles.

nodes.label: Bond Order from MO Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$BO = (N_b - N_a)/2$$. Predicts bond strength and $O_2$ paramagnetism; JEE asks $O_2, N_2, O_2^+$.

nodes.label: Redox Reactions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Oxidation numbers and balancing; the bookkeeping that feeds electrochemistry potential calculations.

nodes.label: Oxidation Number Rules
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Assign O.N. carefully (peroxide, superoxide, metal hydrides) before classifying agents or balancing.

nodes.label: Oxidation Number Conventions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: H = +1 (-1 in metal hydrides), O = -2 (peroxide -1, superoxide -1/2), F = -1, and the O.N. sum equals the species' charge. $$\sum \text{O.N.} = \text{charge on species}$$

nodes.label: Balancing Redox Equations
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Half-reaction or oxidation-number change method; conserve atoms, charge and mass.

nodes.label: Disproportionation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: One element is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction, e.g. $Cl_2$ in cold dilute $NaOH$.

nodes.label: Redox Pair -> Galvanic Cell
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: A spontaneous redox couple sets up a cell: $$\Delta G = -nFE$$, $$E^0_{cell}=E^0_{cathode}-E^0_{anode}$$.

nodes.label: Gaseous State and Kinetic Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ideal-gas laws, gas mixtures and molecular speeds; JEE loves numericals on $v_{rms}$, effusion and van der Waals constants.

nodes.label: Gas Laws (Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Each gas law is one variable held constant between two states of a fixed amount of gas.

nodes.label: Boyle's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: At fixed T, $$PV = const$$. Pressure rises as volume shrinks; basis of lung and piston questions.

nodes.label: Ideal Gas Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: The combined gas law in one line; underpins almost every gas numerical.

nodes.label: Ideal Gas Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$PV = nRT$$, with $R = 0.0821\ L\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. State assumptions: point particles, no intermolecular forces.

nodes.label: ×23 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: ideal gas laws and state mechanics

nodes.label: Dalton's Law and Graham's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Mixture pressures add; rate of effusion scales inversely with sqrt of molar mass.

nodes.label: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$P_{total} = \sum p_i,\quad p_i = x_i P_{total}$$. Each gas behaves as if alone in the volume.

nodes.label: Graham's Law of Effusion
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$r_1/r_2 = \sqrt{M_2/M_1} = t_2/t_1$$. Diffusion and effusion time problems reduce to square-root-of-mass ratios.

nodes.label: Kinetic Theory Postulates
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Gas pressure arises from elastic molecular collisions; average kinetic energy tracks temperature.

nodes.label: Molecular Speeds and Maxwell-Boltzmann
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$v_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M},\ v_{avg}=\sqrt{8RT/\pi M},\ v_{mp}=\sqrt{2RT/M}$$. Ratio $v_{rms}:v_{avg}:v_{mp}=\sqrt3:\sqrt{8/\pi}:\sqrt2$.

nodes.label: Degrees of Freedom
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Translational, rotational and vibrational modes fix $\gamma = C_p/C_v$ and gas heat capacities.

nodes.label: Real Gases and van der Waals Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Finite size (b) and attractions (a) correct the ideal law; $Z$ tracks deviation.

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: real gases and van der waals equation

nodes.label: van der Waals Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\left(P + a n^2/V^2\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$. $a$ measures attraction, $b$ excluded volume; $Z = PV/nRT$.

nodes.label: Critical Constants and Liquefaction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Above $T_c$ no amount of pressure liquefies a gas; critical constants tie back to $a$ and $b$.

nodes.label: Critical Constants from a and b
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb},\ P_c=\frac{a}{27b^2},\ V_c=3nb$$. Easily the most-asked real-gas formula cluster.

nodes.label: Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: State functions, the two laws and Gibbs energy; frames every equilibrium and emf statement in JEE chemistry.

nodes.label: System, Surroundings and State Functions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: State functions (U, H, S, G) depend only on endpoints; q and w are path-dependent.

nodes.label: First Law of Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Energy is conserved: heat added and work done by a system change its internal energy.

nodes.label: ×18 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: first law, PV, work and internal energy enthalpy relations
nodes.formula: $$\Delta U = q + w = q - P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V$$

nodes.label: First Law Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta U = q + w$$ (chemistry sign convention, w = work done on gas: $w = -P\Delta V$). For isothermal ideal gas, $\Delta U=0$.

nodes.label: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isochoric, Isobaric
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Named conditions simplify first-law bookkeeping into one algebraic constraint each.

nodes.label: Entropy and Second Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Spontaneous processes increase universe entropy; $\Delta S$ of a phase or reaction is computable.

nodes.label: Entropy and Second Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta S_{surr} = -\Delta H_{sys}/T,\quad \Delta S_{univ} > 0$$ for spontaneous. Reversible: $q_{rev}/T$.

nodes.label: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $\Delta G$ bundles enthalpy and entropy; negative $\Delta G$ marks a spontaneous process at constant T,P.

nodes.label: ×15 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: second law entropy gibbs free energy and spontaneity

nodes.label: Gibbs Free Energy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$; $\Delta G < 0$ spontaneous, $=0$ equilibrium. Linked to equilibrium: $\Delta G = -RT\ln K$.

nodes.label: Expansion Work
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Every numerical on isothermal/adiabatic change starts from the integral form of w.

nodes.label: Work Formulas
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Isothermal ideal gas: $$w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$$; reversible adiabatic: $$w = (P_2V_2-P_1V_1)/(1-\gamma)$$.

nodes.label: Thermochemistry and Energetics
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Enthalpy changes with Hess's law, bond enthalpy and calorimetry; classic JEE numerical territory.

nodes.label: ×32 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: thermochemistry hess law combustion and bond enthalpies

nodes.label: Enthalpy and Heat of Reaction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: At constant pressure $q_p = \Delta H$; exothermic $\Delta H<0$, endothermic $\Delta H>0$.

nodes.label: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Cycles
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Because H is a state function, enthalpy of reaction is path-independent; cycles with heats of formation save time.

nodes.label: Hess's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta H_{rxn} = \sum \Delta H_{steps}$$. Arrange known formation/combustion data to reach the target reaction.

nodes.label: Bond Enthalpy Calculations
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Break bonds (energy in), form bonds (energy out); difference is $\Delta H$.

nodes.label: Bond Enthalpy Formula
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta H = \sum BE_{\text{broken}} - \sum BE_{\text{formed}}$$. Average bond enthalpies make molecule estimates only.

nodes.label: Calorimetry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Measure q from temperature change with a calorimeter constant; links heat to mass and heat capacity.

nodes.label: Calorimetry Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$q = mc\Delta T + C_{cal}\Delta T$$. Sign and calorimeter constant errors are common traps.

nodes.label: Chemical Equilibrium
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: How far reactions go and how Le Chatelier shifts them; $K_p$–$K_c$ conversions are exam staples.

nodes.label: Law of Mass Action
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Equilibrium constant expression in concentrations of products over reactants, powers = stoichiometric coefficients.

nodes.label: Kp, Kc and Degree of Dissociation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Gas equilibria can use pressures; the two constants differ by $(RT)^{\Delta n}$.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: chemical equilibrium Kp Kc degree of dissociation and le chatelier

nodes.label: Kp = Kc (RT)^delta n
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$$. $\Delta n_g$ counts gaseous moles only; $\Delta n_g=0$ makes them equal.

nodes.label: Degree of Dissociation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Fraction dissociated at equilibrium; connects alpha to K and pressure for dimerisation/dissociation.

nodes.label: Degree of Dissociation Relations
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: For $A \rightleftharpoons 2B$ at pressure P: $$K_p = \frac{4\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$$. Solve for $\alpha$ or P.

nodes.label: Le Chatelier's Principle
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Changing concentration, pressure or temperature shifts a system to partially undo the change.

nodes.label: Le Chatelier Shift Directions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Add reactant -> forward; increase P shifts toward fewer gas moles; raise T for an endothermic reaction -> forward. Catalyst: equilibrium unchanged. $$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$$ links the gas-phase description.

nodes.label: Ionic Equilibrium, pH and Buffers
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Weak electrolytes, pH, buffers, hydrolysis and Ksp; the densest formula cluster in physical chemistry.

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: ionic equilibrium acids bases pH scale and buffer solutions

nodes.label: Acids and Bases: Arrhenius, Bronsted, Lewis
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Each definition is broader than the last; JEE asks for examples fitting each.

nodes.label: Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Bronsted: proton donor/acceptor, e.g. $NH_3/NH_4^+$. Lewis: electron-pair acceptor/donor; $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$ are Lewis acids. $$NH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow NH_4^+$$

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{Bronsted: proton donor/acceptor; Lewis: e}^- \text{ pair acceptor/donor}$$

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{Bronsted: proton donor/acceptor; Lewis: e}^- \text{ pair acceptor/donor}$$

nodes.label: Water Autoionisation and Kw
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Water self-ionises slightly; $K_w$ fixes [H+][OH-] at a given temperature.

nodes.label: Weak Acids/Bases: Ka, Kb
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Degree of dissociation of a weak acid grows as it is diluted (Ostwald).

nodes.label: Buffer Solutions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: A weak acid/conjugate base pair resists pH change; Henderson–Hasselbalch gives the pH directly.

nodes.label: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$pH = pK_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$$ (acidic buffer). Basic buffer: $pOH = pK_b + \log([\text{salt}]/[\text{base}])$.

nodes.label: Salt Hydrolysis
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Salts of weak acid/strong base (or vice versa) hydrolyse, setting solution acidity.

nodes.label: Solubility Product Ksp
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Predicts whether a precipitate forms from a mixing; a Q vs Ksp comparison.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: ionic equilibrium salt hydrolysis and solubility product Ksp

nodes.label: Ksp and Molar Solubility
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: For $M_aX_b$, $$K_{sp} = s^{a+b}a^ab^b$$; e.g. AgCl: $K_{sp}=s^2$, $CaF_2$: $K_{sp}=4s^3$. Common-ion effect lowers s.

nodes.label: Electrochemistry and Ionic Conduction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Conductivity of solutions, Nernst potentials and Faraday's laws; Kohlrausch and Debye-Huckel turn up often.

nodes.label: Conductance and Molar Conductivity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Two ways to report how well a solution conducts; dilution changes them differently.

nodes.label: Molar Conductivity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Lambda_m = \kappa \frac{1000}{c}\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$$. For strong electrolytes $\Lambda_m$ rises on dilution as inter-ionic drag falls.

nodes.label: Kohlrausch's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: At infinite dilution each ion contributes independently to conductance; lets you get $K_w$ and $\Lambda^0$ for weak electrolytes.

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: electrolytic conductance kohlrausch law and ionic mobility

nodes.label: Debye-Huckel-Onsager Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Explains why strong-electrolyte $\Lambda_m$ falls as concentration rises; plots are linear in $\sqrt c$.

nodes.label: Nernst Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Electrode potential under non-standard conditions; the link between emf, concentrations and $\Delta G$.

nodes.label: Nernst Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$E = E^0 - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q = E^0 - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q\ (25^\circ C)$$. Also $\Delta G = -nFE$, $\Delta G^0=-nFE^0$.

nodes.label: ×19 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: galvanic cells, EMF and nernst equation

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: galvanic cells electrochemical series and nernst equation

nodes.label: Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Charge passed deposits a predictable mass; equivalents obey Faraday's constant.

nodes.label: Faraday's Laws
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$m = ZIt/F,\ m \propto Q$$. One faraday ($F = 96487\ C$) deposits one gram-equivalent.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: electrolytic cells faradays laws and electrodeposition

nodes.label: ×12 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: faraday laws of electrolysis and batteries

nodes.label: Solutions and Colligative Properties
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Raoult and Henry laws, vapour-pressure lowering and the four colligative effects with $i$.

nodes.label: ×6 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: colligative properties, RLVP, ebullioscopy and cryoscopy

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: henrys law raoults law and vapor pressure dynamics

nodes.label: Types of Solutions and Concentration
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Solid/liquid/gas mixtures, saturated vs unsaturated, and concentration units used in colligative formulas.

nodes.label: Raoult's Law and Ideal Solutions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Each volatile component contributes partial pressure proportional to its mole fraction.

nodes.label: Raoult's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$P_i = x_i P_i^0,\quad P^0_{mix} = x_A P_A^0 + x_B P_B^0$$. Ideal solutions obey it throughout; positive deviation if $P > \sum x_i P_i^0$.

nodes.label: Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent; related to solute mole fraction.

nodes.label: Elevation of Boiling Point, Depression of Freezing Point
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Dilute solution shifts liquid's boiling/freezing temperatures by amounts proportional to molality.

nodes.label: Delta Tb and Delta Tf
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\Delta T_b = K_b m,\quad \Delta T_f = K_f m$$. $K_b, K_f$ depend on the solvent; used to find molar masses.

nodes.label: Osmotic Pressure
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pressure needed to stop osmosis through a semipermeable membrane; a colligative property like the others.

nodes.label: Osmotic Pressure Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\pi = \frac{n}{V}RT = cRT$$. For polymers/proteins where boiling/freezing changes are tiny, $\pi$ is the metric that works.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: osmotic pressure isotonic systems and vant hoff factor

nodes.label: van't Hoff Factor
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Corrects colligative formulas when a solute associates or dissociates in solution.

nodes.label: van't Hoff Factor i
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$i = \frac{\text{observed colligative effect}}{\text{calculated for no association}};\ i = 1+(n-1)\alpha$$. NaCl: $i\approx2$, acetic acid in benzene: $i\approx 1/2$.

nodes.label: Solid State
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Crystal lattices, packing efficiencies and defects; density/unit-cell numericals are recurring JEE items.

nodes.label: Crystalline vs Amorphous Solids
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ordered lattice vs short-range order; explains anisotropy, fixed melting points and X-ray diffraction patterns.

nodes.label: Unit Cells and Bravais Lattices
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: The 14 Bravais lattices tile 3D space; unit-cell geometry (simple, bcc, fcc) fixes coordination and density.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: cubic lattices geometry and density analytics

nodes.label: Packing Efficiencies
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Simple cubic: 52.4%, bcc: 68%, fcc/ccp: 74%, hcp: 74%. JEE asks for numbers and spheres-per-cell. $$\text{packing efficiency} = \frac{V_{\text{spheres}}}{V_{\text{cell}}}$$

nodes.label: ×11 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: close packing interstitial voids and ionic crystals

nodes.label: FCC, BCC and HCP Geometry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Atoms touch along body diagonal (bcc) or face diagonal (fcc/hcp); radius relates to edge length.

nodes.label: Density of Unit Cell
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Mass of Z atoms in a cube of volume $a^3$ divided by $N_A$ gives crystal density.

nodes.label: Unit Cell Density
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\rho = \frac{Z M}{a^3 N_A}$$. $Z=1$ (sc), 2 (bcc), 4 (fcc). Watch unit conversions: pm to cm.

nodes.label: Defects in Solids
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Point defects create colour and non-stoichiometry; Schottky/Frenkel are the classic pair.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: crystal defects imperfections and non stoichiometry

nodes.label: Schottky and Frenkel Defects
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Schottky: equal cation/anion vacancies (NaCl); Frenkel: cation shifts to interstitial site (AgBr). Both change density/conductivity. $$\text{Schottky: } n_+ = n_-$$

nodes.label: Surface Chemistry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Adsorption, catalysis and colloids; Freundlich and Langmuir isotherms, plus Tyndall/Brownian behaviour.

nodes.label: Adsorption: Physisorption vs Chemisorption
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Surface binding by weak van der Waals or chemical bonds; differ in enthalpy, specificity and reversibility.

nodes.label: Physisorption vs Chemisorption
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Physisorption: low $\Delta H$ (20-40 kJ/mol), multilayer, reversible. Chemisorption: higher $\Delta H$ (40-400), monolayer, specific. $$\Delta H_{ads}: \text{phy} < \text{chem}$$

nodes.label: Adsorption Isotherms
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Amount adsorbed vs pressure at fixed temperature; Freundlich is empirical, Langmuir assumes a monolayer.

nodes.label: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\frac{x}{m} = kP^{1/n}\ (n\ge1)$$. Linear form: $\log(x/m) = \log k + (1/n)\log P$.

nodes.label: Langmuir Isotherm
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Monolayer adsorption with equivalent sites: $$\theta = \frac{bP}{1+bP}$$, approaching saturation at high P.

nodes.label: Heterogeneous Catalysis at Surfaces
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Reactants adsorb, react and desorb on the solid surface; finely divided metals maximise area. Rate tracks exposed surface area: $r \propto A_{surface}$. $$2H_2 + O_2 \xrightarrow{Pt} 2H_2O$$

nodes.label: Colloids, Tyndall Effect and Emulsions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Dispersed phase in a medium with particle size 1-1000 nm; shows Tyndall scattering and Brownian motion.

nodes.label: Chemical Kinetics
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Rate laws, order vs molecularity, half-lives, Arrhenius temperature dependence and catalysis.

nodes.label: Rate of Reaction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Change in concentration per time; average vs instantaneous slopes of concentration-time graphs.

nodes.label: ×23 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: reaction rates rate laws and order

nodes.label: Rate Law, Order and Molecularity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Order is empirical from the rate law; molecularity is theoretical from the rate-determining step.

nodes.label: Rate Law Expression
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\text{rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n$$; overall order $= m+n$. Order can be fractional/zero; molecularity is 1 or 2.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{Rate law comes from the RDS, not the stoichiometry}$$

nodes.label: Zero, First and Second Order
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Each order has a characteristic integrated rate law and half-life pattern.

nodes.label: Integrated Rate Laws
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Zero: $[A]=[A]_0-kt$. First: $$\ln[A]=\ln[A]_0-kt$$. Second: $1/[A]=1/[A]_0+kt$.

nodes.label: ×20 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: integrated rate laws and half life kinetics

nodes.label: Half-Life of Reactions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Time for half the reactant to react; independence of half-life from concentration flags first order.

nodes.label: Arrhenius Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Rate constant rises exponentially with T; higher activation energy means steeper temperature sensitivity.

nodes.label: ×22 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: temperature dependence arrhenius equation and activation energy

nodes.label: Arrhenius Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$. Two-temperature form: $$\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Collision Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Reaction needs effective collisions: correct orientation and energy above $E_a$.

nodes.label: Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Decay laws, half-lives and binding energy; pairs with kinetics via exponential decay mathematics.

nodes.label: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Decay
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Three emission modes with different penetrating power and mass/atomic number bookkeeping.

nodes.label: Radioactive Decay Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Undecayed nuclei fall exponentially; a first-order process.

nodes.label: Radioactive Decay Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t},\quad A = \lambda N$$. Same math as first-order kinetics.

nodes.label: Half-Life of Radioisotopes
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Constant for a given isotope; used in carbon dating and tracer half-thickness.

nodes.label: Radioactive Half-Life
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 0.693/\lambda$$. Viel remnant after n half-lives: $(1/2)^n$.

nodes.label: Fission, Fusion and Binding Energy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Mass defect converts to energy; fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light ones both release binding energy.

nodes.label: Binding Energy and Mass Defect
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$E_b = \Delta m c^2,\quad \Delta m = Z m_p + (A-Z)m_n - M_{nucleus}$$. Per nucleon peaks near Fe-56.

nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Valence Bond Theory (VBT) & Magnetic Moments
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Crystal Field Theory (CFT) & Stabilization Energy (CFSE)
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Organometallic Chemistry & Synergic Bonding in Metal Carbonyls
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — Thermodynamic Stability & Factors Influencing Complex Formation
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — High-Yield Practical & Biological Applications
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds — High-Yield JEE Exam Traps & Problem Archetypes
nodes.subject: chemistry

nodes.label: Periodic Table and Periodicity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Periodic Table and Periodicity. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration and Blocks
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Every element's block is fixed by its valence subshell: $$ns^{1-2}$$ is s-block, $$ns^2np^{1-6}$$ is p-block, $$(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$$ is d-block, and $$(n-2)f^{0-14}$$ is f-block. Expect questions on which orbital holds the differentiating electron.

nodes.label: Atomic and Ionic Radius
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Radius decreases across a period (rising $$Z_{eff}$$) and increases down a group. Cations shrink: $$Na^+ < Na$$; anions expand: $$Cl^- > Cl$$. Isoelectronic size order: $$N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}$$.

nodes.label: Ionisation Enthalpy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Energy to remove the most loosely held electron: $$M(g) \rightarrow M^+(g) + e^-$$. IE rises across a period and falls down a group; successive IEs $$IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3$$ jump when a noble-gas core is broken.

nodes.label: IE Exceptions (N>O, Be>B, Mg>Al)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable, so $$N > O$$ (N has $$2p^3$$) and $$Be > B$$, $$Mg > Al$$. A JEE classic trap: although IE generally increases across a period, these two dips recur every period.

nodes.label: Electron Gain Enthalpy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Energy change on adding an electron: $$X(g) + e^- \rightarrow X^-(g)$$. It usually becomes more negative across a period, but Cl has the most negative EGE, not F, because tiny $$F^-$$ suffers lone-pair repulsion.

nodes.label: Electronegativity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pauling's scale measures an atom's electron-pulling power; F (4.0) is the maximum and decreases down a group and increases across a period. It predicts bond polarity and whether a hydride is ionic or covalent.

nodes.label: Metallic and Non-metallic Character
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Metallic character (ease of losing electrons) increases down a group and decreases across a period, opposite to non-metallic character. Highest metallic: Fr/Cs; highest non-metallic: F.

nodes.label: Periodicity of Oxidation States
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Maximum oxidation state often equals the group number through $$+7$$, then falls after Mn: $$Cr^{+6}$$, $$Mn^{+7}$$ in $$KMnO_4$$, $$Fe^{+6}$$ in $$K_2FeO_4$$. Lower states stabilise down a group (inert pair effect, later).

nodes.label: S Block Elements
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: S Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Group 1: Alkali Metals
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Soft, low-melting metals with configuration $$ns^1$$: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. Very low IE makes them powerful reducing agents; hydration enthalpy of $$Li^+$$ is the largest in the group.

nodes.label: Oxides, Peroxides, Superoxides
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Combustion in air gives oxides (Li: $$Li_2O$$), peroxides (Na: $$Na_2O_2$$) and superoxides (K, Rb, Cs: $$KO_2$$). Superoxides like $$KO_2$$ liberate $$O_2$$, used in submarine air supply: $$4KO_2 + 2CO_2 \rightarrow 2K_2CO_3 + 3O_2$$.

nodes.label: Solution in Liquid NH3 (Blue)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Dissolved alkali metals give a deep blue paramagnetic solution from solvated electrons: $$M + (x+y)NH_3 \rightarrow [M(NH_3)_x]^+ + [e(NH_3)_y]^-$$. On standing it decomposes to $$NaNH_2$$ plus $$H_2$$.

nodes.label: Group 2: Alkaline Earth Metals
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Harder, denser metals $$ns^2$$: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra. Solubility of hydroxides rises down the group while solubility of sulfates falls: $$BeSO_4, MgSO_4$$ soluble, $$BaSO_4$$ insoluble.

nodes.label: Anomalous Be and Mg
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Small Be shows covalent character: $$BeCl_2$$ is polymeric and $$BeCO_3$$ is unstable; Mg forms a nitride $$Mg_3N_2$$ unlike other group members and its carbonate decomposes most easily. These are fixed JEE favourites.

nodes.label: Diagonal Relationship (Li-Mg, Be-Al)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Li resembles Mg and Be resembles Al: similar polarising power gives amphoteric hydroxides, covalent chlorides and nitride formation. Example: both Li and Mg form nitrides, $$Li_3N$$ and $$Mg_3N_2$$, on heating in air.

nodes.label: Flame Test Colors (s-Block)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Characteristic flame emission: Li crimson red, Na golden yellow, K lilac (violet), Ca brick red, Sr crimson red, Ba apple green. Be and Mg show no characteristic flame since their excitation energies lie in the UV.

nodes.label: Thermal Stability of Carbonates and Nitrates
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Stability of carbonates and nitrates increases down a group because the larger cation polarises the anion less: $$MCO_3 \rightarrow MO + CO_2$$, $$2MNO_3 \rightarrow 2MNO_2 + O_2$$. $$Li_2CO_3$$ and $$LiNO_3$$ decompose most easily in Group 1.

nodes.label: Important Sodium Compounds
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: NaOH (caustic soda, Castner-Kellner cell), $$Na_2CO_3$$ (washing soda, Solvay process) and $$NaHCO_3$$ (baking soda, mild) dominate JEE. $$Na_2CO_3$$ on heating does not decompose (unlike $$Li_2CO_3$$).

nodes.label: Solvay Process for Na2CO3
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Industrial preparation: $$NaCl + NH_3 + CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow NaHCO_3 + NH_4Cl$$, then $$2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2CO_3 + CO_2 + H_2O$$. Note $$K_2CO_3$$ cannot be made this way because $$KHCO_3$$ is too soluble.

nodes.label: Important Calcium Compounds
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Key substances: quicklime $$CaO$$, slaked lime $$Ca(OH)_2$$, lime water, bleaching powder $$CaOCl_2$$, and plaster of Paris $$CaSO_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O$$. Setting of POP is crystallisation of gypsum: $$CaSO_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O + \tfrac{3}{2}H_2O \rightarrow CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$$.

nodes.label: P Block Elements
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: P Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Group 13: Boron Family
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Boron is a metalloid with electron-deficient $$BCl_3$$; Al is amphoteric: $$Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O$$. Gallium, indium and thallium show increasing inert-pair stability of the $$+1$$ state down the group.

nodes.label: Group 14: Carbon Family
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb with states $$+4$$ and $$+2$$; stability of $$+2$$ grows down the group (inert pair effect). $$CO_2$$ is a gas while $$SiO_2$$ is a giant covalent solid; watch oxidation states: $$PbO_2$$ is a strong oxidiser, $$PbCl_4$$ unstable.

nodes.label: Group 15: Nitrogen Family
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: N, P, As, Sb, Bi. Nitrogen shows $$p\pi-p\pi$$ back-bonding ($$N_2$$, $$N_2O$$, NO) unlike heavier congeners. $$NH_3$$ is basic, $$HNO_3$$ is a strong oxidising acid, and $$PCl_5$$ exists while $$NCl_5$$ does not (no d-orbitals).

nodes.label: Haber Process for Ammonia
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Industrial synthesis: $$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$$, exothermic, favoured by high pressure ~200 atm and Fe catalyst with Mo promoter. A high-pressure, moderately heated equilibrium compromise.

nodes.label: Oxoacids of Nitrogen
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Key acids: $$HNO_2$$ (nitrous, unstable), $$HNO_3$$ (nitric), $$H_2N_2O_2$$ (hyponitrous). Basicity = number of $$-OH$$ groups; $$H_3PO_2$$ and $$H_3PO_3$$ are reducing, $$HNO_3$$ oxidising.

nodes.label: Group 16: Oxygen Family
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: O, S, Se, Te, Po. $$O_3$$ (ozone) is a bent triatomic allotrope: $$2O_3 \rightarrow 3O_2$$. Sulfur's acids dominate: $$H_2SO_4$$ (contact process, strong dehydrating agent) and $$H_2S_2O_8$$ (peroxodisulfuric, has $$-O-O-$$ linkage).

nodes.label: Contact Process for H2SO4
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Sulfur burned to $$SO_2$$, catalytically oxidised: $$2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons[V_2O_5]{} 2SO_3$$, then absorbed in $$H_2SO_4$$ to give oleum $$H_2S_2O_7$$, diluted to $$H_2SO_4$$.

nodes.label: Ozone Layer Chemistry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: CFCs release Cl radicals that destroy ozone: $$Cl + O_3 \rightarrow ClO + O_2$$, $$ClO + O \rightarrow Cl + O_2$$. This radical chain thins the stratospheric ozone layer, increasing harmful UV-B at the surface.

nodes.label: Group 17: Halogens
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: F, Cl, Br, I with configuration $$ns^2np^5$$. Bond dissociation anomaly: $$F_2$$ has lower bond energy than $$Cl_2$$ due to lone-pair repulsion. All form $$HX$$; $$HF$$ is the weakest acid yet forms $$HF_2^-$$ ($$F^- \cdots HF$$).

nodes.label: Halogen Oxoacids
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Order of acid strength $$HOCl < HClO_2 < HClO_3 < HClO_4$$; oxidising power decreases down the order. $$HClO_4$$ is the strongest halogen acid; perhalates are powerful oxidisers.

nodes.label: Group 18: Noble Gases
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn with closed shells $$ns^2np^6$$ (He: $$1s^2$$). Only heavier noble gases form compounds: $$XeF_2$$ (linear), $$XeF_4$$ (square planar), $$XeO_3$$ (pyramidal) via VSEPR with lone pairs.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{Noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn}$$

nodes.label: Xenon Fluorides (XeF2, XeF4, XeF6)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Direct fluorination: $$Xe + F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 673K} XeF_2$$, $$Xe + 2F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 873K} XeF_4$$, $$Xe + 3F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 1173K} XeF_6$$. Hydrolysis of $$XeF_6$$: $$XeF_6 + H_2O \rightarrow XeOF_4 + 2HF$$.

nodes.label: Inert Pair Effect
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Down groups 13-15 the $$ns^2$$ pair resists bonding, stabilising lower oxidation states: $$Tl^+ > Tl^{3+}$$, $$Pb^{2+} > Pb^{4+}$$, $$Bi^{3+} > Bi^{5+}$$. A direct periodicity consequence examiners love.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{inert pair effect: } ns^2 \ \text{stable down the group}$$

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\text{Ox. state trends: inert pair effect in heavier p-block}$$

nodes.label: Hydrogen
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Hydrogen. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Isotopes and Preparation of H2
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Protium $$^1H$$, deuterium $$^2H$$ (D), radioactive tritium $$^3H$$. Lab preparation: $$Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2$$; large scale via steam reforming: $$CH_4 + H_2O \xrightarrow{1273K} CO + 3H_2$$.

nodes.label: Water Gas Shift Reaction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: To increase $$H_2$$ yield, CO in water gas is shifted: $$CO + H_2O \xrightarrow{673K} CO_2 + H_2$$. Iron-chrome or copper-zinc oxide catalysts are used industrially.

nodes.label: Types of Hydrides
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ionic (saline): $$NaH, CaH_2$$; covalent: $$CH_4, NH_3, H_2O, HF$$; interstitial (metallic): non-stoichiometric, e.g. $$PdH_{0.6}$$, electrically conducting. Trend in boiling points: $$H_2O$$ anomalously high due to H-bonding.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Prepared by anthraquinone process; structure has $$-O-O-$$ bridge: $$H-O-O-H$$ with dihedral angle ~109.8 deg in gas. $$H_2O_2$$ acts as both oxidiser and reducer: $$H_2O_2 + 2KI \rightarrow 2KOH + I_2$$, $$H_2O_2 + Ag_2O \rightarrow 2Ag + H_2O + O_2$$.

nodes.label: Structure and Bond Angle of H2O2
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Open book (skewed) structure with O-O single bond; gas dihedral 111.5 deg, crystalline altered by H-bonding. Oxidation state of O is $$-1$$, between $$-2$$ (water) and $$0$$ ($$O_2$$).

nodes.label: Water and Heavy Water
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$H_2O$$ is a bent molecule ($$\angle H-O-H \approx 104.5^\circ$$) with strong H-bonding giving high boiling point. Heavy water $$D_2O$$ is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors and in NMR/tracer studies.

nodes.label: D and F Block Elements
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: D and F Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: General Properties of d-Block
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Transition metals show variable oxidation states, coloured ions, paramagnetism and catalytic activity. Config: $$(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$$ with the exception of $$Cr: [Ar]3d^54s^1$$ and $$Cu: [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1$$.

nodes.label: Oxidation States and Trends
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Max oxidation state peaks at group 7: $$Mn^{+7}$$ in $$Mn_2O_7$$; $$Sc^{+3}$$ and $$Zn^{+2}$$ are common. High states are oxidising ($$Cr_2O_7^{2-}$$), low states often reducing ($$V^{2+}$$).

nodes.label: Spin-Only Magnetic Moment
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: For unpaired electrons n: $$\mu_{so} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$$ BM. Used to count d-electrons, e.g. $$Fe^{3+}$$ (d5): $$\mu = \sqrt{5 \cdot 7} = 5.92$$ BM.

nodes.label: Lanthanoid Contraction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks radii across the lanthanoids: $$La^{3+}$$ (106 pm) to $$Lu^{3+}$$ (85 pm). Consequence: 4d and 5d pairs (Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta, Mo/W) have nearly equal radii and chemistry.

nodes.label: Important d-Block Compounds
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$KMnO_4$$ (purple, strong oxidiser), $$K_2Cr_2O_7$$ (orange, oxidiser in acid), $$K_2CrO_4$$ (yellow), and $$FeSO_4 \cdot (NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O$$ (Mohr's salt). Colour: $$MnO_4^-$$ purple, $$CrO_4^{2-}$$ yellow, $$Cr_2O_7^{2-}$$ orange.

nodes.label: KMnO4 as Oxidant
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: In acid: $$MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$$ (purple to colourless). In neutral/alkaline medium it reduces to $$MnO_2$$: $$MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- \rightarrow MnO_2 + 4OH^-$$.

nodes.label: Cr2O7^2- / CrO4^2- Equilibrium
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 2OH^- \rightleftharpoons 2CrO_4^{2-} + H_2O$$. Orange dichromate in acid, yellow chromate in base - classic Le Chatelier demo.

nodes.label: Transition Metal Catalysts
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Fe (Haber, with Mo promoter), $$V_2O_5$$ (contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt/Pd (petroleum reforming). Adsorption of reactants on the surface and availability of d-orbitals explain activity.

nodes.label: F-Block: Lanthanoids and Actinoids
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Lanthanoids (4f) are silvery, with common state $$+3$$; $$Ce^{4+}$$ and $$Eu^{2+}$$ are notable. Actinoids (5f) are radioactive, all show $$+3$$, and heavier ones have low stability; $$U^{6+}$$ in uranyl $$UO_2^{2+}$$.

nodes.label: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Ionic Bond and Lattice Enthalpy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Formed by electron transfer giving a cation-anion lattice; lattice enthalpy is the energy released when gaseous ions form a solid, $$Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g) \rightarrow NaCl(s)$$. Higher charges and smaller ions give larger lattice enthalpy.

nodes.label: Born-Haber Cycle
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Hess-law bookkeeping of formation: $$\Delta H_f = S + \tfrac{1}{2}D + IE + EA - U$$. Lets you estimate lattice energy or electron affinity that cannot be measured directly.

nodes.label: Covalent Bonding and VBT
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: VBT: bonds form by overlap of half-filled orbitals with paired spins ($$\sigma$$ by head-on, $$\pi$$ by sideways overlap). $$\sigma$$ is stronger than $$\pi$$; $$N_2$$'s triple bond $$N \equiv N$$ has one $$\sigma$$ and two $$\pi$$.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: valence bond theory and magnetic moments

nodes.label: ×27 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: valence bond theory hybridization and back bonding

nodes.label: VSEPR Theory and Geometries
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Geometry follows electron-pair repulsion: $$AX_2$$ linear, $$AX_3$$ trigonal planar, $$AX_4$$ tetrahedral, $$AX_2E_2$$ bent ($$H_2O$$, 104.5 deg), $$AX_3E$$ pyramidal ($$NH_3$$, 107 deg). Lone pairs compress bond angles.

nodes.label: ×21 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: VSEPR molecular geometries shapes and bond angles
nodes.formula: $$\text{Lone Pair}-\text{Lone Pair} > \text{Lone Pair}-\text{Bond Pair} > \text{Bond Pair}-\text{Bond Pair}$$

nodes.label: Hybridization
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Mixing of orbitals gives directed geometry: $$sp$$ (linear), $$sp^2$$ (trigonal planar), $$sp^3$$ (tetrahedral), $$dsp^2$$ (square planar), $$sp^3d^2$$ (octahedral). Count $$\sigma$$ bonds + lone pairs to assign.

nodes.label: Molecular Orbital Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: MOs form by LCAO; for Z <= 7 the order is $$\sigma 1s < \sigma^*1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^*2s < \pi 2p < \sigma 2p < \pi^*2p < \sigma^*2p$$, and for O, F, Ne the $$\sigma 2p$$ and $$\pi 2p$$ swap. Bond order $$BO = \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$$ sets stability: $$O_2$$ has BO = 2 and is paramagnetic.

nodes.label: ×22 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: molecular orbital theory bond orders and magnetism

nodes.label: Dipole Moment and Molecular Polarity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$\mu = q \cdot d$$. $$CO_2$$ (linear, two opposing dipoles) has $$\mu = 0$$ though C=O is polar; $$H_2O$$ and $$NH_3$$ are polar. $$NF_3 < NH_3$$ in $$\mu$$ because lone-pair and bond dipoles oppose in $$NF_3$$.

nodes.label: ×11 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: classical bonding octet rule lattice energy and dipole moments

nodes.label: Fajan's Rules of Polarization
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Small highly charged cations and large polarisable anions increase covalent character: $$LiI$$ more covalent than $$LiF$$; $$AlCl_3$$ covalent, $$AlF_3$$ ionic. Explains solubility and colour trends.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Bonding
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: H covalently bound to F/O/N is attracted to a lone pair on F/O/N: $$O-H \cdots O$$. Explains high bp of $$H_2O, HF, NH_3$$ and why ice (open cage) floats: max density of water at 4 deg C.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: hydrogen bonding intermolecular forces and physical properties

nodes.label: Open Cage Structure of Ice
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Each water in ice H-bonds tetrahedrally to four neighbours, leaving cavities; volume expands on freezing so ice is less dense (0.917 g/cm3) and floats. This is vital for aquatic life in winter.

nodes.label: Intermolecular Forces (vdW)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: London dispersion (all molecules, rises with size), dipole-dipole, and H-bonding (strongest). Boiling points: $$He < Ar < Kr$$ from rising dispersion; polar $$HCl$$ boils above non-polar $$F_2$$ of similar mass.

nodes.label: Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Equilibrium Constant Kc and Kp
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: For $$aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$$, $$K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$$ and $$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$$. Solids and pure liquids are omitted. Large K means products dominate at equilibrium.

nodes.label: Le Chatelier's Principle
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: A system at equilibrium shifts to counter any imposed change. For $$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$$ ($$\Delta H < 0$$), high pressure and low temperature favour $$NH_3$$; a catalyst only speeds attainment of equilibrium.

nodes.label: Degree of Dissociation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Fraction dissociated $$\alpha$$; for $$N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2$$, $$K_p = \frac{4\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$$. Higher temperature shifts toward more $$NO_2$$ (browner gas) since dissociation is endothermic.

nodes.label: Acids, Bases and pH
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$pH = -\log[H^+]$$, $$pOH = 14 - pH$$ at 25 deg C. Strong acid $$HCl$$: $$pH = -\log C$$; weak acid $$CH_3COOH$$: $$[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a C}$$. $$K_w = 10^{-14}$$ links $$K_a$$ and $$K_b$$: $$K_w = K_a K_b$$.

nodes.label: Buffer Solutions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: A weak acid plus its conjugate base resists pH change; Henderson-Hasselbalch: $$pH = pK_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$$. Blood ($$H_2CO_3/HCO_3^-$$) is the classic biological buffer.

nodes.label: Salt Hydrolysis
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Salts of weak acid + strong base give basic solutions ($$CH_3COONa$$, $$pH > 7$$): $$CH_3COO^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_3COOH + OH^-$$. Salt of strong acid + weak base gives $$pH < 7$$ ($$NH_4Cl$$); weak+weak depends on $$K_a$$ vs $$K_b$$.

nodes.label: Solubility Product Ksp
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: For $$MX_2(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{2+} + 2X^-$$, $$K_{sp} = [M^{2+}][X^-]^2 = 4s^3$$. Precipitation starts when ionic product $$Q > K_{sp}$$; common ion effect suppresses solubility - basis of Group I/II cation separation.

nodes.label: Redox Reactions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Redox Reactions. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Oxidation Number Rules
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Rules: free element 0, $$O$$ is $$-2$$ (except peroxides $$-1$$, $$OF_2$$ $$+2$$), $$H$$ is $$+1$$ (except hydrides $$-1$$), sum equals charge. $$K_2Cr_2O_7$$: Cr is $$+6$$; $$H_2SO_5$$: one peroxy O pair makes S $$+6$$.

nodes.label: Oxidising and Reducing Agents
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Oxidiser gains electrons (is reduced); reducer loses electrons (is oxidised). $$KMnO_4, K_2Cr_2O_7, HNO_3$$ are common oxidisers; $$Zn, NaBH_4, H_2S$$ are common reducers. Disproportionation: same species oxidised and reduced, e.g. $$Cl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_2O$$.

nodes.label: Balancing Redox (Ion-Electron)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Split into half-reactions, balance atoms (O with $$H_2O$$, H with $$H^+$$ in acid), then electrons, then combine. Example: $$MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$$.

nodes.label: Redox Titrations
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Self-indicator titrations: $$MnO_4^-$$ (purple) vs oxalate or $$Fe^{2+}$$; endpoint is first permanent pink. Iodometric titration: $$I_2 + 2Na_2S_2O_3 \rightarrow 2NaI + Na_2S_4O_6$$ with starch blue-black endpoint.

nodes.label: Electrochemistry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Electrochemistry. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Galvanic Cell and Daniell Cell
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Spontaneous redox drives current: Daniell cell $$Zn|Zn^{2+}||Cu^{2+}|Cu$$, $$E^\circ_{cell} = 1.10$$ V, $$Zn$$ anode oxidised, $$Cu^{2+}$$ reduced at cathode. Salt bridge maintains electroneutrality.

nodes.label: Electrode Potential and Nernst Equation
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Potential vs SHE (0.00 V). Nernst: $$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q$$ at 298 K. At equilibrium $$E = 0$$ and $$E^\circ = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log K$$. Connects EMF to $$\Delta G = -nFE$$.

nodes.label: Electrolytic Cell and Faraday's Laws
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: External EMF drives non-spontaneous reaction; products: cathode reduction, anode oxidation. Faraday: $$w = ZIt = \frac{M}{nF}It$$. Electrolysis of brine gives $$H_2$$, $$Cl_2$$ at cathode/anode; molten $$NaCl$$ gives Na and $$Cl_2$$.

nodes.label: Conductivity and Kohlrausch's Law
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Molar conductivity $$\Lambda_m$$ rises on dilution for weak electrolytes; Debye-Huckel-Onsager: $$\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$$. Kohlrausch: $$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda_+^\circ + \lambda_-^\circ$$; used to find $$K_a$$ of weak acids and $$K_{sp}$$ of sparingly soluble salts.

nodes.label: Batteries and Fuel Cells
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Lead-acid (secondary): anode $$Pb + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow PbSO_4 + 2e^-$$, cathode $$PbO_2 + SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow PbSO_4 + 2H_2O$$, $$E \approx 2$$ V per cell. Fuel cell: $$2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$$, high efficiency ~75%.

nodes.label: Corrosion and Rusting
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Rusting needs both $$O_2$$ and $$H_2O$$: anode $$Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-$$, cathode $$O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-$$; rust is $$Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O$$. Prevention: galvanising (Zn), sacrificial Mg/Al, or coating.

nodes.label: Coordination Compounds
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Coordination Compounds. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Ligands and Denticity
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ligands donate lone pairs to the metal: unidentate ($$NH_3, H_2O, Cl^-, CO$$), bidentate ($$en, C_2O_4^{2-}$$), polydentate (EDTA, hexadentate). Ambidentate: $$NO_2^-$$ (N or O), $$SCN^-$$ (S or N). Chelates ring the metal and add stability (chelate effect).

nodes.label: Coordination Number and Oxidation State
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: In $$[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$$: CN = 6, Co is $$+3$$. EAN = metal electrons + donated electrons, e.g. $$[Fe(CO)_5]$$: $$26 + 10 = 36$$ (Kr). Distinguishes coordination vs ionic sphere: ionisable Cl gives ppt with $$Ag^+$$.

nodes.label: IUPAC Nomenclature
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ligands named alphabetically (anionic end in -o: chloro, ammine for $$NH_3$$, aqua, carbonyl); metal oxidation state in Roman numerals; anionic complex gets -ate: $$K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$$ potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).

nodes.label: Werner's Theory
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Primary valency (ionisable, satisfied by anions outside sphere) and secondary valency (directed in space, inside sphere). $$CoCl_3 \cdot 6NH_3$$: all Cl inside, only 1 ionisable in $$[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2$$-type? Classic series: $$[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$$ (3 ionisable Cl), $$[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2$$ (2), $$[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]Cl$$ (1).

nodes.label: Isomerism in Complexes
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Structural: ionisation, hydrate, linkage ($$[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}$$ vs $$[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}$$), coordination. Stereo: geometrical ($$cis/trans$$ in $$[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$$ - cisplatin is the $$cis$$ isomer) and optical ($$[Co(en)_3]^{3+}$$).

nodes.label: VBT for Complexes
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Geometry from hybridisation: $$[NiCl_4]^{2-}$$ $$sp^3$$ tetrahedral paramagnetic; $$[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$$ $$dsp^2$$ square planar diamagnetic. Octahedral: inner-orbital $$d^2sp^3$$ (strong field, e.g. $$[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$$) vs outer-orbital $$sp^3d^2$$ (weak field).

nodes.label: Crystal Field Theory and CFSE
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ligands split d-orbitals: octahedral $$t_{2g}$$ (lower, 3 orbitals) and $$e_g$$ (higher, 2), gap $$\Delta_o$$; CFSE $$= (-0.4n_{t2g} + 0.6n_{eg})\Delta_o$$. Strong field gives low-spin (pairing), weak field high-spin.

nodes.label: ×54 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.pattern: crystal field theory, CFSE and spectra

nodes.label: Spectrochemical Series
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Ligand field strength: $$I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < H_2O < NH_3 < en < NO_2^- < CN^- < CO$$. Weak-field halides give high-spin coloured complexes; $$CN^-, CO$$ give low-spin, often colourless diamagnetic ones.

nodes.label: Jahn-Teller Distortion
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Unequal occupancy of degenerate orbitals (e.g. $$d^9$$ $$Cu^{2+}$$, $$d^4$$ high-spin $$Mn^{3+}$$) distorts octahedron, usually elongating two axial bonds. Common in $$[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$$.

nodes.label: Stability Constants and EDTA
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Stepwise stability constants $$K_1 > K_2 > ...$$; overall $$\beta_n = K_1K_2\cdots K_n$$. Chelation (EDTA, en) greatly increases stability (chelate effect). EDTA titrates $$Ca^{2+}/Mg^{2+}$$ in water hardness with Eriochrome Black T indicator: $$Ca^{2+} + Y^{4-} \rightarrow [CaY]^{2-}$$.

nodes.label: Isolation of Elements
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Isolation of Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Principles of Metallurgy
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Steps: concentration of ore, conversion to oxide, reduction, refining. Choice of reducing agent from Ellingham diagram ($$\Delta G$$ vs T): carbon reduces most oxides at high T, $$Al$$ reduces $$Cr_2O_3$$ (thermite).

nodes.label: ×9 questions
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.formula: $$\Delta G^\circ \text{ vs } T;\ \text{lower } \Delta G^\circ \text{ fixes oxide stability}$$

nodes.label: Concentration of Ores
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Froth flotation for sulfide ores ($$ZnS$$, $$PbS$$) with pine oil; magnetic separation for $$Fe_3O_4/MnO_2$$; leaching: bauxite $$Al_2O_3 \cdot 2H_2O$$ dissolved in $$NaOH$$ as $$NaAlO_2$$.

nodes.label: Extraction of Aluminium (Hall-Heroult)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Electrolysis of $$Al_2O_3$$ in molten cryolite $$Na_3AlF_6$$: cathode $$Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al$$, anode $$C + O^{2-} \rightarrow CO + 2e^-$$, overall $$2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2$$.

nodes.label: Thermite Reaction
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$2Al + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2Fe$$, highly exothermic (~3000 K), used to weld railway rails. $$Mg$$ and $$Ca$$ similarly reduce $$TiCl_4$$ (Kroll process).

nodes.label: Extraction of Iron (Blast Furnace)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: In a blast furnace, coke reduces haematite: $$C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2$$, $$CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO$$, then $$Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$$. Limestone removes gangue: $$CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$$, $$CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3$$.

nodes.label: Refining of Metals
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Electrolytic refining (Cu, Ag, Au): impure anode, pure cathode in metal salt solution. Zone refining (Ge, Si) for semiconductors; Mond process for Ni: $$Ni + 4CO \xrightarrow{330K} Ni(CO)_4 \xrightarrow{450K} Ni + 4CO$$.

nodes.label: Mond Process for Nickel
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Impure Ni heated with CO forms volatile $$Ni(CO)_4$$, which decomposes at 450 K to pure Ni. Basis of high-purity nickel production.

nodes.label: Qualitative Analysis (Salt Analysis)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Qualitative Analysis (Salt Analysis). Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Analysis of Cations (Groups 0-VI)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Systematic separation by selective precipitation using $$K_{sp}$$: Group 0 $$NH_4^+$$; I $$Ag^+, Pb^{2+}, Hg_2^{2+}$$ (dil HCl); II $$Cu^{2+}, Cd^{2+}, Bi^{3+}, Sn^{2+}, As^{3+}$$ ($$H_2S$$ in dil HCl); III $$Fe^{3+}, Al^{3+}, Cr^{3+}$$ ($$NH_4OH/NH_4Cl$$); IV $$Zn^{2+}, Mn^{2+}, Ni^{2+}, Co^{2+}$$ ($$H_2S$$ in basic); V $$Ba^{2+}, Sr^{2+}, Ca^{2+}$$ ($$(NH_4)_2CO_3$$); VI $$Mg^{2+}$$.

nodes.label: Group I: Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2^2+
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Dil HCl precipitates white chlorides: $$AgCl, PbCl_2, Hg_2Cl_2$$. Hot water dissolves $$PbCl_2$$; $$NH_4OH$$ dissolves $$AgCl$$ as $$[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+$$ and blackens $$Hg_2Cl_2$$: $$Hg_2Cl_2 + 2NH_3 \rightarrow Hg + Hg(NH_2)Cl + NH_4Cl$$.

nodes.label: Group III: Fe3+, Al3+, Cr3+
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$NH_4OH$$ in presence of $$NH_4Cl$$ precipitates hydroxides: $$Fe(OH)_3$$ (red-brown), $$Al(OH)_3$$ (white gelatinous), $$Cr(OH)_3$$ (green). $$Fe^{3+}$$ confirmed by blood-red $$[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$$ or Prussian blue with $$K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$$.

nodes.label: Group IV Confirmatory Tests
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$Ni^{2+}$$ gives rosy-red $$Ni(DMG)_2$$ with dimethylglyoxime; $$Co^{2+}$$ gives blue $$[Co(SCN)_4]^{2-}$$; $$Zn^{2+}$$ gives white $$ZnS$$/ash test (Rinmann's green $$CoO \cdot ZnO$$ with cobalt nitrate); $$Mn^{2+}$$ gives pink sulfide and purple $$MnO_4^-$$ with oxidiser.

nodes.label: Analysis of Anions (Classes A/B/C)
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Class A (dil acid, gases): $$CO_3^{2-}, SO_3^{2-}, S^{2-}, NO_2^-, S_2O_3^{2-}, CH_3COO^-$$. Class B (conc $$H_2SO_4$$): $$Cl^-, Br^-, I^-, NO_3^-, C_2O_4^{2-}$$. Class C (precipitation): $$SO_4^{2-}, PO_4^{3-}, BO_3^{3-}$$. Soda extract $$Na_2CO_3$$ fusion makes salts water-soluble.

nodes.label: Brown Ring Test for Nitrate
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$NO_3^- + 3Fe^{2+} + 4H^+ \rightarrow 3Fe^{3+} + NO + 2H_2O$$; then $$Fe^{2+} + NO + 5H_2O \rightarrow [Fe(H_2O)_5(NO)]^{2+}$$ (brown ring at acid-water interface). Nitrite also gives a similar ring - destroy $$NO_2^-$$ with urea first.

nodes.label: Chromyl Chloride Test for Chloride
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$K_2Cr_2O_7 + 4NaCl + 6H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2CrO_2Cl_2 + 2KHSO_4 + 4NaHSO_4 + 2H_2O$$; orange-red vapours ($$CrO_2Cl_2$$) turn NaOH yellow ($$Na_2CrO_4$$), and $$Ag^+$$ gives brown $$Ag_2CrO_4$$. Fails for $$AgCl, PbCl_2, HgCl_2$$.

nodes.label: Borax Bead Test
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Heat borax $$Na_2B_4O_7 \cdot 10H_2O \rightarrow NaBO_2 + B_2O_3 + 10H_2O$$; the glassy bead dissolves metal oxides to coloured metaborates: Cu blue/green, Co blue, Cr green, Fe yellow/brown, Mn violet. A dry preliminary test for transition-metal cations.

nodes.label: Thenard's Blue and Rinmann's Green
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Charcoal cavity + cobalt nitrate: $$Al^{3+}$$ gives Thenard's blue ($$CoO \cdot Al_2O_3$$), $$Zn^{2+}$$ gives Rinmann's green ($$CoO \cdot ZnO$$). Classic flame-colour-free dry tests in qualitative analysis.

nodes.label: Dry Heating and Flame Tests
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Dry heating clues: blue/green $$Cu^{2+}$$ flame, $$ZnO$$ yellow when hot white when cold, decrepitation of $$Pb(NO_3)_2$$. Flame tests: Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green, Na golden yellow, K lilac (viewed through cobalt glass).

nodes.label: Environmental Chemistry
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Environmental Chemistry. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Atmospheric Pollution
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Key pollutants: $$CO$$ (carboxyhaemoglobin, reduces $$O_2$$ transport), $$SO_2$$ (acid rain precursor: $$SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3$$, oxidised to $$H_2SO_4$$), $$NO_x$$ (photochemical smog), particulates (PM2.5/PM10). Green chemistry aims to prevent waste at source.

nodes.label: Acid Rain
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Rain with $$pH < 5.6$$ from $$SO_2, NO_x$$ oxidation: $$2SO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4$$, $$4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4HNO_3$$. Damages marble ($$CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4$$) and acidifies lakes.

nodes.label: Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: $$CO_2, CH_4, N_2O, CFCs$$ absorb outgoing IR, raising Earth's mean temperature. Methane is ~25x more potent than $$CO_2$$ over 100 years; rising from fossil fuels, rice paddies and landfills.

nodes.label: Ozone Layer and CFC Depletion
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: Stratospheric $$O_3$$ absorbs UV ($$O_3 \xrightarrow{h\nu} O_2 + O$$). CFCs ($$CFCl_3, CF_2Cl_2$$) photolyse to Cl radicals catalysing $$2O_3 \rightarrow 3O_2$$; Montreal Protocol phased CFCs out. More UV-B reaches surface, causing skin cancer risk.

nodes.label: Water Pollution and BOD
nodes.subject: chemistry
nodes.note: BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) measures organic load; high BOD depletes dissolved $$O_2$$, killing fish. Eutrophication from phosphates triggers algal blooms. Heavy metals $$Hg, Pb, Cd$$ bioaccumulate; Minamata disease from methyl-Hg.
