nodes.label: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Empirical gas laws combine into the ideal gas equation $$PV = nRT$$, with $R = 8.314\ \text{J}/\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}$.

nodes.label: Boyle's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At fixed temperature, pressure and volume are inverse: $$P \propto \frac{1}{V}, \ P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$. The isotherm is a rectangular hyperbola on the P-V plane.

nodes.label: Charles's and Gay-Lussac's Laws
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At fixed pressure $V \propto T$; at fixed volume $P \propto T$: $$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}, \ \frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$$. Absolute temperature in kelvin is mandatory.

nodes.label: Combined Gas Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: One relation covers all three variables: $$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$$. It applies to a fixed mass of ideal gas between two equilibrium states.

nodes.label: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total pressure is the sum of partial pressures of non-reacting components: $$P = p_1 + p_2 + p_3 + \dots, \ p_i = \frac{n_i}{n}P$$. Moist gas questions subtract water vapour pressure.

nodes.label: Dalton Mixture Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A $2\ \text{L}$ vessel holds $1\ \text{mol}$ N$_2$ and $1\ \text{mol}$ O$_2$ at $300\ \text{K}$: each partial pressure is $p_i = \frac{n_iRT}{V} \approx 12.5\ \text{atm}$, so $P \approx 25\ \text{atm}$.

nodes.label: Graham's Law of Diffusion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Effusion rates are inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass: $$\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \sqrt{\frac{M_2}{M_1}}$$. It explains isotopic separation of uranium hexafluoride.

nodes.label: Graham Ratio Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: He vs O$_2$: $$\frac{r_{He}}{r_{O_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{4}} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$$. Helium effuses nearly three times faster.

nodes.label: Avogadro's Hypothesis and Molar Volume
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Equal volumes of gases at the same $T$ and $P$ contain equal molecules: at STP one mole occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$. Density then scales as $$\rho = \frac{PM}{RT}$$.

nodes.label: Open Vessel Heating
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An open vessel at fixed $P$ and $V$ loses molecules on heating: $$\frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{T_1}{T_2}$$. The fraction expelled is $$1 - \frac{T_1}{T_2}$$.

nodes.label: Moist Gas Correction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Gas collected over water contains water vapour: $$P_{gas} = P_{atm} - P_{water}$$. Vapour pressure of water depends only on temperature.

nodes.label: Kinetic Theory Postulates and Pressure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ideal gas molecules are point masses with elastic collisions and no intermolecular forces. Pressure follows from momentum transfer: $$P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N}{V}m\overline{v^2}$$.

nodes.label: Postulates of KTG
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Molecules move randomly, collisions are perfectly elastic, and collision time is negligible. Between collisions the gas obeys Newtonian mechanics with pressure emerging statistically.

nodes.label: Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average translational kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: $$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$$. This is why $T = 0\ \text{K}$ means zero kinetic energy.

nodes.label: Why Ideal Model Fails at High Density
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At high pressure, finite molecular size and attractions matter. The van der Waals correction is $$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$.

nodes.label: Collision Frequency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Molecules of one species collide at rate $$Z_1 = \sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n \bar{v}$$. Total intermolecular collisions per unit volume per second scale as $$Z_{11} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\pi d^2 n^2 \bar{v}$$.

nodes.label: Molecular Speeds
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A Maxwell-Boltzmann ensemble yields three characteristic speeds: most probable, mean, and rms. Their ranking is $$v_{mp} < \bar{v} < v_{rms}$$.

nodes.label: ×9 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: kinetic theory molecular speeds and equipartition

nodes.label: RMS Speed
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Root-mean-square speed is $$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_BT}{m}}$$. It grows as $\sqrt{T}$ and falls as $\sqrt{M}$.

nodes.label: Mean and Most Probable Speeds
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\bar{v} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}, \ v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$$. The ratio $v_{mp} : \bar{v} : v_{rms} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.225$ is a frequent JEE ask.

nodes.label: Speed Ratio Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For O$_2$ at $300\ \text{K}$, $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} \approx 483\ \text{m}/\text{s}$, while $v_{mp} \approx 395\ \text{m}/\text{s}$.

nodes.label: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The speed probability density is $$f(v) = 4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-mv^2/2k_BT}$$. Higher $T$ flattens and right-shifts the curve.

nodes.label: Mean Free Path
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average distance between collisions is $$\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n} = \frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P}$$. It falls as pressure rises.

nodes.label: Temperature and Molar Mass Shift
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The most probable speed scales as $$v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$$. Heating shifts the Maxwell peak right; heavier gases shift it left.

nodes.label: Degrees of Freedom and Equipartition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each quadratic energy term contributes $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule. For $f$ degrees of freedom, $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$$.

nodes.label: Degrees of Freedom by Gas Type
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Monatomic gases have $f = 3$ (translation only), diatomic have $f = 5$ at ordinary temperatures (3 translational + 2 rotational), and polyatomic have $f = 6$ with vibrations active.

nodes.label: Law of Equipartition of Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Energy is shared equally among all accessible quadratic modes: $$E_{mode} = \frac{1}{2}k_BT$$ per molecule. This explains why adding rotational modes raises heat capacity.

nodes.label: Heat Capacities and Gamma
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Molar heats satisfy $$C_P - C_V = R, \ \gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$$. So $\gamma = 5/3$ for monatomic and $7/5$ for diatomic gases.

nodes.label: Gas Mixtures
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Internal energy is additive: $$U = \frac{1}{2}(n_1f_1 + n_2f_2)RT$$. Effective gamma is $$\gamma_{mix} = \frac{n_1C_{P1} + n_2C_{P2}}{n_1C_{V1} + n_2C_{V2}}$$.

nodes.label: Vibrational Modes and High-Temperature Failure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Vibrations add 2 degrees of freedom per mode, giving $f = 7$ classically. Quantum freezing of modes explains why measured $C_V$ falls below classical predictions at low $T$.

nodes.label: Internal Energy of Ideal Gas
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT = nC_V T$$. Since $U$ depends only on $T$, any isothermal ideal-gas process has $\Delta U = 0$.

nodes.label: Speeds in Reaction and Effusion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Effusion rate through a small hole is $$r = \frac{P}{\sqrt{2\pi m k_B T}}$$ per unit area. It yields Graham's law on integration over the Maxwell distribution.

nodes.label: Real Gases
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Real gases deviate from ideality, captured by the compressibility factor $$Z = \frac{PV}{nRT}$$.

nodes.label: Compressibility Factor Z
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $Z = 1$ marks ideality; $Z < 1$ shows attraction dominance; $Z > 1$ shows repulsion/finite size. Z vs P curves at fixed $T$ are classic graph questions.

nodes.label: Z Curve Reading
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For H$_2$ and He, $Z > 1$ at all pressures near room temperature because repulsions dominate. For CO$_2$, $Z$ dips below 1 at moderate pressures before rising.

nodes.label: Van der Waals Equation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$ with $a$ correcting attraction and $b$ correcting volume. Both constants are material-specific.

nodes.label: Critical Constants
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At the critical point the isotherm has an inflection: $$P_c = \frac{a}{27b^2}, \ V_c = 3b, \ T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$$. Above $T_c$ no liquefaction is possible.

nodes.label: Boyle Temperature
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At $T_B$ a real gas mimics ideal behavior over a wide pressure range: $$T_B = \frac{a}{Rb}$$. Below $T_B$ attractions dominate at low pressure.

nodes.label: Virial Equation of State
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\frac{PV}{RT} = 1 + \frac{B(T)}{V} + \frac{C(T)}{V^2} + \dots$$. From van der Waals, $B(T) = b - a/(RT)$.

nodes.label: Liquefaction of Gases
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A gas liquefies only below its critical temperature: $$T < T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$$. Cooling plus compression along the Andrews isotherm produces the liquid phase.

nodes.label: Elements and Wave Propagation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A communication system encodes information into a carrier, propagates it, and decodes it at the receiver. Block flow: transducer $\to$ modulator $\to$ channel $\to$ detector $\to$ transducer.

nodes.label: Block Diagram
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Transmitter converts a message into a modulated signal for the channel; the receiver reverses the process. Blocks: transducer, modulator, channel, demodulator, transducer. A communication chain is transducer, modulator, channel, demodulator, transducer.

nodes.label: Atmospheric Layers
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Troposphere (weather, up to $\sim 12$ km), stratosphere (ozone, to $50$ km), mesosphere (to $80$ km), and ionosphere ($80$-$400$ km) hosting ions that reflect RF. Ionosphere spans roughly $$80 \text{ km} \le h \le 400 \text{ km}$$.

nodes.label: Propagation Modes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ground wave for $f < 1.5$ MHz along Earth, sky wave $1.5$ to $30$ MHz via ionospheric reflection, space wave $f > 40$ MHz line-of-sight. The ionosphere cannot reflect space waves. Space wave needs $f > 40$ MHz; sky wave uses $1.5$-$30$ MHz band.

nodes.label: Critical Frequency and Skip Distance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Critical frequency $$f_c = 9\sqrt{N_{max}}$$ sets vertical reflection. Skip distance $$d = 2h\sqrt{(f/f_c)^2 - 1}$$ and MUF $= f_c \sec\theta$.

nodes.label: Radio Horizon and Coverage
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Distance to the radio horizon from antenna height $h$ is $$d_T = \sqrt{2 R_e h_T}$$ Total LOS range: $d_T + d_R$. Covered area $A = 2\pi R_e h_T$.

nodes.label: Modulation and Bandwidth
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Baseband audio cannot be radiated efficiently, so it modulates a high-frequency carrier. Modulation index: $$\mu = A_m/A_c$$.

nodes.label: Need for Modulation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Antenna size must be $\sim \lambda/4$; a $20$ kHz audio signal has $\lambda = 15$ km. Modulating to RF ($1$ MHz) drops this to $\sim 75$ m. Radiated power scales as $P \propto (l/\lambda)^2 \propto f^2$. Radiated power scales as $$P \propto (l/\lambda)^2 \propto f^2$$.

nodes.label: Amplitude Modulation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Carrier $c(t) = A_c\sin\omega_c t$, message $m(t) = A_m\sin\omega_m t$: $$c_m(t) = A_c(1 + \mu\sin\omega_m t)\sin\omega_c t, \ \mu = A_m/A_c \le 1$$. Envelope extremes give $\mu = (A_{max}-A_{min})/(A_{max}+A_{min})$.

nodes.label: AM Spectrum and Bandwidth
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: AM splits into carrier plus two sidebands at $f_c \pm f_m$: $$BW = 2f_m$$ Amplitudes of sidebands are $\mu A_c/2$ each.

nodes.label: Power in AM Wave
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total average power $$P_t = P_c\left(1 + \frac{\mu^2}{2}\right)$$ with $P_c = A_c^2/(2R)$. Sideband fraction is $\mu^2/(2+\mu^2)$; for $\mu = 1$ one third of power is in sidebands.

nodes.label: FM and PM
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: FM makes carrier frequency follow the message: $$f(t) = f_c + \Delta f \sin\omega_m t, \ m_f = \Delta f/f_m$$. Carson's rule: $BW_{FM} \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)$.

nodes.label: Channels and Optical Communication
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Channels carry modulated signals; optical fibers use total internal reflection for high-speed links. Coaxial cable works up to about $$f \sim 1 \text{ GHz}$$.

nodes.label: Transmission Lines
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two-wire lines: simple, lossy, under $200$ MHz. Coaxial cables: braided shield, up to $\sim 1$ GHz, low radiation loss. Two-wire lines are limited to roughly $$f < 200 \text{ MHz}$$.

nodes.label: Optical Fiber Communication
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Light pulses travel in a glass core by TIR. Advantages: huge bandwidth, low attenuation, immune to EMI, and small size. TIR condition: $$\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$$.

nodes.label: Core-Cladding Guidance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Core refractive index $n_1$ exceeds cladding $n_2$. TIR needs incidence angle above critical: $$\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$$. Rays steeper than this reflect repeatedly.

nodes.label: Acceptance Angle and Numerical Aperture
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Maximum entry angle from air that still yields TIR inside the core: $$\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = NA$$. Larger NA collects more light but increases modal dispersion.

nodes.label: Problem Archetypes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: JEE traps connect modulation index, antenna height formulas, and fiber geometry. Skip distance: $$d = 2h\sqrt{(f/f_c)^2 - 1}$$.

nodes.label: Reading Modulation Index
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Given an oscilloscope trace, $\mu = (A_{max} - A_{min})/(A_{max} + A_{min})$. Overmodulation $\mu > 1$ distorts the envelope and cannot be demodulated cleanly. Modulation index from trace: $$\mu = (A_{max}-A_{min})/(A_{max}+A_{min})$$.

nodes.label: Tree and Tower Range
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two towers of heights $h_T$, $h_R$: $$d_{max} = \sqrt{2R_e h_T} + \sqrt{2R_e h_R}$$. Doubling height multiplies range by $\sqrt{2}$, a common JEE scaling question.

nodes.label: NA from Geometry
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Combine $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ with Snell's law at entry to get $\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$. Questions often swap $n_1, n_2$ in options. Numerical aperture: $$NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$.

nodes.label: Information Signal
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Speech occupies roughly $$20\text{ Hz} - 20\text{ kHz}$$ while music extends to about $20$ kHz. A transducer converts this audio into an electrical waveform.

nodes.label: Attenuation and Noise
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Signal strength falls with distance as attenuation, measured in $$\text{dB} = 10\log_{10}(P_{out}/P_{in})$$. Random noise added in the channel must be overcome by boosting the signal.

nodes.label: Weather Effect on Propagation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Tropospheric temperature inversions can trap waves and extend the normal line-of-sight range. This is a standard short-answer fact in JEE Main. Carrier relation: $$c = f\lambda$$ with $c \approx 3\times 10^8$ m/s.

nodes.label: Frequency Bands
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The bands used are roughly $$\text{MF: } \text{sky wave}, \ \text{VHF/UHF: } \text{space wave}, \ \text{microwave: satellite links}$$. Each band suits a different propagation mode.

nodes.label: Ground Wave Attenuation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ground wave energy is lost to eddy currents in the conducting Earth, with loss rising as $$\propto f^2$$. This confines ground waves to low frequencies below about $1.5$ MHz.

nodes.label: Maximum Usable Frequency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For incidence angle $\theta$ with the vertical, the maximum usable frequency is $$MUF = \frac{f_c}{\cos\theta} = f_c\sec\theta$$. Operating above MUF loses the sky wave.

nodes.label: Practical Antenna Size
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Efficient radiation needs antenna length comparable to wavelength: $$l \gtrsim \lambda/4$$. For a $100$ m radio wave this means a $25$ m tower.

nodes.label: Demodulation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An envelope detector of diode and RC circuit recovers the message because its time constant satisfies $$\frac{1}{f_c} \ll RC \ll \frac{1}{f_m}$$. This strips the high-frequency carrier.

nodes.label: FM Advantage
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: FM noise performance improves as $$SNR_{out} \propto m_f^2$$, much better than AM at the same power. The cost is a bandwidth $$BW_{FM} \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)$$.

nodes.label: Coaxial Cable Use
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The inner conductor and braided outer screen confine the field, giving low radiation loss up to $$f \sim 1 \text{ GHz}$$. Cable TV distribution relies on this.

nodes.label: Why Fibers Dominate
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Optical carrier frequencies near $$f \sim 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$$ give enormous bandwidth, plus immunity to electromagnetic interference. Attenuation in modern fiber can be below $0.2$ dB/km.

nodes.label: Modal Dispersion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In multimode fiber, different rays take different path lengths, spreading pulses by $$\Delta t \approx \frac{L}{c}\cdot\frac{n_1^2}{n_2}\Delta\theta$$. Single-mode fiber avoids this.

nodes.label: Acceptance Cone
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Light entering within the cone of half-angle $\theta_a$ is guided; outside rays refract into the cladding and are lost. Hence $$\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$.

nodes.label: Satellite Link Basics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Geostationary satellites sit at height $$h \approx 36000 \text{ km}$$ above the equator with period $24$ h. Three such satellites can cover nearly the whole globe.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic Wave Speed
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In vacuum an EM wave travels at $$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \approx 3\times 10^8\text{ m/s}$$. This ties electricity and magnetism into one wave picture.

nodes.label: TV Range Estimate
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: TV signals use space waves, so the range is set by the radio horizon: $$d = \sqrt{2 R_e h_T}$$. Raising the antenna height by $4\times$ only doubles the range.

nodes.label: Single Sideband Idea
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Sending both sidebands wastes power, so SSB keeps only one: the RF power in one sideband is $$P_{USB} = \frac{\mu^2 A_c^2}{8R}$$. SSB roughly halves the transmission bandwidth.

nodes.label: Waveguides at Microwave
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Hollow metallic guides carry microwaves without a center conductor, avoiding dielectric loss. The lowest mode cutoff wavelength satisfies $$\lambda_c = 2a$$ for a rectangular guide of width $a$.

nodes.label: Probability Foundations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Sample space, events, and the axioms.

nodes.label: Sample Space and Events
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The sample space S is all outcomes; an event E is a subset: $$P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$$ for equally likely outcomes. Sure event $P(S)=1$, impossible event $P(\emptyset)=0$.

nodes.label: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Events
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Disjoint events never co-occur: $$A \cap B = \emptyset \Rightarrow P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$$. Exhaustive events cover S, so their probabilities sum to 1.

nodes.label: Addition Theorem for Events
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$. Extends to three events with the full inclusion-exclusion pattern.

nodes.label: Classical vs Empirical Probability
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Classical probability assumes equally likely outcomes, while empirical probability uses observed frequency: $$P(E) \approx \frac{\text{favourable trials}}{\text{total trials}}$$. Law of large numbers justifies the approximation.

nodes.label: Odds in Favour and Against
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Odds convert probabilities: $$\text{odds in favour} = \frac{P(E)}{1 - P(E)}$$. A probability $3/7$ corresponds to odds $3 : 4$ in favour.

nodes.label: Complement Rule
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(\bar{A}) = 1 - P(A)$$ resolves 'at least one' counts: compute the none-case and subtract.

nodes.label: Conditional Probability and Bayes
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Dependence, independence, and updating.

nodes.label: Conditional Probability
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \ P(B) > 0$$. It reweights the space to outcomes where B already happened.

nodes.label: Tree Diagrams
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Sequential experiments draw branching trees; probabilities along a branch multiply, and probabilities of distinct branches add. Two-stage draws of balls from an urn are standard tree-diagram items.

nodes.label: Multiplication Rule
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Chain of conditional probabilities: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$$. Drawing balls without replacement uses it directly.

nodes.label: Independence of Events
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A and B are independent when $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$$. Independent coin tosses and dice rolls are the canonical examples.

nodes.label: Law of Total Probability
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For a partition $\{E_i\}$ of S: $$P(A) = \sum_i P(E_i)\,P(A \mid E_i)$$. Bayes problems always start with this expansion in the denominator.

nodes.label: Example: Two Machines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Machine A makes 60% of parts with 2% defect, B makes 40% with 5% defect. $P(A \mid \text{defect}) = \frac{0.6 \cdot 0.02}{0.6 \cdot 0.02 + 0.4 \cdot 0.05} = \frac{3}{8}$.

nodes.label: Bayes' Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(E_i \mid A) = \frac{P(E_i)P(A \mid E_i)}{\sum_j P(E_j)P(A \mid E_j)}$$. Use it to invert cause and effect, e.g. defect rates across two machines.

nodes.label: Random Variables and Expectation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: From experiments to numeric outcomes.

nodes.label: Discrete Random Variable
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A variable X mapping outcomes to numbers has a probability mass function $p(x) = P(X = x)$ with $\sum p(x) = 1$. Number of heads in 3 tosses is the standard RV.

nodes.label: Expectation (Mean)
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$E(X) = \sum_i x_i\, p(x_i)$$ is the long-run average. Linearity $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$ simplifies most JEE items.

nodes.label: Variance and Standard Deviation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 p(x_i)$$. SD is the square root of variance, so variance questions often test the shortcut formula.

nodes.label: Example: Expected Winnings
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A game pays Rs 100 with probability 0.1 and loses Rs 20 with 0.9: $E = 0.1(100) - 0.9(20) = -8$, so it is unfavourable on average.

nodes.label: Distribution Tables
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A valid distribution lists all x_i with probabilities summing to 1. Unknown constants in such problems come from $\sum p(x_i) = 1$.

nodes.label: Binomial Distribution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Bernoulli trials counted over n repetitions.

nodes.label: Bernoulli and Binomial Trials
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Each trial has success probability p and failure q = 1 - p, independent of others. n trials give the binomial setting.

nodes.label: Binomial Probability Mass Function
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = {}^nC_r\, p^r q^{\,n-r}$$. The probability of exactly r successes in n trials drives every JEE binomial PYQ.

nodes.label: Mean and Variance of Binomial
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$E(X) = np, \quad \text{Var}(X) = npq$$. Maximum probability occurs at the integer part of $(n+1)p$.

nodes.label: At Least One Success
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - q^n$$. Use the complement instead of summing the binomial tail.

nodes.label: Example: Coin Tosses
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Probability of exactly 3 heads in 5 tosses: ${}^5C_3 (1/2)^3 (1/2)^2 = \frac{10}{32} = \frac{5}{16}$.

nodes.label: Other Distributions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Poisson, geometric, and normal appear as named limits or models.

nodes.label: Poisson Distribution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^r}{r!}$$ models rare events with rate lambda. It arises as the $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ limit of binomial.

nodes.label: Normal Distribution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A continuous curve with mean mu and SD sigma; about 68% of data lies within one sigma. Standardizing with $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ converts lookups to the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Example: Standardisation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If marks are $N(60, 10^2)$, then $P(X \ge 80) = P(Z \ge 2) \approx 0.0228$ from the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Geometric Distribution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Number of trials until the first success: $$P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p$$. Its mean $1/p$ measures waiting time for the first success.

nodes.label: Statistics
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Central tendency, dispersion, and correlation.

nodes.label: Mean, Median and Mode
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$, median is the middle ordered value, mode the most frequent. Skewed JEE data questions often distinguish which one misleads.

nodes.label: Variance, SD and Range
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$ and the computational form $\sigma^2 = \overline{x^2} - \bar{x}^2$. Coefficient of variation $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ compares data sets.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}$$ lies in $[-1, 1]$: $r = 1$ perfect positive linear relation, $r = -1$ perfect negative, $r = 0$ no linear relation.

nodes.label: Weighted Mean
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Combine group means with weights: $$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}$$. JEE uses it for combined averages of two sections with different sizes.

nodes.label: Coefficient of Variation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: $$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$$ compares relative spread of two data sets. The set with higher CV is less consistent.

nodes.label: Regression Lines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Least-squares lines of y on x and x on y both pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$: $$y - \bar{y} = r\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}(x - \bar{x})$$. The product of the two slopes is $r^2$.

nodes.label: Charge and Coulomb's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Charge comes in integer units of $$e$$ and obeys an inverse-square force between resting point charges. Everything downstream starts here.

nodes.label: Quantization and Conservation of Charge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Any isolated charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge: $$q = \pm ne$$ for $$n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$. Charge can only move between bodies, so the total of an isolated system stays fixed.

nodes.label: Coulomb's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two point charges pull or push along the line joining them with magnitude $$F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$$. The constant evaluates to $$k = 9 \times 10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$$.

nodes.label: Force in a Dielectric Medium
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A medium of dielectric constant $$K$$ weakens the force between fixed charges because bound charge screens them. The reduction is $$F_{med} = \frac{F_{vac}}{K}$$.

nodes.label: Superposition of Electrostatic Forces
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each pair contributes independently, so net force is the vector sum over all partners: $$\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i} \vec{F}_i$$. Resolve into components before adding; the forces are never collinear in JEE setups.

nodes.label: Permittivity of Free Space
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Permittivity fixes the strength of electric interactions in vacuum: $$\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F/m}$$. It is bundled into $$k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$$ to shorten algebra.

nodes.label: Electric Field and Field Lines
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The field is force per unit test charge, so it exists even with no charge present. Standard geometries give closed-form results such as $$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$.

nodes.label: Definition of Electric Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The field is defined by a vanishing test charge so the source is undisturbed: $$\vec{E} = \lim_{q_0 \to 0}\frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$$. Field vectors from several sources add like any vectors.

nodes.label: Field of an Infinite Line Charge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Cylindrical symmetry makes Gauss's law trivial for linear density $$\lambda$$, giving a field that falls as $$1/r$$. The result is $$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$, or $$E = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Field on the Axis of a Charged Ring
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Off-axis components cancel and the axial field peaks at a finite distance. It reads $$E(x) = \frac{kQx}{(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$$, with maximum at $$x = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$$.

nodes.label: Field of a Uniformly Charged Disc
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A disc is a stack of rings, and its field rises from zero at the centre to the sheet value far away. The closed form is $$E(x) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Field of Charged Spheres
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A shell shields its interior, while a solid sphere's enclosed charge grows with $$r$$. Outside both, $$E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$$, inside a solid sphere $$E = \frac{kQr}{R^3}$$, and inside a shell $$E = 0$$.

nodes.label: Field of Infinite Charged Sheets
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A non-conducting sheet sends the same field to both sides, independent of distance: $$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$. Just outside a charged conductor the field doubles to $$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$.

nodes.label: Potential and Potential Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Potential trades vectors for scalars, since it stores the work done against the field. The link to field is $$\Delta V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$$.

nodes.label: Potential Difference
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Potential difference is work per unit charge moved by an external agent against the field: $$\Delta V = V_B - V_A = \frac{W_{ext}}{q}$$. The minus sign in $$\vec{E} = -\nabla V$$ says field points down the potential slope.

nodes.label: Potential of Standard Geometries
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Scalars superpose directly, so a shell gives $$V = \frac{kQ}{r}$$ outside and $$V = \frac{kQ}{R}$$ throughout. Inside a solid sphere $$V(r) = \frac{kQ}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$$, maximum at the centre.

nodes.label: Equipotential Surfaces
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Moving a charge on an equipotential costs nothing, so field lines meet these surfaces at right angles. Numerically $$W = q\Delta V = 0$$, and the field strength along the normal is $$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$$.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Potential Energy of a System
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Assembling a charge distribution costs energy pair by pair: $$U = \sum_{i < j}\frac{kq_i q_j}{r_{ij}} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i q_i V_i$$. The factor of half avoids double counting each pair.

nodes.label: Work Done by an External Agent
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The electrostatic force is conservative, so work depends only on endpoints: $$W_{ext} = \Delta U = q(V_f - V_i)$$. Kinetic energy then comes from $$\Delta K = -\Delta U$$ when released.

nodes.label: Electric Dipole
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two equal opposite charges separated by a small distance form the standard non-uniform field source. Its strength is $$\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$$.

nodes.label: Dipole Moment
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Dipole moment points from the negative to the positive charge with magnitude charge times separation: $$\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$$. Far-field formulas assume $$r \gg a$$ throughout.

nodes.label: Axial and Equatorial Fields
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On the axis the dipole field runs along $$\vec{p}$$ while on the equatorial plane it runs opposite: $$E_{axial} = \frac{2kp}{r^3}$$ and $$E_{eq} = -\frac{kp}{r^3}$$. The axial value is exactly twice the equatorial one at equal distance.

nodes.label: Field and Potential at a General Point
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At angle $$\theta$$ from the axis the components combine as $$E = \frac{kp}{r^3}\sqrt{1 + 3\cos^2\theta}$$, while potential is $$V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$$. The equatorial plane stays at $$V = 0$$ everywhere.

nodes.label: Torque and Energy in an External Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A uniform field exerts no net force but does torque the dipole toward alignment: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$$ with $$\tau = pE\sin\theta$$. Its potential energy is $$U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta$$.

nodes.label: Angular Oscillation of a Dipole
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Released near alignment the restoring torque makes simple harmonic motion for small angles. The period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{pE}}$$ with $$I$$ the moment of inertia.

nodes.label: Gauss's Law and Conductors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Gauss's law converts hard integrals into bookkeeping of enclosed charge: $$\Phi_E = \frac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$. It also fixes how charge sits on a conductor at rest.

nodes.label: Gauss's Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total flux through any closed surface depends only on the charge inside it, never on the surface shape: $$\Phi_E = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$. Choose a surface matching the symmetry of the source.

nodes.label: Flux Through Symmetric Portions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When a charge sits at a symmetric point, flux splits evenly among the pieces seen from it. A charge at a cube corner leaks $$\Phi = \frac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}$$ through that cube, and one at the centre gives $$\frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$$ per face.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Equilibrium of Conductors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Free charges rearrange until the bulk field vanishes and all excess charge lives on the surface. Just outside the surface $$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$, and the whole conductor sits at one potential.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Shielding
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A Gaussian surface inside conductor material carries no flux, so a cavity with no charge is field-free: $$E_{cavity} = 0$$. This is why instruments are housed in metal enclosures.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Pressure on a Surface
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each surface element is pulled outward by the field of the rest of the charge, which is half the total field. The resulting pressure is $$P = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$$.

nodes.label: Capacitors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A capacitor stores separated charge at a fixed ratio set by geometry, not by charge: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$. Networks then combine exactly like resistors, but inverted.

nodes.label: Capacitance Definition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Capacitance measures charge stored per volt and depends only on shape, size, and medium: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$. An isolated sphere of radius $$R$$ is a capacitor with $$C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$$.

nodes.label: Standard Capacitances
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Parallel plates give $$C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$$, while concentric shells of radii $$a < b$$ give $$C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0\frac{ab}{b - a}$$. Coaxial cylinders of length $$L$$ give $$C = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Building up the charge costs work that ends up in the field: $$U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$$. That energy lives in space as density $$u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$$.

nodes.label: Force Between the Plates
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each plate feels only the field of the other, which is half the total field, so a factor of half appears. The attraction is $$F = \frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A} = \frac{1}{2}QE$$.

nodes.label: Capacitor Networks
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Series capacitors share charge while parallel capacitors share voltage, inverting the resistor rules: $$\frac{1}{C_{series}} = \sum \frac{1}{C_i}$$ and $$C_{parallel} = \sum C_i$$. Balanced ladders and infinite grids reduce to these two cases.

nodes.label: Series Combination
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In series every capacitor carries the same charge $$Q$$ while voltages split: $$\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{C_i}$$. The equivalent capacitance is always smaller than the smallest member.

nodes.label: Parallel Combination
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In parallel every capacitor sees the same voltage and charges simply add: $$C_{eq} = \sum_i C_i$$. Charge divides in proportion to capacitance, $$Q_i = C_i V$$.

nodes.label: Dielectrics and Charge Sharing
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Inserting an insulator raises capacitance and lowers the internal field, and the boundary conditions decide whether charge or voltage is fixed. The rule of thumb is $$C \to KC_0$$.

nodes.label: Partially Filled Dielectric Slab
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A slab of thickness $$t$$ and constant $$K$$ shortens the effective gap of the capacitor. The capacitance becomes $$C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t\left(1 - \frac{1}{K}\right)}$$, and a conductor slab is the limit $$K \to \infty$$.

nodes.label: Field Inside a Dielectric
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Polarization produces an opposing field that reduces the applied one: $$E_{in} = \frac{E_0}{K}$$. The material response is $$K = 1 + \chi_e$$ with susceptibility $$\chi_e$$.

nodes.label: Battery Disconnected or Connected
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With the battery removed charge is trapped, so inserting the slab drops energy: $$U_{disc} = \frac{U_0}{K}$$. With the battery kept the voltage is pinned and energy rises: $$U_{conn} = K U_0$$, the surplus supplied by the battery.

nodes.label: Charge Sharing and Energy Loss
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Connecting charged capacitors equalizes voltage at $$V_{common} = \frac{C_1V_1 + C_2V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$ while total charge is conserved. The missing energy leaves as heat: $$\Delta H = \frac{C_1 C_2 (V_1 - V_2)^2}{2(C_1 + C_2)}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Density with a Dielectric
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Inside the filled region the field is weaker but permittivity is higher, and the product sets the stored density. It reads $$u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 K E_{in}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0 E_{in}$$.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law and Current Fields
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Every current element contributes a field that falls as $$1/r^2$$ and curls around the wire. Integration over standard shapes gives all the results JEE asks for.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A current element sends out a field along the cross product of its direction and the radial vector: $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$$. The constant is $$\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$$.

nodes.label: Straight Current-Carrying Conductors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A finite wire at perpendicular distance $$d$$ gives $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha_1 + \sin\alpha_2)$$ with angles measured from the foot of the perpendicular. Infinite wires double to $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$$, and a semi-infinite wire gives half that.

nodes.label: Circular Arc and Loop Centre Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On a circular arc only the perpendicular components survive, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I \phi}{4\pi R}$$ for angle $$\phi$$. A full loop therefore has $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$$ at its centre, or $$\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$$ with $$N$$ turns.

nodes.label: Circular Loop on Its Axis
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Off-axis components cancel and only the axial part remains: $$B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$$. Two coaxial coils a radius $$R$$ apart give a nearly uniform field of $$B = \frac{8\mu_0 N I}{5\sqrt{5}R}$$, the Helmholtz case.

nodes.label: Solenoid and Toroid
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A long solenoid packs turns into a uniform interior field $$B = \mu_0 n I$$, falling to half at the end. A toroid closes the flux on itself, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi R}$$ inside and zero outside.

nodes.label: Ampere's Circuital Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ampere's law turns hard integrals into a counting of enclosed current: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$. It works only where symmetry makes $$B$$ constant on the loop.

nodes.label: Statement of Ampere's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The circulation of $$\vec{B}$$ around any closed path depends only on current threading it: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}$$. It is the magnetic counterpart of Gauss's law for charges.

nodes.label: Field Inside and Outside a Thick Conductor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current spreads uniformly through a wire of radius $$R$$, so only part of it is enclosed at radius $$r < R$$. That gives $$B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$$ inside and $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$ outside, peaking at the surface.

nodes.label: Choosing an Amperian Loop
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pick a loop on which $$B$$ is constant and parallel to $$d\vec{l}$$, usually a circle centred on the current. Then $$B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$ solves for $$B$$ in one line.

nodes.label: Gauss's Law for Magnetism
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end because isolated poles do not exist. Every closed surface therefore collects zero net flux: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Motion of Charged Particles
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A magnetic force perpendicular to velocity bends motion without changing speed, so the trajectory is circular or helical. The radius is always $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Lorentz Force and Zero Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The full force law combines both fields: $$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$$. Since the magnetic part is perpendicular to motion it does no work, $$W_B = 0$$, and kinetic energy stays fixed.

nodes.label: Circular Motion in a Uniform Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Entering perpendicular to $$\vec{B}$$, the Lorentz force plays the centripetal role, giving $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$. The orbit period $$T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$$ is independent of speed, which is why cyclotrons work.

nodes.label: Helical Motion at an Angle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Only the perpendicular velocity component circles, while the parallel component slides undisturbed. With entry angle $$\theta$$ the pitch is $$p = v_{\parallel}T = \frac{2\pi mv\cos\theta}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Time Spent in a Field Region
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Inside a magnetic strip a particle turns through angle $$\theta$$ before leaving, and the turn time follows from the period. The time is $$t = \frac{m\theta}{qB}$$, independent of speed.

nodes.label: Velocity Selector
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Crossed electric and magnetic fields can cancel exactly for one speed, letting undeflected particles through. The selected velocity is $$v = \frac{E}{B}$$, set only by the field ratio.

nodes.label: Cyclotron
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An alternating voltage at the resonant frequency kicks the particle each half turn, while $$B$$ keeps it on a spiral. Resonance needs $$f = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$, and the Dee radius $$R$$ caps energy at $$K = \frac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m}$$.

nodes.label: Force and Torque on Currents
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Summing the Lorentz force over a wire gives a macroscopic force and, for loops, a torque. The wire result is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$.

nodes.label: Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A straight segment in a field feels $$\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$$, so magnitude is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$. The force vanishes when the wire runs parallel to the field.

nodes.label: Force Between Parallel Currents
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each wire sits in the other's field, so force per unit length is $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite directions repel.

nodes.label: Torque on a Current Loop
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Opposite sides of a loop push opposite ways, so the net force cancels but a couple survives: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$$ with $$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$$. This is exactly what spins a galvanometer coil.

nodes.label: Magnetic Moment and Potential Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A loop is a dipole with moment $$\vec{M} = NIA\hat{n}$$, and it aligns to lower energy: $$U = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B} = -MB\cos\theta$$. Stable equilibrium is at $$\theta = 0$$, unstable at $$\theta = 180^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Closed Loop in a Uniform Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For any closed current loop in a uniform field the forces around the perimeter cancel exactly: $$\vec{F}_{net} = 0$$. Only a non-uniform field can translate the loop, which is how magnetic traps and dipoles behave.

nodes.label: Galvanometer and Instruments
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A coil in a radial field converts current into deflection against a spring, and shunts or multipliers turn it into meters. Balance reads $$NIAB = C\theta$$.

nodes.label: Moving Coil Galvanometer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A cylindrical core makes the field radial, so torque stays at right angles to the plane of the coil. Deflecting torque then balances the restoring torque of the strip: $$NIAB = C\theta$$, giving $$I = \frac{C}{NAB}\theta$$.

nodes.label: Why the Field Is Made Radial
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With the field always in the plane of the coil, the angle stays at 90 degrees and the scale becomes linear. Torque is then $$\tau = NIAB$$ at every deflection, independent of $$\theta$$.

nodes.label: Current and Voltage Sensitivity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current sensitivity is deflection per ampere, $$S_i = \frac{NAB}{C}$$, while voltage sensitivity divides by coil resistance, $$S_v = \frac{S_i}{R_g}$$. Doubling turns doubles both $$S_i$$ and $$R_g$$, leaving $$S_v$$ unchanged.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as an Ammeter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A low shunt resistor diverts most current past the delicate coil. For range $$0$$ to $$I$$ the shunt is $$S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$$, and the finished ammeter has very low resistance.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as a Voltmeter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A high series resistance limits current so the meter reads potential difference across it: $$R = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g$$. The ideal voltmeter draws nothing, meaning $$R_V \to \infty$$.

nodes.label: Earth's Magnetism
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet whose field is resolved into horizontal and vertical parts. The dip angle ties them as $$\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$$.

nodes.label: Magnetic Elements of the Earth
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Declination gives the angle between geographic and magnetic meridians, and dip gives the tilt of the total field below horizontal. Components follow $$B_H = B_e\cos\delta$$ and $$B_V = B_e\sin\delta$$.

nodes.label: True and Apparent Dip
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Dip measured outside the magnetic meridian reads low, so two perpendicular readings recover the true value. They obey $$\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2$$, with true dip the smallest possible reading.

nodes.label: Tangent Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A needle under two perpendicular fields settles where their torques balance, turning angle into a field ratio. The law is $$B = B_H\tan\theta$$ for the applied field $$B$$.

nodes.label: Tangent Galvanometer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A vertical circular coil in the magnetic meridian adds its own field perpendicular to $$B_H$$. Combining coil field and tangent law gives $$I = \frac{2RB_H}{\mu_0 N}\tan\theta$$.

nodes.label: Vibration Magnetometer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A magnet displaced in the meridian oscillates about equilibrium under the restoring torque of $$B_H$$. The period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{MB_H}}$$, which lets moments be compared by timing.

nodes.label: Neutral Points
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A neutral point is where the magnet's own field exactly cancels the horizontal component of Earth's field. There the net field is zero, $$B_{mag} = B_H$$, and a compass refuses to turn.

nodes.label: Magnetic Properties of Matter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Matter magnetizes in response to an applied field, and its susceptibility classifies it. The constitutive link is $$B = \mu_0(H + I)$$.

nodes.label: Magnetization and Permeability
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Magnetization is magnetic moment per unit volume, $$I = \frac{M_{net}}{V}$$, and permeability measures how easily the medium supports flux. They combine as $$B = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H$$ with $$\chi = \frac{I}{H}$$.

nodes.label: Classification of Magnetic Materials
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Diamagnets have small negative susceptibility, paramagnets small positive susceptibility, and ferromagnets enormous positive susceptibility. The values run $$-1 \le \chi < 0$$ for diamagnets, $$0 < \chi < 10^{-3}$$ for paramagnets, and $$\chi \sim 10^2$$ upward for ferromagnets.

nodes.label: Curie's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Heat jostles paramagnetic alignment, so susceptibility falls with absolute temperature: $$\chi = \frac{C}{T}$$. Above its Curie temperature a ferromagnet obeys $$\chi = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$$ instead.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loop
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The B versus H curve lags behind the applied field, marking saturation, residual flux, and the coercive field. Retentivity $$B_r$$ is the flux left at $$H = 0$$, and coercivity $$H_c$$ is the reverse field needed to reach $$B = 0$$.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loss and Material Choice
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Energy lost per cycle per unit volume equals the enclosed loop area: $$W = \oint B\,dH$$. Narrow-loop soft iron suits transformer cores at 50 Hz, while broad-loop steel with high coercivity makes permanent magnets.

nodes.label: Superconductors and Perfect Diamagnetism
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Below its critical temperature a superconductor expels every field line from its interior. That makes it a perfect diamagnet with $$\chi = -1$$ and $$\mu_r = 0$$, so $$B = 0$$ inside.

nodes.label: Current and Microscopic Transport
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Charge in motion is current, and drift velocity explains why a slow electron still delivers steady current. The definitions are $$I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$$ and $$I = neAv_d$$.

nodes.label: Definition of Current
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current is the rate of charge crossing a cross-section, positive by convention: $$I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$$. It is a scalar, and in networks the junction rule keeps it consistent.

nodes.label: Current from a Single Moving Charge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A charge $$q$$ sweeping a length $$d$$ at speed $$v$$ completes a crossing every $$d/v$$ seconds. The average current is therefore $$I = \frac{qv}{d}$$.

nodes.label: Drift Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Electrons zig-zag between collisions and are nudged only slightly by the field, giving a slow net drift. Its size is $$v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m} = \frac{eV\tau}{mL}$$, typically under a millimetre per second.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: drift velocity ohms law and resistance dynamics

nodes.label: Current Density and Mobility
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current density counts amperes per area and links directly to drift: $$I = neAv_d$$. Mobility is drift per field, $$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$$.

nodes.label: Conductivity and Resistivity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Microscopic Ohm's law reads $$\vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E}$$ with conductivity set by carrier density and collision time: $$\sigma = \frac{ne^2\tau}{m}$$. Resistivity is its reciprocal, $$\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma}$$.

nodes.label: Resistance and Resistivity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Resistance scales with length and shrinks with area, while resistivity belongs to the material alone. The master relation is $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$.

nodes.label: Ohm's Law and Resistance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For ohmic materials voltage and current stay proportional at fixed temperature: $$V = IR$$. Geometry then gives $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$, so shape and material separate cleanly.

nodes.label: Temperature Dependence of Resistance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Metal resistance rises with temperature as lattice vibrations scatter electrons more often: $$R(T) = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$$. Semiconductors have negative $$\alpha$$ because thermal carriers multiply.

nodes.label: Stretching and Reducing Wires
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Stretching a wire keeps its volume, so gaining length means losing area. If length becomes $$n$$ times, then area becomes $$1/n$$ and $$R' = n^2 R$$; a wire of half the radius has four times the resistance.

nodes.label: Geometry Versus Material
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Resistivity depends only on material and temperature, so it survives any reshaping: $$\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$$. Charging the temperature changes $$\rho$$, but cutting the wire never does.

nodes.label: Resistor Networks
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Complex circuits collapse once series, parallel, and symmetry are recognised. Series adds resistances while parallel adds reciprocals: $$R_{eq} = \sum R_i$$.

nodes.label: ×1 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: resistor networks cell groupings and electric power

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Combinations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Series resistors share current so voltages add, while parallel resistors share voltage so conductances add. $$R_{eq} = \sum_i R_i$$ in series and $$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{R_i}$$ in parallel.

nodes.label: Current and Voltage Division
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a parallel pair current takes the inverse-resistance path, so the bigger resistor gets less: $$I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$. In series the voltage splits in proportion, $$V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$$.

nodes.label: Delta to Star Transformation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A triangle of resistors can be replaced by a three-legged star whose arms reproduce terminal behaviour. The arms are $$R_1 = \frac{R_bR_c}{R_a + R_b + R_c}$$ and its two cyclic partners.

nodes.label: Cube of Resistors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Symmetry lets the cube's twelve identical edges be folded into three groups of parallel branches. Across an edge the equivalent resistance is $$R_{eq} = \frac{7}{12}R$$, and across a face diagonal it is $$\frac{3}{4}R$$.

nodes.label: Symmetry and Equipotential Removal
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Mirror symmetry can force two nodes to the same potential, so no current flows along a bridge between them. Such a branch is deleted, $$I = 0$$, and the circuit factorises.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Laws
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: These two laws encode charge and energy conservation for any multi-loop circuit. Together they give $$\sum I = 0$$ at a junction and $$\sum IR = \sum \mathcal{E}$$ around a loop.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Current Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so whatever enters leaves: $$\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$$. It applies to any element, not just ideal wires.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Going once around a closed loop returns to the same potential, so the total voltage change vanishes: $$\sum \Delta V = 0$$. In practice drops $$IR$$ balance the emfs, giving $$\sum IR = \sum \mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Sign Conventions for Loops
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Guess a current direction first and keep it fixed; a negative answer then simply reverses the guess. Traversing a resistor against the assumed current adds $$IR$$, while crossing a cell from minus to plus adds $$\mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Wheatstone and Metre Bridges
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Bridges detect the null state, where a galvanometer reads zero and the arms balance exactly. The balance condition is $$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$$.

nodes.label: Balanced Wheatstone Bridge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When the galvanometer current vanishes, the mid-points are at equal potential and the arms are proportional: $$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$$. Unbalanced bridges need full Kirchhoff analysis or symmetry tricks.

nodes.label: Metre Bridge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A one-metre wire of uniform resistance acts as two proportional arms with a sliding contact. Balance at $$l$$ cm gives $$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$$, which is why readings cluster near 50 cm.

nodes.label: Why Null Methods Are Preferred
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At balance no current flows through the detector, so neither the source nor the meter affects the reading. Accuracy then depends only on length ratios, $$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$$, not on meter calibration.

nodes.label: Cells and Grouping
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A real cell has emf $$\mathcal{E}$$ plus internal resistance $$r$$, so terminal voltage shifts with current. Discharging gives $$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$$.

nodes.label: Terminal Potential Difference
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Delivering current makes the terminal voltage sag by the internal drop: $$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$$. Charging reverses it to $$V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$$, and open circuit leaves $$V = \mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Short Circuit and Load Matching
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Shorting a cell drives current limited only by its own resistance: $$I_{sc} = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{r}$$. With a load $$R$$ the delivered current is $$I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}$$.

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Grouping
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Series cells add emf and resistance, giving $$I = \frac{n\mathcal{E}}{R + nr}$$ for $$n$$ identical cells. Parallel cells keep emf but divide internal resistance, giving $$I = \frac{m\mathcal{E}}{mR + r}$$, and a reversed cell reduces the net emf.

nodes.label: Mixed Grouping and Maximum Current
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With $$n$$ cells in series per row and $$m$$ rows in parallel the current is $$I = \frac{mn\mathcal{E}}{mR + nr}$$. Maximising it requires the external load to equal the bank's internal resistance, $$R = \frac{nr}{m}$$.

nodes.label: Heating, Power and Fuses
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Resistive dissipation converts electrical energy to heat, which is both a loss and a design tool. The standard measure is $$H = I^2Rt$$.

nodes.label: Joule's Law of Heating
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Heat generated depends on current squared, resistance, and time: $$H = I^2Rt = \frac{V^2}{R}t$$. This is why thin, high-resistance elements run hot.

nodes.label: Electric Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Power is energy delivered per second in any of the equivalent forms: $$P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$$. Rating an appliance fixes which form is convenient.

nodes.label: Maximum Power Transfer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Power to the load peaks when load resistance equals source internal resistance: $$R = r$$. The peak is $$P_{max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}$$, delivered at only $$50\%$$ efficiency.

nodes.label: Fuse Wire
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A fuse melts when generation outruns cooling along its surface, so only radius matters for rating. That gives $$I^2 \propto r^3$$, hence $$I_{rated} \propto r^{3/2}$$ independent of length.

nodes.label: Potentiometer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A potentiometer compares potentials by balancing them against a uniform wire drop, drawing no current at balance. Its sensitivity is set by the potential gradient $$k = \frac{V}{L}$$.

nodes.label: Principle and Potential Gradient
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The wire potential falls linearly with length, so position maps directly to voltage: $$k = \frac{V_{AB}}{L}$$ in volts per metre. A smaller $$k$$ means finer resolution.

nodes.label: Comparison of EMFs
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At balance the cell emf equals the wire drop over its balance length, with zero current drawn from the cell. Two cells therefore compare as $$\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{\mathcal{E}_2} = \frac{l_1}{l_2}$$.

nodes.label: Measurement of Internal Resistance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Balance length falls from $$l_1$$ to $$l_2$$ when a shunt $$R$$ across the cell draws current. The internal resistance follows as $$r = R\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)$$.

nodes.label: RC Transients
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A capacitor charges and discharges exponentially, with the resistor setting the clock. The governing time constant is $$\tau = RC$$.

nodes.label: Charging a Capacitor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Charge builds toward its ceiling while current decays from the initial surge: $$q(t) = Q_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$$ and $$i(t) = I_0 e^{-t/RC}$$. One time constant reaches $$63.2\%$$ of full charge.

nodes.label: Discharging and Half Life
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With no source the stored charge drains exponentially: $$q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t/RC}$$. Charge halves every $$t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 \approx 0.693RC$$.

nodes.label: Time Constant and Energy Balance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The time constant sets the response speed, $$\tau = RC$$, after which the circuit is effectively steady. Charging always wastes half the battery's work as heat, $$H = \frac{1}{2}C\mathcal{E}^2$$, whatever $$R$$ is.

nodes.label: Principles and AC Generation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: AC varies sinusoidally; a rotating coil in a magnetic field is the canonical generator. Angular frequency is $$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$$.

nodes.label: Definition of AC
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Alternating current reverses direction periodically: $$I(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$. One full reversal takes $T = 1/f = 2\pi/\omega$.

nodes.label: Dynamo Principle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A coil of area $A$, $N$ turns, rotating at $\omega$ in field $B$ has flux $NAB\cos\omega t$, so $$\varepsilon = NBA\omega \sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0 \sin\omega t$$. Peak EMF scales with $N, B, A, \omega$.

nodes.label: Average and RMS Values
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average and RMS values connect sinusoidal waveforms to equivalent DC heating effect. RMS of a sine is $$I_{rms} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$$.

nodes.label: ×8 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: AC waveforms, RMS, average and pure reactive elements

nodes.label: Average Value
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Over a full half-cycle the mean of $I_0\sin\omega t$ is $$I_{av} = \frac{2 I_0}{\pi}$$. Full-cycle average is zero because positive and negative halves cancel.

nodes.label: RMS Value
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: RMS is defined by equal heating in a resistor: $$I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}, \ V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ for pure sinusoids. Mains $230\text{ V}$ means $V_0 \approx 325\text{ V}$.

nodes.label: Form Factor and Hot Wire
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Form factor $= I_{rms}/I_{av} = (\pi/2)/\sqrt{2} \approx 1.11$ for a sine wave. Hot-wire instruments read RMS because expansion tracks $I^2R$ heating. Form factor $$= \frac{I_{rms}}{I_{av}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.11$$.

nodes.label: Pure Element Response and Phasors
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each pure element responds with a characteristic phase shift between voltage and current. Reactances: $$X_L = \omega L, \ X_C = 1/(\omega C)$$.

nodes.label: Pure Resistor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $V = V_0\sin\omega t$ across $R$, $$I = \frac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t$$ in phase with voltage. Average power $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}$ is dissipated as heat.

nodes.label: Pure Inductor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$ gives $$I = \frac{V_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$ Current lags voltage by $90^\circ$.

nodes.label: Pure Capacitor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Capacitive reactance $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ gives $$I = \omega C V_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$ Current leads voltage by $90^\circ$.

nodes.label: Phasor Diagrams
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Phasors are rotating vectors of amplitude equal to peak value; phase differences come from angles. Adding voltages uses vector sums, e.g. $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$. Phasor amplitude equals peak value and angle gives phase lag.

nodes.label: Two-Element Series Circuits
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two-element series circuits combine resistance with reactance in an impedance triangle. Series RL: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}$$.

nodes.label: Series RL
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}$ and phase $\tan\phi = \omega L/R$. Current lags voltage: $$I_{rms} = \frac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Series RC
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (1/\omega C)^2}$ and $$\tan\phi = -\frac{1}{\omega C R}$$ Current leads voltage. Used as phase-shift networks.

nodes.label: Series LC
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pure $L$-$C$ has $Z = |X_L - X_C| = |\omega L - 1/\omega C|$, zero at resonance $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Voltages across $L$ and $C$ can far exceed the source. Series LC impedance: $$Z = \left|\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right|$$.

nodes.label: Series LCR and Impedance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Series LCR generalizes impedance and phase for arbitrary frequency; operating regimes split by $X_L$ versus $X_C$. Series LCR impedance: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: series, LCR, circuits impedance and power factor

nodes.label: Impedance Triangle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total impedance combines resistance and net reactance: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$ Voltage triangle: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$.

nodes.label: Phase Angle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The phase of current relative to voltage satisfies $$\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$. Inductive above resonance, capacitive below, zero at resonance.

nodes.label: Operating Regimes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If $\omega L > 1/\omega C$ circuit is inductive; if less, capacitive; equality gives unity power factor. JEE graphs ask sign of $\phi$ versus $\omega$. Phase sign of $$\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$$ tells the circuit character.

nodes.label: Resonance and Quality Factor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At resonance the series LCR current is maximum, phase is zero, and the $Q$ factor measures sharpness. Resonance frequency: $$\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$$.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: electrical resonance quality factor and transformers

nodes.label: Series Resonance Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Resonance occurs when reactances cancel: $$X_L = X_C \Rightarrow \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$. Impedance is minimum and purely resistive.

nodes.label: Half-Power Bandwidth
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current falls to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of peak at $\omega_{1,2}$ with $$\Delta \omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1 = \frac{R}{L}$$. Narrower bandwidth means sharper tuning.

nodes.label: Quality Factor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Quality factor is resonance sharpness and voltage magnification: $$Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta \omega}$$. $V_L = V_C = QV$ at resonance.

nodes.label: Power and Power Factor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average power depends on resistive voltage and current alignment; wattless current and chokes matter for efficiency. Average power: $$P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$$.

nodes.label: Average Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, $I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, average power is $$P = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi = \frac{V_0 I_0}{2}\cos\phi$$ only the resistive part dissipates.

nodes.label: Apparent, Real, Reactive Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Real power $P = VI\cos\phi$ (watt), reactive $Q = VI\sin\phi$ (VAR), apparent $S = VI$ (VA). Power factor is $\cos\phi = P/S$. Power triangle: $$S^2 = P^2 + Q^2$$ with $S = VI$.

nodes.label: Wattless Current
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Current with $\phi = \pi/2$, as in a pure inductor or capacitor, gives zero average power. Energy oscillates between source and element. Wattless current has $$\phi = \pi/2 \Rightarrow \cos\phi = 0$$.

nodes.label: Choke Coil
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A choke is a high-inductance coil that drops AC voltage with small $R$, limiting AC current without much heating. Ideal choke has $Z = \omega L$. Ideal choke impedance: $$Z = \omega L$$.

nodes.label: Free LC Oscillations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A lossless LC tank exchanges electric and magnetic energy at its natural frequency. Natural frequency: $$\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Exchange
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total energy sloshes between capacitor and inductor: $$U = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \text{constant}$$ At charge maximum all energy is electric; at $q=0$ all is magnetic.

nodes.label: Natural Frequency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Charge obeys $$\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0, \ \omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$$. Adding resistance damps this like a damped oscillator.

nodes.label: Electromechanical Analogy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $L$ plays the role of mass, $1/C$ of spring constant, $R$ of damping: $$m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + b\frac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0 \leftrightarrow L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + R\frac{dq}{dt} + \frac{q}{C} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Transformers
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Transformers step voltage using mutual induction while conserving power up to efficiency losses. Turns ratio: $$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$$.

nodes.label: Construction and Principle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Primary and secondary coils share flux in an iron core; the turns ratio sets $$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{I_p}{I_s}$$ (ideal). Step-up raises voltage, lowers current.

nodes.label: Step-Up and Step-Down
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Step-up: $N_s > N_p$, used for transmission at high voltage and low current to cut $I^2R$ loss. Step-down: $N_s < N_p$, used near consumers. Ideal transformer conserves power: $$V_p I_p = V_s I_s$$.

nodes.label: Power Conservation and Efficiency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ideal: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Real efficiency $$\eta = \frac{V_s I_s \cos\phi_s}{V_p I_p \cos\phi_p} \times 100\%$$ Losses drop as load rises toward rated value.

nodes.label: Energy Losses
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Copper loss $I^2R$ in windings, eddy currents in the core (reduced by laminations), hysteresis (soft iron core), and flux leakage between coils. Copper loss scales as $$P_{loss} = I^2 R$$.

nodes.label: Problem Archetypes and Shortcuts
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Traps mix DC and AC readings, resonance switching, and hot-wire instruments. Hot-wire reading: $$I_{rms}^2 = I_{DC}^2 + I_0^2/2$$.

nodes.label: DC and AC on Hot Wire
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A hot-wire meter reads RMS of the total waveform: $$I_{rms}^2 = I_{DC}^2 + \frac{I_0^2}{2}$$. Superpose mean-square values, not amplitudes.

nodes.label: Voltmeter Across Series LCR
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ideal voltmeters read RMS node voltages. Across $L$ and $C$ at resonance, $V_L = V_C = QV$ while the source reads only $V_R$. At resonance $$V_L = V_C = QV_{source}$$.

nodes.label: Q and Parallel Resonance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: High $Q$ circuits respond sharply. Parallel resonance gives maximum impedance and minimum line current, dual to the series case. Quality factor: $$Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$$.

nodes.label: Waveform Parameters
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $I = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, peak value is $I_0$, frequency $f = \omega/2\pi$, and time period $T = 1/f$. Phase constant $\phi$ shifts the wave along the time axis. Sinusoidal quantities use $$I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

nodes.label: Average over Half Cycle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The mean of a sine over its positive half-cycle is $$I_{av} = \frac{2I_0}{\pi}$$. This is why rectified average meters need correction factors for different waveforms.

nodes.label: Hot-Wire Instrument
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A hot wire heats as $I^2R$, so its expansion responds to the mean square. Its reading is therefore the RMS value $$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle}$$ regardless of waveform shape.

nodes.label: Reactance Trends
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Inductive reactance $$X_L = \omega L$$ grows with frequency; capacitive reactance $$X_C = 1/(\omega C)$$ falls. At DC an inductor acts like a wire and a capacitor like an open circuit.

nodes.label: Energy Transfer View
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At the series LC resonance the inductor and capacitor exchange energy each cycle with no net draw from the source. Source current is limited only by resistance $R$. Sinusoidal quantities use $$I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

nodes.label: Power Factor Correction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Industrial loads are inductive, so a capacitor in parallel supplies the reactive part $$Q_C = V^2 \omega C$$. This raises $\cos\phi$ toward unity and cuts line current.

nodes.label: Why High-Voltage Transmission
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For the same power, raising voltage by $k$ cuts current by $k$, so line loss $$P_{loss} = I^2R$$ drops by $k^2$. Transformers make this practical.
