nodes.label: Fluid Statics and Pressure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pressure at rest, Pascal's law, hydrostatic variation, and liquids in accelerated frames. Statics means no shear: pressure is isotropic.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: fluid statics pressure and archimedes principle

nodes.label: Pressure Definition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pressure is normal force per unit area: $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$, in pascals (N/m$^2$). In a static fluid it acts equally in all directions at a point.

nodes.label: Pascal's Law and Hydraulics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An applied pressure transmits undiminished through the fluid: $$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$. Hydraulic lifts trade distance for force by a factor $A_2/A_1$.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic Variation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pressure grows linearly with depth: $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$. Shape of the container is irrelevant; only the depth of the free surface matters.

nodes.label: Accelerated Container
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a frame accelerating horizontally the free surface tilts: $$\tan\theta = \frac{a}{g}$$. Effective gravity becomes the vector sum $\vec{g} - \vec{a}$.

nodes.label: Rotating Liquid Column
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Steady rotation makes the surface a paraboloid: $$z = \frac{\omega^2 r^2}{2g}$$. The pressure gradient balances both gravity and centrifugal acceleration.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic Paradox
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The force on the base of a vessel is $$F = \rho g h\, A$$, regardless of the vessel's shape or the total volume of water. Containers of different shapes with the same base and fill height push down with equal force.

nodes.label: Buoyancy and Flotation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Archimedes' principle, apparent weight, floating equilibrium, and buoyancy in non-inertial frames. Weight minus upthrust is what a spring balance reads.

nodes.label: Archimedes' Principle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid: $$F_B = \rho_f V_{sub} g$$. It depends on the fluid and submerged volume, never on the object's material.

nodes.label: Apparent Weight
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Immersion reduces the measured weight: $$W_{app} = W - F_B = (\rho_{obj} - \rho_f) V g$$. A body denser than the fluid still sinks but weighs less.

nodes.label: Flotation Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A floating body displaces its own weight: $$\rho_{obj} V_{obj} = \rho_f V_{sub} \Rightarrow \frac{V_{sub}}{V_{obj}} = \frac{\rho_{obj}}{\rho_f}$$. Ice floats with about 92% of its volume below water.

nodes.label: Floating Ice Melting
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Since the displaced water volume equals the water the ice will form, the level in the glass is unchanged: $$V_{disp} = \frac{m_{ice}}{\rho_w}$$. Adding salt or alcohol changes the answer.

nodes.label: Buoyancy in Accelerated Frames
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Replace g by the effective gravity: $$F_B = \rho V (g \pm a)$$. In free fall, buoyancy and apparent weight both vanish.

nodes.label: Fluid Dynamics and Bernoulli
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ideal flow, continuity, Bernoulli's theorem, and efflux applications. Energy conservation per unit volume is the master key.

nodes.label: ×6 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: fluid dynamics bernoulli principle and efflux

nodes.label: Ideal Fluid Assumptions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Ideal flow is incompressible, non-viscous, and irrotational: $\nabla \cdot \vec{v} = 0$ and streamlines never cross. Real problems assume this before corrections.

nodes.label: Gauge vs Absolute Pressure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Instruments read gauge pressure above atmosphere: $$P_{gauge} = P - P_{atm} = \rho g h$$. Hydrostatic problems inside open tanks use gauge pressure unless stated otherwise.

nodes.label: Equation of Continuity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Mass conservation for incompressible flow: $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$. Where the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up.

nodes.label: Bernoulli's Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Energy per unit volume is conserved along a streamline: $$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = const$$. Fast streamlines carry low pressure (Venturi effect).

nodes.label: Venturimeter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Measuring two pressures across a contraction yields the flow speed: $$v_2 = A_1\sqrt{\frac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho(A_1^2 - A_2^2)}}$$. Continuity plus Bernoulli convert pressure difference into discharge.

nodes.label: Torricelli's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Efflux speed from a small hole at depth $h$: $$v = \sqrt{2gh}$$. The emerging jet follows projectile motion from the orifice.

nodes.label: Range of the Efflux Jet
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A horizontal jet from a hole at depth $y$ below the surface of a tank of height $H$ lands at $$R = 2\sqrt{y\,(H - y)}$$. Maximum range $2H$ occurs for a hole at mid-depth $y = H/2$.

nodes.label: Hydraulic Press Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pascal multiplication gives the press force: $$F_2 = F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1}$$, while the work input equals work output since $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$. A press multiplies force, not energy.

nodes.label: Viscosity and Fluid Friction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Newton's law of viscosity, Poiseuille flow, Stokes drag, and the Reynolds number. Dissipation enters only when layers slide.

nodes.label: Newton's Law of Viscosity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient: $$F = \eta A \frac{dv}{dy}$$. Coefficient $\eta$ (Pa.s) measures internal friction.

nodes.label: Poiseuille's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Laminar discharge through a capillary: $$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \eta L}$$. The $R^4$ dependence makes small changes in radius dominant.

nodes.label: Stokes' Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Drag on a sphere at low speed: $$F = 6\pi \eta r v$$. Opposing weight and buoyancy this gives terminal velocity.

nodes.label: Terminal Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Balancing Stokes drag with net weight: $$v_t = \frac{2 r^2 (\rho_s - \rho_f) g}{9 \eta}$$. It scales with the square of the drop radius.

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: viscous flow stokes law and terminal velocity

nodes.label: Drag Regimes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At low Reynolds number drag is viscous and linear, $F \propto v$ (Stokes); at high Reynolds number it is inertial and quadratic, $F = \tfrac{1}{2} C_d \rho A v^2$. Terminal speed follows from setting drag equal to weight in the right regime.

nodes.label: Temperature and Viscosity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Liquid viscosity falls rapidly with temperature, roughly $$\eta \propto e^{E_a/RT}$$ (Andrade), while gases get more viscous as they warm. Heating honey makes it pour faster; heating air thickens its internal friction.

nodes.label: Reynolds Number
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces is $$R_e = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$$. Flow is laminar below $\sim 2000$ and turbulent above $\sim 4000$ in pipes.

nodes.label: Surface Tension and Capillarity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Surface energy, excess pressure in curved interfaces, contact angle, and capillary rise. Molecular cohesion at the free surface, made measurable.

nodes.label: ×7 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: surface tension excess pressure and capillarity

nodes.label: Surface Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Creating area costs energy: $$W = \sigma \Delta A$$, so surface tension $\sigma$ (N/m) is energy per unit area. Liquids minimise surface area into spheres.

nodes.label: Young-Laplace Pressure
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A curved interface sustains excess pressure: $$\Delta P = \sigma\left(\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$, giving $2\sigma/R$ for a drop and $4\sigma/R$ for a soap bubble (two surfaces). Smaller bubbles are over-pressured more.

nodes.label: Bubble Coalescence
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two soap bubbles merging into one release surface energy, which becomes sound and heat: $$\Delta E = \sigma \Delta A_{total}$$. For a cluster of $n$ drops coalescing, $\Delta A = 4\pi r^2 (n - n^{2/3})$.

nodes.label: Angle of Contact
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Young's equation balances the three interfacial tensions: $$\sigma_{SA} = \sigma_{SL} + \sigma_{LA}\cos\theta$$. $\theta < 90^\circ$ (water on glass) gives a concave meniscus and capillary rise.

nodes.label: Force on a Sliding Wire
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A soap film on a U-frame pulls the slider with $$F = 2\sigma L$$ (two surfaces). Equilibrium balances this against an applied load plus the film's weight.

nodes.label: Capillary Depression
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A non-wetting liquid like mercury is depressed: $$h = \frac{2\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g r} < 0$$ since $\theta > 90^\circ$. The same Jurin formula, with negative h, covers it.

nodes.label: Jurin's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rise in a clean wetting tube: $$h = \frac{2\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$$. Narrower tubes lift the column higher, inversely with radius.

nodes.label: Tube Too Short
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If the tube is shorter than $h$, the liquid rises to the top and flattens its meniscus so that $\frac{2\sigma\cos\theta'}{r} = \rho g L$; it does not overflow. The contact angle adjusts instead.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Kinematics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Definition of a rigid body, invariance of angular velocity, and the rotational kinematic equations. Geometry of a rotating body, before any force discussion.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Definition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A rigid body keeps fixed inter-particle distances, so its motion is fully described by the translation of one point plus rotation about it. Every point shares the same angular velocity.

nodes.label: Invariance of Angular Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At any instant every particle has the same $\omega$ about any fixed axis: $$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$$. Thus $\omega$ is a property of the body, not of the chosen point.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinematic Equations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Under constant angular acceleration the rotational analogues of the translational laws hold: $$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t,\quad \theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2,\quad \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$$. Use them exactly like the linear equations.

nodes.label: Angular Displacement
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Angle in radians ties arc length to radius: $$\theta = \frac{s}{r},\quad v = r\omega,\quad a_t = r\alpha$$. Every circular quantity is just the linear one divided by r.

nodes.label: Centripetal Acceleration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Even steady rotation needs inward acceleration: $$a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$. Total acceleration combines it with the tangential part: $$a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$.

nodes.label: Linear-Rotational Analogy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Every translational law has a rotational twin: $$s \leftrightarrow \theta,\ v \leftrightarrow \omega,\ m \leftrightarrow I,\ F \leftrightarrow \tau,\ p \leftrightarrow L$$. Translate a familiar result rather than memorising a new one.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rotational inertia about axes, radius of gyration, axis-shift theorems, and the standard values. The quantity that plays the role of mass in rotation.

nodes.label: ×16 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: moment of inertia radius of gyration and axis theorems

nodes.label: Definition and Radius of Gyration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rotational inertia is $$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2 dm$$, with radius of gyration $$k = \sqrt{I/M}$$. Mass far from the axis dominates I.

nodes.label: Parallel Axis Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Shifting from the centre of mass to a parallel axis adds $Md^2$: $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$. The CM axis always carries the smallest I.

nodes.label: Perpendicular Axis Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a planar lamina, the out-of-plane moment equals the sum of the two in-plane moments: $$I_z = I_x + I_y$$. This quickly yields, for a disc, $$I_z = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$$.

nodes.label: Standard Moments of Inertia
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Memorise the hierarchy $$I_{ring} = MR^2,\quad I_{disc} = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2,\quad I_{solid\ sphere} = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2,\quad I_{rod} = \tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$$. Smaller $I/MR^2$ means the body rolls faster.

nodes.label: Cavity by Negative Mass
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A body with a cavity is the superposition of the full body minus the removed part: $$I = I_{full} - I_{removed}$$. The cavity piece's own CM offset then uses the parallel-axis theorem.

nodes.label: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Torque as the rotational force, the rotational second law, and rotational work-energy. Dynamics of a body when the line of action misses the centre.

nodes.label: ×11 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: torque rotational equilibrium and fixed axis dynamics

nodes.label: Definition of Torque
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Torque is the moment of force about a point: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F},\quad \tau = rF\sin\phi$$. Its lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force.

nodes.label: Rotational Second Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Net torque produces angular acceleration: $$\tau_{net} = I\alpha$$, with the constraint equations of the problem supplying $\alpha$. It is the direct analogue of $F = ma$.

nodes.label: Angular Impulse and Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Impulse of torque changes angular momentum, and torque does work through angle: $$\int \tau\, dt = \Delta L,\quad W = \int \tau\, d\theta,\quad P = \tau\omega$$. These are the rotational analogues of impulse and work.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinetic Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A spinning body stores $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis this replaces $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$; compare energies of differently shaped wheels at equal $\omega$.

nodes.label: Couple
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two equal opposite parallel forces form a pure moment: $$\tau = F \times d$$, independent of the pivot chosen. A couple spins a body without translating its CM.

nodes.label: Unwinding Yo-Yo and Hanging Mass
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a hanging mass $m$ on a string wrapped around a disc, Newton plus $\tau = I\alpha$ give $$a = \frac{g}{1 + I/mR^2}$$. The disc's inertia slows the descent.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Definition, conservation, and classic applications like the cue-ball strike. Conserved whenever external torque vanishes, exactly like linear momentum.

nodes.label: ×8 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: angular momentum conservation and impulse dynamics

nodes.label: Definition of L
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Angular momentum about a point is $$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times m\vec{v}$$, and for a rigid body $$L = I\omega$$. Its direction follows the right-hand rule about the pivot.

nodes.label: Conservation of L
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With zero net external torque, angular momentum is conserved: $$\tau_{ext} = 0 \Rightarrow L = const,\quad I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$$. A skater pulling in her arms spins faster because $I$ drops.

nodes.label: Direction and Precession Idea
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Torque changes L along its own direction: $$\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$$. A spinning top precesses because gravity torques its angular momentum sideways, not downward.

nodes.label: Cue Ball Strike Height
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A horizontal cue strike produces immediate pure rolling when $$h = \frac{R}{2}\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$$ above the centre, i.e. $7R/10$ for a solid sphere. Below this height the ball skids forward; above it, it back-spins.

nodes.label: Rolling Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Combined translation and rotation, the rolling constraint, instantaneous centre, incline dynamics, and energy partitioning. The richest rigid-body topic in JEE.

nodes.label: Konig's Theorem for KE
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total kinetic energy splits into CM translation and rotation about the CM: $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}I_{cm}\omega^2$$. Each part is computed independently, then added.

nodes.label: Pure Rolling Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rolling without slipping locks translation to rotation: $$v_{cm} = \omega R,\quad a_{cm} = \alpha R$$. Static friction enforces it and does no net work on the contact point.

nodes.label: Instantaneous Centre of Rotation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The contact point is momentarily at rest and acts as the pivot: every point's speed is $v = \omega d$ where $d$ is its distance from the contact. The top of a rolling wheel moves at $2v_{cm}$.

nodes.label: Rolling Down an Incline
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Combining $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$ with $fR = I\alpha$ gives $$a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/MR^2}$$. The race down the incline ranks ring last and solid sphere first.

nodes.label: ×14 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: rolling motion energy partition and incline dynamics

nodes.label: Great Incline Race
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Acceleration depends only on shape factor $\beta = I/MR^2$: smaller $\beta$ wins. Solid sphere ($2/5$) beats disc ($1/2$), which beats ring ($1$), independent of mass and radius.

nodes.label: Speed at the Base
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Energy conservation gives $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + I/MR^2}}$$, and travel time follows from $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. No slipping means static friction, so mechanical energy is conserved.

nodes.label: Toppling versus Sliding
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When a block tips over instead of sliding, set by geometry against friction. Decides the angle at which a block on an incline first gives way.

nodes.label: Normal Reaction Migration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: As the incline steepens, the normal shifts toward the downhill edge: $$x = \frac{h}{2}\tan\theta$$-style balance of torques. Toppling begins when the normal reaches the lower corner.

nodes.label: Toppling vs Sliding Criterion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Sliding starts at $$\tan\theta = \mu_s$$ while toppling starts at $$\tan\theta = \frac{b}{h}$$ (base over height). The smaller of $\mu_s$ and $b/h$ decides the failure mode.

nodes.label: High-Yield Traps
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Frequent exam pitfalls in rotational mechanics, gathered as quick diagnostics. Read after every problem for a one-line self-check.

nodes.label: Axis Choice Trap
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Always write $\tau = I\alpha$ about an axis fixed in direction; for moving axes add the $M a_{cm} \times r$ correction. Mixing axes between L and alpha silently breaks conservation arguments.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia Axis Trap
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $I$ is always about a specified axis; quoting a single value without its axis is meaningless. Shift with $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$ only between parallel axes through the same orientation.

nodes.label: Rolling Energy Trap
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In pure rolling on a fixed surface, static friction does no work, yet friction is essential to enforce $v = \omega R$. Do not add a $f \cdot s$ dissipation term.

nodes.label: SHM Fundamentals
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The defining condition is linear restoring force: $$F = -kx \Rightarrow a = -\frac{k}{m}x$$.

nodes.label: Defining Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Acceleration is always directed toward the mean position and proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. Any system satisfying this oscillates in SHM.

nodes.label: Differential Equation of SHM
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2 x = 0$$ with solution $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.

nodes.label: Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$v = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi), \ a = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. Maximum speed at mean position: $$v_{max} = A\omega$$; maximum acceleration at extremes: $$a_{max} = A\omega^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinematics Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $x = 2\sin(3t)$ cm: $A = 2\ \text{cm}$, $\omega = 3\ \text{rad/s}$, so $$v_{max} = A\omega = 6\ \text{cm/s}, \ a_{max} = A\omega^2 = 18\ \text{cm/s}^2$$.

nodes.label: ×19 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: SHM kinematics phasor circle and energy dynamics

nodes.label: Phase and Reference Circle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ maps to projection of uniform circular motion of radius $A$ and angular speed $\omega$. Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$.

nodes.label: Time Period and Frequency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \ f = \frac{1}{T}, \ \omega = 2\pi f$$. Period is independent of amplitude for ideal SHM.

nodes.label: Period Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass on a $200\ \text{N/m}$ spring: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.5/200} \approx 0.31\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Energy in SHM
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total mechanical energy is conserved and fixed by amplitude: $$E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinetic Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$$. It is maximum at the mean position and zero at extremes.

nodes.label: KE at Half Amplitude
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At $x = A/2$: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2\left(A^2 - \frac{A^2}{4}\right) = \frac{3}{4}E$$. Three-quarters of the energy is kinetic there.

nodes.label: Potential Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$. Stored energy grows quadratically with displacement from equilibrium.

nodes.label: Point Where K Equals U
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Setting $K = U$ gives $$x = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$$. At this point half the energy is kinetic and half potential.

nodes.label: Double-Frequency Energy Oscillation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Both $K$ and $U$ vary as $\sin^2$ or $\cos^2$, so each pulsates at twice the SHM frequency: $$f_{energy} = 2f_{SHM}$$.

nodes.label: Time-Average vs Position-Average Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Time-averaged over a cycle, $$\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle = \frac{E}{2}$$. Position-averaged over the path from $-A$ to $A$ gives a different split, a classic trap.

nodes.label: Spring-Mass Systems
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Spring networks reduce to one equivalent constant. For springs, $$k = \frac{F}{x}$$ and $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{eq}}}$$.

nodes.label: ×8 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: spring mass networks and oscillating systems

nodes.label: Springs in Series
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{k_{eq}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$$. Equivalent constant is smaller, so the period increases.

nodes.label: Series Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two $100\ \text{N/m}$ springs in series give $k_{eq} = 50\ \text{N/m}$. A $2\ \text{kg}$ mass then oscillates with $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{2/50} \approx 1.26\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Springs in Parallel
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2$$. Stiffness adds, shortening the period.

nodes.label: Spring Cutting Rule
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Cutting a spring into $n$ equal parts makes each part $n$ times stiffer: $$k' = nk$$. Shorter springs stretch less for the same force.

nodes.label: Two-Body Oscillator and Reduced Mass
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two masses on a spring oscillate with $$\mu = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}}$$. This collapses the two-body problem to one effective body.

nodes.label: Vertical Spring-Mass SHM
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Gravity only shifts the equilibrium by $$x_0 = \frac{mg}{k}$$. Oscillation about the new equilibrium obeys $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$$, unchanged.

nodes.label: Pendulum Dynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A pendulum is SHM for small angles. The simple pendulum period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$.

nodes.label: Simple Pendulum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For small angular displacement, restoring torque gives $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$. Period grows with length and shrinks with gravity.

nodes.label: Seconds Pendulum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A pendulum with $T = 2\ \text{s}$ needs $$L = \frac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.994\ \text{m}$$. It is the classic seconds pendulum.

nodes.label: Pendulum in Accelerating Frames
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a lift accelerating at $a$, use $g_{eff} = g \pm a$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{eff}}}$$. Free fall ($a = g$) gives infinite period.

nodes.label: Physical (Compound) Pendulum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$$, where $I$ is moment of inertia about the pivot and $d$ is pivot-to-COM distance. It generalizes the simple pendulum.

nodes.label: Torsional Pendulum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{\kappa}}$$, with $\kappa$ the torsional constant of the wire. Used to measure moments of inertia.

nodes.label: Large-Angle Correction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For amplitude $\theta_0$, the period lengthens: $$T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\left(1 + \frac{\theta_0^2}{16}\right)$$. Small-angle formula underestimates $T$.

nodes.label: Pendulum in a Lift
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Downward acceleration $a$ reduces effective gravity: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g - a}}$$. Upward acceleration increases it; $a = g$ downward freezes the pendulum.

nodes.label: Superposition, Damping, Resonance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: SHMs combine by superposition; real oscillators lose energy and respond to driving. Resonance occurs when $$\omega_{drive} = \omega_0$$.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: pendulums physical oscillations superposition and damped resonance

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: pendulums superposition and damped forced resonance

nodes.label: Superposition of Collinear SHMs
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two same-frequency SHMs give a single SHM: $$A' = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$$. Phase difference $\phi$ decides constructive or destructive addition.

nodes.label: Superposition Example
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two equal SHMs $x_1 = A\sin\omega t$, $x_2 = A\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$ add to $$A' = \sqrt{A^2 + A^2} = A\sqrt{2}$$ with phase lead $\pi/4$.

nodes.label: Lissajous Figures
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Perpendicular SHMs trace Lissajous patterns whose shape depends on the frequency ratio and phase. Equal frequencies with $\pi/2$ phase give a circle or ellipse: $$\frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = 1$$.

nodes.label: Damped Harmonic Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$x = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}\cos(\omega' t + \phi), \ \omega' = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \frac{b^2}{4m^2}}$$. Amplitude decays exponentially while frequency drops slightly.

nodes.label: Damping Time Constant
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Amplitude halves when $e^{-bt/2m} = 1/2$, i.e. $$t_{1/2} = \frac{2m\ln 2}{b}$$. Energy falls four times faster.

nodes.label: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A driven oscillator peaks in amplitude when driving frequency matches natural frequency: $$A_{max} \text{ at } \omega = \omega_0$$. Light damping gives a sharp, tall resonance peak.

nodes.label: Resonance Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A swing pushed at its natural frequency $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g/L}$ grows in amplitude even with small pushes. Pushing off-frequency yields small response.

nodes.label: Quality Factor
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$Q = \frac{\omega_0 m}{b}$$ measures sharpness of resonance and energy stored per cycle lost. High $Q$ means light damping and a narrow bandwidth.

nodes.label: Rectilinear Motion Fundamentals
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: One-dimensional motion along a straight line: distance, displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

nodes.label: Distance vs Displacement
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the straight-line vector from initial to final position. The fundamental inequality is $$s \ge |\Delta \vec{r}|$$, with equality only for straight unidirectional motion.

nodes.label: Equality Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Distance equals displacement magnitude if and only if the particle moves along a strictly straight line without ever reversing direction.

nodes.label: Speed and Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average velocity is displacement over time; average speed is total distance over time. Always $$v_{\text{avg, scalar}} \ge |\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}|$$.

nodes.label: Average Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i}{t_f - t_i}$$. Instantaneous velocity is the limit as $$\Delta t \to 0$$: $$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$$.

nodes.label: Mean Speed Theorems
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For equal distance segments, $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$$ (harmonic mean). For equal time intervals, $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$$ (arithmetic mean).

nodes.label: Acceleration and Calculus
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: $$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \frac{d^2\vec{r}}{dt^2}$$. In one dimension, $$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$$ by the chain rule.

nodes.label: Differential Form
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The spatial form $$a = v \frac{dv}{dx}$$ is derived from $$\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}$$. It is essential for position-dependent acceleration problems.

nodes.label: Uniformly Accelerated Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Motion with constant acceleration: the master equations, vertical free fall, and graph calculus.

nodes.label: Equations of Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The three master equations for constant acceleration: $$v = u + at$$, $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = \frac{u+v}{2}t$$, and $$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$.

nodes.label: Displacement in nth Second
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The displacement in the $$n$$-th second is $$s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$$. This is not the total distance in $$n$$ seconds.

nodes.label: Vertical Motion Under Gravity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Taking upward as positive, a body projected up with speed $$u$$ decelerates at $$g$$. Time of ascent equals time of descent: $$t_a = t_d = \frac{u}{g}$$.

nodes.label: Maximum Height
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At maximum height $$v = 0$$, so $$H_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{2g}$$. The body returns to projection level with the same speed $$u$$.

nodes.label: Dual Time Conjugates
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For any height $$h < H_{\max}$$, the two times $$t_1$$ (ascending) and $$t_2$$ (descending) satisfy $$t_1 + t_2 = \frac{2u}{g}$$ and $$t_1 t_2 = \frac{2h}{g}$$.

nodes.label: Kinematics Graphs
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The slope of an $$x$$-t graph gives velocity; the slope of a $$v$$-t graph gives acceleration. The area under a $$v$$-t graph gives signed displacement.

nodes.label: Area Under v-t Graph
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The algebraic area under a $$v$$-t curve yields displacement ($$\Delta x = \int v\,dt$$). For total distance, take the absolute value: $$s = \int |v|\,dt$$.

nodes.label: Area Under a-x Graph
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The area under an acceleration-displacement curve gives $$\int a\,dx = \frac{v_f^2 - v_i^2}{2}$$. This is the work-energy relation per unit mass.

nodes.label: Galileo's Law of Odd Numbers
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a particle starting from rest under uniform acceleration, displacements in consecutive equal time intervals follow the ratio $$s_1 : s_2 : s_3 : \dots = 1 : 3 : 5 : \dots : (2n-1)$$.

nodes.label: Stopping Distance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Total stopping distance combines reaction distance and braking distance: $$D_{\text{stop}} = u t_r + \frac{u^2}{2a}$$. Reaction distance scales linearly with speed; braking distance scales quadratically.

nodes.label: Projectile Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two-dimensional motion under uniform gravity: independence of horizontal and vertical components, flight parameters, and trajectory geometry.

nodes.label: Independence of Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A projectile's horizontal motion is uniform ($$v_x = u\cos\theta = \text{const}$$) and vertical motion is uniformly accelerated ($$a_y = -g$$). The two components are completely independent.

nodes.label: Flight Parameters
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Time of flight, maximum height, and range are the three canonical flight parameters for ground-to-ground projectiles.

nodes.label: Time of Flight
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Setting $$y = 0$$ gives $$T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$$. Time of ascent equals time of descent: $$t_a = t_d = \frac{T}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Height and Range
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Maximum height is $$H_{\max} = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$$ and horizontal range is $$R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$$. The geometric link is $$\tan\theta = \frac{4H_{\max}}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Maximum Range
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For fixed $$u$$, range is maximized at $$\theta = 45^\circ$$ giving $$R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$$. The height at maximum range is $$H = \frac{u^2}{4g}$$.

nodes.label: Equation of Trajectory
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Eliminating time from the kinematic equations yields the parabolic trajectory $$y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$$.

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: trajectory equations elevated projections and curvature

nodes.label: Factorized Range Form
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The trajectory can be rewritten as $$y = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)$$. This form is ideal for clearance problems over walls and obstacles.

nodes.label: Complementary Angles
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two projectiles launched at the same speed $$u$$ at angles $$\theta$$ and $$90^\circ - \theta$$ have identical ranges: $$R(\theta) = R(90^\circ - \theta)$$.

nodes.label: ×5 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: oblique projectile kinematics and complementary angles

nodes.label: Inter-Trajectory Relations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For complementary angles, $$T_1 T_2 = \frac{2R}{g}$$ and $$R = 4\sqrt{H_1 H_2}$$. Also $$H_1 + H_2 = \frac{u^2}{2g}$$ and $$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \tan\theta$$.

nodes.label: Radius of Curvature
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The radius of curvature at any point on the trajectory is $$\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$$ where $$a_\perp$$ is the normal component of acceleration.

nodes.label: Curvature at Peak
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At the topmost point, $$v = u\cos\theta$$ and $$a_\perp = g$$, so $$\rho_{\text{top}} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$$. This is the global minimum radius of curvature.

nodes.label: Inclined Plane Ballistics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On an incline of angle $$\beta$$, choose axes along and perpendicular to the incline. The launch angle $$\alpha$$ is measured relative to the incline surface.

nodes.label: Optimal Launch Angles
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Maximum range up the incline occurs at $$\alpha = 45^\circ - \frac{\beta}{2}$$ giving $$R_{\text{up,max}} = \frac{u^2}{g(1+\sin\beta)}$$. Down the incline, $$\alpha = 45^\circ + \frac{\beta}{2}$$ gives $$R_{\text{down,max}} = \frac{u^2}{g(1-\sin\beta)}$$.

nodes.label: Relative Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Frame transformations, closest approach geometry, and classic 2D relative motion problems.

nodes.label: Frame Transformations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Relative position, velocity, and acceleration follow vector subtraction: $$\vec{r}_{B/A} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$$, $$\vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A$$, $$\vec{a}_{B/A} = \vec{a}_B - \vec{a}_A$$.

nodes.label: Two-Projectile Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two projectiles in flight under gravity have $$\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{g} - \vec{g} = 0$$. Their relative motion is uniform straight-line at constant velocity $$\vec{v}_{2/1} = \vec{u}_2 - \vec{u}_1$$.

nodes.label: Closest Approach
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The velocity of approach is $$v_{\text{app}} = -\frac{dr}{dt}$$. At closest approach, $$v_{\text{app}} = 0$$ and the relative velocity is perpendicular to the line of sight.

nodes.label: Closest Approach Geometry
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For initial separation $$r_0$$ and relative velocity at angle $$\theta$$ to the line of sight, $$d_{\min} = r_0\sin\theta$$ and $$t_{\min} = \frac{r_0\cos\theta}{|\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}|}$$.

nodes.label: River-Boat Crossing
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A boat crosses a river of width $$d$$ with current speed $$v_r$$ and boat speed $$u$$ relative to water. Shortest time and shortest path are different strategies.

nodes.label: Shortest Time
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Steer perpendicular to the bank ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$): $$t_{\min} = \frac{d}{u}$$. The downstream drift is $$x = \frac{v_r d}{u}$$. Crossing time is independent of river speed.

nodes.label: Zero Drift
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: To land directly opposite, steer upstream with $$\sin\alpha = \frac{v_r}{u}$$ (requires $$u > v_r$$). The crossing time is $$t = \frac{d}{\sqrt{u^2 - v_r^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Drift When Slower
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When $$u < v_r$$, zero drift is impossible. The minimum drift is $$x_{\min} = d\sqrt{\frac{v_r^2}{u^2} - 1}$$ achieved at $$\sin\alpha = \frac{u}{v_r}$$.

nodes.label: Rain-Man Problem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Rain falls with velocity $$\vec{v}_r$$ and a person moves with velocity $$\vec{v}_m$$. The apparent rain velocity is $$\vec{v}_{r/m} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_m$$.

nodes.label: Umbrella Tilt
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: To stay dry, hold the umbrella opposite to the apparent rain direction. The tilt angle from vertical is $$\tan\theta = \frac{|v_{rx} + v_m|}{v_{ry}}$$. For vertical rain, $$\tan\theta = \frac{v_m}{v_r}$$.

nodes.label: Polygon Pursuit
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$N$$ particles at the vertices of a regular $$N$$-gon each move toward their cyclic neighbor at speed $$v$$. They spiral into the center.

nodes.label: Pursuit Time
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The approach speed is $$v_{\text{app}} = v[1 - \cos(2\pi/N)]$$, so the meeting time is $$t_{\text{meet}} = \frac{d}{v[1 - \cos(2\pi/N)]}$$. For a triangle, $$t = \frac{2d}{3v}$$; for a square, $$t = \frac{d}{v}$$.

nodes.label: Circular Kinematics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Angular variables, linear-angular relations, and acceleration decomposition in circular motion.

nodes.label: ×3 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: circular kinematics radius of curvature and acceleration vectors

nodes.label: Angular Variables
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Angular velocity is $$\vec{\omega} = \frac{d\vec{\theta}}{dt}$$ and angular acceleration is $$\vec{\alpha} = \frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt}$$. Infinitesimal angular displacement is a vector; finite angular displacement is not.

nodes.label: Linear-Angular Relations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Linear velocity is $$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$$ with magnitude $$v = \omega r$$. The total acceleration is $$\vec{a} = \vec{a}_t + \vec{a}_c$$.

nodes.label: Centripetal Acceleration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The radial component is $$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = v\omega$$, directed inward. It changes only the direction of velocity, not the speed.

nodes.label: Tangential Acceleration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The tangential component is $$a_t = \frac{dv}{dt} = \alpha r$$. It changes only the speed, not the direction. Net acceleration: $$a_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$.

nodes.label: Relative Angular Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The angular velocity of $$B$$ relative to $$A$$ is $$\omega_{B/A} = \frac{v_{B/A,\perp}}{r_{AB}}$$. A particle on a circle has half the angular speed about a point on the circumference compared to the center.

nodes.label: Uniform Circular Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In UCM, speed is constant: $$a_t = 0$$ and $$a_{\text{net}} = a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$. The acceleration is always perpendicular to velocity.

nodes.label: Non-Uniform Circular Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In NUCM, speed varies: $$a_t \ne 0$$ and $$a_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$. The angle between net acceleration and tangent is $$\tan\psi = \frac{a_c}{a_t}$$.

nodes.label: Finite Angular Displacement
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Finite angular displacement does not obey the commutative law: $$\Delta\theta_1 + \Delta\theta_2 \ne \Delta\theta_2 + \Delta\theta_1$$. Only infinitesimal angular displacement is a true vector.

nodes.label: Dynamics of Circular Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Centripetal force is the net real force along the inward normal. It is not an additional force.

nodes.label: Centripetal Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The required centripetal force is $$F_c = ma_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$$. It must be supplied by real forces: tension, gravity, normal reaction, friction, or electrostatic attraction.

nodes.label: Centrifugal Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In a rotating frame, the pseudo force is $$\vec{F}_{\text{cf}} = m\omega^2\vec{r}$$ directed radially outward. It exists only in non-inertial frames and has no reaction partner.

nodes.label: Conical Pendulum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A bob on a string of length $$L$$ rotating at angle $$\theta$$: $$T\cos\theta = mg$$ and $$T\sin\theta = m\omega^2 L\sin\theta$$. The angular speed is $$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L\cos\theta}} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{h}}$$.

nodes.label: Conical Pendulum Period
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The period is $$T_p = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L\cos\theta}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$$ where $$h = L\cos\theta$$. String tension is $$T = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$$.

nodes.label: Centripetal Force Misconception
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Centripetal force is not an extra force in the FBD. It is the name for the net real force along the radial direction: $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{radial}} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Vehicle Turning and Banking
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Turning on flat and banked roads, overturning, and rotor mechanics.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: horizontal circular dynamics turntable slipping and road banking

nodes.label: Unbanked Road
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On a flat curve, friction supplies the centripetal force: $$\frac{mv^2}{r} \le \mu_s mg$$. The maximum speed is $$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s rg}$$.

nodes.label: Cyclist Leaning
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A cyclist leans inward at angle $$\theta$$ with the vertical: $$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} \le \mu_s$$.

nodes.label: Frictionless Banked Road
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On a banked road at angle $$\theta$$ with no friction: $$N\sin\theta = \frac{mv_0^2}{r}$$ and $$N\cos\theta = mg$$. The rated speed is $$v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$$.

nodes.label: Rough Banked Road
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With friction on a banked road, the safe speed window is $$v_{\min} = \sqrt{rg\tan(\theta - \lambda)}$$ to $$v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg\tan(\theta + \lambda)}$$ where $$\lambda = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$$.

nodes.label: Parking on Bank
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If $$\tan\theta \le \mu_s$$, a car can park stationary on the bank without sliding down, so $$v_{\min} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Overturning of Vehicles
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a four-wheeler with track width $$d$$ and COM height $$h$$: the overturning speed is $$v_{\text{overturn}} = \sqrt{\frac{grd}{2h}}$$. Skidding occurs first if $$\mu_s < \frac{d}{2h}$$.

nodes.label: Skidding vs Overturning
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A vehicle skids before overturning if $$\mu_s < \frac{d}{2h}$$. It overturns before skidding if $$\mu_s > \frac{d}{2h}$$.

nodes.label: Rotor (Death Well)
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A rider inside a vertical cylinder of radius $$R$$: normal reaction provides centripetal force and friction balances gravity. The minimum angular speed is $$\omega_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\mu_s R}}$$.

nodes.label: Rotor Minimum Speed
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The minimum linear speed in a rotor is $$v_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{gR}{\mu_s}}$$.

nodes.label: Banking Angle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The banking angle is designed so that at the rated speed, no lateral friction is needed: $$\tan\theta = \frac{v_0^2}{rg}$$. This prevents tyre wear.

nodes.label: Vertical Circular Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: String and rod vertical loops, critical speeds, and detachment from spherical surfaces.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: vertical circular motion and energy conservation

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: vertical circular motion tension invariants and looping limits

nodes.label: String Vertical Loop
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a particle on a string of length $$R$$: tension at angle $$\theta$$ from the bottom is $$T(\theta) = \frac{mv^2}{R} + mg\cos\theta$$. Energy conservation gives $$v^2 = u^2 - 2gR(1-\cos\theta)$$.

nodes.label: Tension Difference Invariant
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The tension difference between bottom and top is universal: $$T_L - T_T = 6mg$$, independent of launch speed.

nodes.label: Critical Looping Triad
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a string: $$v_L \ge \sqrt{5gR}$$ at the bottom, $$v_M \ge \sqrt{3gR}$$ at horizontal, $$v_T \ge \sqrt{gR}$$ at the top. Critical bottom tension is $$T_L = 6mg$$.

nodes.label: Three Motion Regimes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Based on launch speed $$u$$: oscillation ($$u \le \sqrt{2gR}$$), slacking with projectile flight ($$\sqrt{2gR} < u < \sqrt{5gR}$$), and complete loop ($$u \ge \sqrt{5gR}$$).

nodes.label: Oscillation Regime
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $$0 < u \le \sqrt{2gR}$$: velocity vanishes at $$\theta \le 90^\circ$$ where $$T = mg\cos\theta > 0$$. The body oscillates like a simple pendulum.

nodes.label: Slacking Regime
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $$\sqrt{2gR} < u < \sqrt{5gR}$$: tension vanishes in the upper semicircle while velocity is still non-zero. The particle leaves the circle and follows a parabola.

nodes.label: Complete Loop Regime
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For $$u \ge \sqrt{5gR}$$: tension remains strictly positive throughout the entire circle. The body completes full circular revolution.

nodes.label: Rigid Rod Vertical Loop
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A rigid rod can support compression, so it cannot slack. The looping condition is only $$v_T \ge 0$$, giving $$v_L \ge \sqrt{4gR} = 2\sqrt{gR}$$.

nodes.label: Rod Critical Triad
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a rigid rod: $$v_L \ge 2\sqrt{gR}$$ at the bottom, $$v_M \ge \sqrt{2gR}$$ at horizontal, $$v_T \ge 0$$ at the top.

nodes.label: Detachment from Sphere
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A particle sliding from the top of a smooth sphere of radius $$R$$: $$N = mg(3\cos\theta - 2)$$. Detachment occurs at $$\cos\theta = \frac{2}{3}$$, so $$h = \frac{R}{3}$$ and $$v_{\text{detach}} = \sqrt{\frac{2gR}{3}}$$.

nodes.label: String Slacking
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When tension reaches zero before velocity, the string slacks and the particle enters parabolic projectile motion. This occurs in the upper semicircle for $$\sqrt{2gR} < u < \sqrt{5gR}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Conservation in VCM
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Mechanical energy is conserved in vertical circular motion: $$\frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgR(1-\cos\theta)$$. This relates speed at any point to the launch speed.

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — Fundamentals of Mechanical Work: Calculus & Frame Dynamics
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — The Universal Work-Energy Theorem & Conservation Laws
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — Potential Energy Curves $U(x)$ & Equilibrium Stability
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — Mechanical Power Formulations & Constant Power Kinematics
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — Advanced Energy Applications: Chains & Conveyor Systems
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Work Power and Energy — Master Formula Sheet & High-Yield Diagnostic Traps
nodes.subject: physics

nodes.label: Mechanical Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement. It can be positive, negative, or zero depending on the angle between force and displacement.

nodes.label: Work by Constant Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a constant force, $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s} = Fs\cos\theta$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle between force and displacement. The SI unit is the joule: $$[W] = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$$.

nodes.label: Dimensions and Units
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Work has dimensions $$[M L^2 T^{-2}]$$. $$1\text{ J} = 10^7\text{ erg}$$. The CGS unit of work is the erg.

nodes.label: Work by Variable Force
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a variable force along a path $$C$$: $$W = \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int F_x\,dx + \int F_y\,dy + \int F_z\,dz$$.

nodes.label: ×4 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: mechanical work variable forces and cable potential energy

nodes.label: Area Under F-x Curve
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The work done by a 1D variable force equals the signed area between the $$F$$-$$x$$ curve and the displacement axis: $$W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$$.

nodes.label: Sign of Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Positive work ($$0 \le \theta < 90^\circ$$) transfers energy into the body. Negative work ($$90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$$) extracts energy. Zero work occurs when $$\theta = 90^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Zero Work Cases
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Zero work occurs when force is perpendicular to displacement: centripetal force in circular motion, magnetic Lorentz force $$q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$$, and normal reaction on a fixed surface.

nodes.label: Work by Canonical Forces
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Gravity, spring force, and internal tension have standard work formulas that appear repeatedly in JEE problems.

nodes.label: Gravitational Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Near Earth's surface, $$W_g = -mg\Delta y = mg(y_i - y_f)$$. Gravitational work depends only on initial and final vertical coordinates, not on the path taken.

nodes.label: Spring Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For an ideal spring, $$W_s = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2) = -\Delta U_s$$. The work done by a spring equals the negative change in spring potential energy.

nodes.label: Internal Tension Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For an ideal string connecting multiple masses, internal tension transfers energy without net work: $$\sum W_T = \sum \vec{T} \cdot d\vec{s} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Friction and Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Static friction does zero net work on a system; kinetic friction always dissipates mechanical energy as heat.

nodes.label: Static Friction Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Static friction can do positive, negative, or zero work on an individual body. But across the entire interacting system, the net work is identically zero: $$\sum W_{f_s} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Static Friction Work Cases
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A crate accelerating in a truck bed: static friction does positive work. A person walking: the contact foot has zero displacement, so $$W_{f_s} = 0$$. Static friction never dissipates energy.

nodes.label: Kinetic Friction Dissipation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: When two bodies slide with relative displacement $$s_{\text{rel}}$$, the net work of kinetic friction is strictly negative: $$\sum W_{f_k} = -f_k s_{\text{rel}} < 0$$.

nodes.label: Heat Generation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The lost mechanical energy becomes thermal energy: $$Q_{\text{heat}} = f_k s_{\text{rel}}$$. This dissipation is irreversible and independent of the friction coefficient.

nodes.label: Frame Dependence of Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Work is frame-dependent because displacement changes: $$W' = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}' \ne W$$. However, the work-energy theorem $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$$ holds in every inertial frame.

nodes.label: Work-Energy Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy. This is the cornerstone of energy methods in mechanics.

nodes.label: Work-Energy Theorem
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The net work equals the change in kinetic energy: $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$$.

nodes.label: WET Derivation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: From $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$$: $$W_{\text{net}} = \int m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} \cdot \vec{v}\,dt = \int m\vec{v} \cdot d\vec{v} = \left[\frac{1}{2}mv^2\right]_{v_i}^{v_f}$$.

nodes.label: Force Partitioning
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Partitioning work into conservative, non-conservative, and external parts: $$W_C + W_{\text{NC}} + W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta K$$. Since $$W_C = -\Delta U$$, this gives $$W_{\text{NC}} + W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta E_{\text{mech}}$$.

nodes.label: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If only conservative forces do work, mechanical energy is conserved: $$\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = 0 \iff K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f = \text{constant}$$.

nodes.label: Conservative Fields
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A force field is conservative if its work is path-independent or equivalently if it can be derived from a scalar potential.

nodes.label: Curl Condition
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A force field is conservative if and only if $$\vec{\nabla} \times \vec{F} = \vec{0}$$. This is the irrotational condition.

nodes.label: Force from Potential
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A conservative force is the negative gradient of potential energy: $$\vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla}U = -\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Potential Energy Curves
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The $$U(x)$$ curve reveals force, equilibrium stability, and allowed regions of motion.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: work energy theorem spring systems and potential energy curves

nodes.label: Force-Potential Gradient
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In one dimension, $$F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$$. The force points toward decreasing potential energy.

nodes.label: Equilibrium Stability
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Equilibrium occurs where $$\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$$. The second derivative determines stability.

nodes.label: Stable Equilibrium
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At a local minimum ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$$), the force is restoring. The particle executes SHM with $$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Unstable Equilibrium
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At a local maximum ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$$), the force reinforces displacement. The particle accelerates away from equilibrium.

nodes.label: Neutral Equilibrium
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On a flat plateau ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 0$$), the force remains zero. The particle stays at rest in its new position.

nodes.label: Classical Turning Points
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Since $$K(x) = E - U(x) \ge 0$$, motion is confined to $$U(x) \le E$$. Turning points occur where $$U(x_t) = E$$ and the particle reverses direction.

nodes.label: Allowed and Forbidden Regions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The allowed region is where $$U(x) \le E$$. Regions where $$U(x) > E$$ would require negative kinetic energy and are classically forbidden.

nodes.label: Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Power is the rate of doing work. Constant power motion has distinctive kinematic scaling laws.

nodes.label: Instantaneous Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Instantaneous power is $$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = Fv\cos\theta$$. Net power equals the rate of change of kinetic energy: $$P_{\text{net}} = \frac{dK}{dt}$$.

nodes.label: Average Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Average power is $$P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t} = \frac{W_{\text{total}}}{\Delta t}$$.

nodes.label: Motion Under Constant Power
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An engine delivering constant power $$P$$ to a vehicle of mass $$m$$ from rest produces characteristic scaling laws.

nodes.label: ×2 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: power dynamics constant power scaling and conveyor belts

nodes.label: Velocity Scaling
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: From $$P = mv\frac{dv}{dt}$$: $$v(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}}\,t^{1/2} \propto t^{1/2}$$.

nodes.label: Displacement Scaling
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Integrating velocity: $$x(t) = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}}\,t^{3/2} \propto t^{3/2}$$. Acceleration decreases as $$a = \frac{P}{mv} \propto t^{-1/2}$$.

nodes.label: Advanced Applications
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Hanging chain work and conveyor belt mechanics involve continuous mass redistribution and energy dissipation.

nodes.label: Hanging Chain Work
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a uniform chain of mass $$M$$ and length $$L$$ with fraction $$1/n$$ hanging, the work to pull it up is $$W = \frac{MgL}{2n^2}$$. This uses the center of mass of the hanging segment.

nodes.label: Conveyor Belt 50% Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Sand falling on a conveyor belt moving at speed $$v$$: motor power is $$P_{\text{motor}} = v^2\frac{dm}{dt}$$. Exactly 50% becomes kinetic energy; 50% is dissipated as heat.

nodes.label: Heat and Calorimetry
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Heat is energy in transit; calorimetry measures it. The working relation is $$Q = mc\Delta T$$ for a temperature change without phase change.

nodes.label: Mechanical Equivalent of Heat
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Joule's paddle-wheel experiment fixed the conversion between work and heat: $$W = JQ, \ J = 4.2\ \text{J}/\text{cal}$$. It unified mechanical and thermal energy.

nodes.label: Specific Heat Capacity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Heat needed to raise unit mass by one degree: $$Q = mc\Delta T$$. Water's high specific heat $c = 4186\ \text{J}/\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}$ makes it a thermal buffer in nature and exam tricks.

nodes.label: Thermal Capacity and Molar Heat
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Thermal capacity of a body is $C = mc$, and molar heat capacity is $$C_m = \frac{Q}{n\Delta T}$$. The solid-liquid distinction appears when comparing $C_V$ and $C_P$ for gases.

nodes.label: Principle of Calorimetry
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In an isolated system the heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies: $$\sum Q_{\text{lost}} = \sum Q_{\text{gained}}$$. Mixing problems are solved by this single balance equation.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: specific heat latent heat and principle of calorimetry

nodes.label: Water Equivalent of Calorimeter
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A calorimeter absorbs heat like an equivalent mass of water: $$(m_1c_1 + W)\Delta T_1 = m_2c_2\Delta T_2$$. Omitting water equivalent is the most common JEE calorimetry error.

nodes.label: Calorimetry Mixing Algorithm
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For a hot body in cold water: $$m_h c_h (T_h - T_f) = m_c c_c (T_f - T_c)$$. Solve iteratively when ice is present by first checking whether all ice melts.

nodes.label: Ice-Water Mixture Check
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Before mixing, compare heat needed to melt all ice, $$Q_{melt} = m_{ice}L_f$$, with heat available from cooling water. The comparison decides whether the final state is all-liquid or a mixture at $0^\circ\text{C}$.

nodes.label: Change of State
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Phase changes absorb latent heat at constant temperature: $$Q = mL$$, where $L$ is the latent heat of fusion or vaporisation.

nodes.label: Latent Heat
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Latent heat of fusion for ice is about $3.34 \times 10^5\ \text{J}/\text{kg}$: $$Q = mL_f$$. During $L_f$ transfer the temperature stays pinned at $0^\circ\text{C}$.

nodes.label: Heating Curve Analysis
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: On a temperature vs heat graph, sloped parts follow $Q = mc\Delta T$ and flat plateaus follow $Q = mL$. The slope inverts between solid, liquid, and gas because the $c$ values differ.

nodes.label: Regelation and Melting Point
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Pressure lowers the melting point of ice (anomalous), enabling regelation: $$\frac{dT}{dP} = \frac{T(V_l - V_s)}{L}$$. The negative sign of $V_l - V_s$ for ice is the entire physics.

nodes.label: Sublimation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Solids passing directly to vapour absorb latent heat of sublimation: $$Q = mL_s, \ L_s = L_f + L_v$$. Dry ice and camphor are textbook cases.

nodes.label: Triple Point of Water
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The unique $(T, P)$ where solid, liquid, and vapour coexist: $$T = 273.16\ \text{K}, \ P = 611.657\ \text{Pa}$$. It defines the kelvin.

nodes.label: Thermal Expansion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Solids, liquids, and gases expand on heating; linear expansion is $$\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$$.

nodes.label: Linear Expansion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Fractional length change is linear in temperature: $$\frac{\Delta L}{L_0} = \alpha \Delta T$$. The coefficient $\alpha$ differs by material and sets bimetallic behavior.

nodes.label: Superficial and Volumetric Expansion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For isotropic solids, area and volume coefficients relate as $$\beta \approx 2\alpha, \ \gamma \approx 3\alpha$$. Liquids are quoted by $\gamma$ since only volume matters.

nodes.label: ×9 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: linear superficial and cubical thermal expansion

nodes.label: Bimetallic Strip
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two bonded strips bend toward the lower-$\alpha$ side on heating: $$\Delta L_{rel} = (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1)L_0\Delta T$$. This differential expansion drives thermostat switches.

nodes.label: Thermal Stress in Clamped Rods
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A rod prevented from expanding develops compressive stress: $$\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$$, with force $F = YA\alpha\Delta T$. It is why bridges have expansion joints.

nodes.label: Anomalous Expansion of Water
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Water contracts from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $4^\circ\text{C}$ and is densest at $4^\circ\text{C}$. Density variation follows $$\rho(T) \approx \rho_0[1 - \gamma (T - 4)]$$ in that window.

nodes.label: Real vs Apparent Expansion of Liquids
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A liquid in a vessel expands apparently because the vessel expands too: $$\gamma_{real} = \gamma_{app} + \gamma_{vessel}$$. Overflow method problems use exactly this bookkeeping.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: liquid apparent expansion pendulum clocks and buoyancy

nodes.label: Density Variation with Temperature
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\rho_T = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} \approx \rho_0(1 - \gamma \Delta T)$$. Mass is conserved during thermal expansion, so density falls.

nodes.label: Laws of Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: The laws define temperature, constrain energy conversion, and forbid perfect engines. The first law is an energy ledger: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$.

nodes.label: Zeroth Law and Temperature
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and C are at equal temperature: symmetry and transitivity of equilibrium. Temperature is the only state function this defines.

nodes.label: First Law of Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$, with $W$ the work done by the gas and $\Delta U$ depending only on endpoints: $$W = \int P\,dV$$. Sign conventions flip $W$ in chemistry texts.

nodes.label: Internal Energy of an Ideal Gas
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Internal energy is kinetic only, hence temperature-only for an ideal gas: $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$$. This is why isothermal ideal-gas processes have $\Delta U = 0$.

nodes.label: Second Law Statements
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Kelvin-Planck: no engine converts heat from a single reservoir fully into work. Clausius: heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot. Both imply entropy increases: $$\Delta S_{univ} \ge 0$$.

nodes.label: Thermodynamic Processes
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Each canonical process pins one variable or constraint, simplifying the first law. For a polytropic change $$PV^x = \text{constant}$$.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: first law thermodynamic processes and polytropic gas expansions

nodes.label: Isochoric Process
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Constant volume gives $W = 0$, so all heat changes internal energy: $$Q = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$$. On a P-V diagram it is a vertical line.

nodes.label: Isobaric Process
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: At constant pressure, work is $$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$$ and heat absorbed is $$Q = nC_P\Delta T$$. The gap $C_P - C_V = R$ measures expansion work.

nodes.label: Isothermal Process
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: For an ideal gas at constant $T$, $\Delta U = 0$ and $$W = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$. The P-V curve is a rectangular hyperbola $PV = $ const.

nodes.label: Adiabatic Process
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: With $Q = 0$, the gas obeys $$PV^\gamma = \text{constant}, \ T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$$ and $W = \frac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$. Compression heats the gas rapidly.

nodes.label: Free Expansion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: An ideal gas expanding into vacuum does no work and exchanges no heat, so $$\Delta U = 0, \ \Delta T = 0$$. Entropy still rises: $$\Delta S = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$.

nodes.label: Work on P-V, V-T, P-T Diagrams
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Work equals the enclosed area in a cyclic process: $$W_{cycle} = \oint P\,dV$$. Clockwise cycles output positive net work.

nodes.label: Role of Gamma in Adiabatics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Steeper adiabats on a P-V plot follow $$P \propto V^{-\gamma}$$ with $\gamma > 1$. The isotherm is $PV = \text{const}$, noticeably flatter.

nodes.label: Heat Engines and Entropy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Engines convert heat between reservoirs with bounded efficiency. Carnot sets the ceiling: $$\eta_{max} = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: cyclic processes heat engines and carnot refrigerators

nodes.label: Heat Engine Efficiency
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Efficiency is work output over heat input: $$\eta = \frac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$$. Real engines underperform Carnot because of friction and finite-rate heat flow.

nodes.label: Carnot Cycle
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Two isotherms and two adiabatics give the reversible benchmark: $$\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$. Kelvin temperatures must be used, so $T_2 < T_1$ always.

nodes.label: Entropy and Clausius Inequality
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Entropy change for a reversible path is $$\Delta S = \int \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T}$$, and for any cycle $$\oint \frac{dQ}{T} \le 0$$. Free expansion of a gas creates entropy with no heat transfer at all.

nodes.label: Refrigerator and Heat Pump
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: A reversed engine moves heat from cold to hot using work: $$K_{fridge} = \frac{Q_2}{W} = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2}$$. Heat pump COP exceeds 1 because it delivers $Q_1 = Q_2 + W$.

nodes.label: Heat Transfer
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Heat moves by conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction through a slab follows Fourier's law: $$\frac{dQ}{dt} = -kA\frac{dT}{dx}$$.

nodes.label: Conduction and Thermal Resistance
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: In series, resistances add; in parallel, conductances add: $$R_{th} = \frac{x}{kA}, \ R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2$$. Composite-wall JEE problems are resistor problems in disguise.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: thermal conduction resistance networks and ice formation

nodes.label: Newton's Law of Cooling
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Cooling rate is proportional to the excess temperature: $$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0)$$. Integrating gives exponential approach to ambient.

nodes.label: ×10 questions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.pattern: newtons law of cooling and calorimetric heat loss

nodes.label: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.note: Radiated power scales as the fourth power of absolute temperature: $$P = \sigma e A T^4, \ \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W}/\text{m}^2\text{K}^4$$. Net exchange uses $T^4 - T_0^4$.
