nodes.label: Expansion for Positive Integral Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For a positive integer $$n$$ the expansion of $$(a + b)^n$$ has exactly $$n + 1$$ terms in which the powers of $$a$$ fall and the powers of $$b$$ rise, always summing to $$n$$. The compact form is $$(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$.

nodes.label: Theorem Statement and General Term
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The theorem states $$(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$ and the $$(r+1)$$-th term from the beginning is $$T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$. The subscript $$r$$ is always one less than the term position, a detail that drives most indexing questions.

nodes.label: General Term
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$, so to find the term containing a particular power one solves for $$r$$ from the exponent of $$a$$ or $$b$$. The coefficient of that term is the binomial coefficient $$\binom{n}{r}$$ times any numerical factors carried by $$a$$ and $$b$$.

nodes.label: Number of Terms and Homogeneity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The expansion of $$(a + b)^n$$ has exactly $$n + 1$$ terms, one more than the index, and in every term the exponents of $$a$$ and $$b$$ add up to $$n$$. This homogeneity $$(n - r) + r = n$$ is the quickest check that an expansion has been written correctly.

nodes.label: Canonical Form with Unity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Setting $$a = 1$$ and $$b = x$$ gives the canonical expansion $$(1 + x)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} x^r = C_0 + C_1 x + C_2 x^2 + \dots + C_n x^n$$ where $$C_r = \binom{n}{r}$$. Almost every coefficient-series identity is derived from this single form by substituting values of $$x$$.

nodes.label: Middle Term Analytics
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The location of the middle term depends on the parity of $$n$$: an even index gives one middle term and an odd index gives two. This is because the total number of terms $$n + 1$$ is odd for even $$n$$ and even for odd $$n$$.

nodes.label: Middle Term for Even Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $$n$$ is even there is a unique middle term, the $$\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)$$-th term, equal to $$T_{\frac{n}{2} + 1} = \binom{n}{n/2} a^{n/2} b^{n/2}$$. Its coefficient $$\binom{n}{n/2}$$ is the largest binomial coefficient in the whole expansion.

nodes.label: Middle Terms for Odd Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $$n$$ is odd there are two middle terms, the $$\frac{n+1}{2}$$-th and the $$\frac{n+3}{2}$$-th, given by $$T_{\frac{n+1}{2}} = \binom{n}{\frac{n-1}{2}} a^{\frac{n+1}{2}} b^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$$ and $$T_{\frac{n+3}{2}} = \binom{n}{\frac{n+1}{2}} a^{\frac{n-1}{2}} b^{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$. The two coefficients $$\binom{n}{\frac{n-1}{2}}$$ and $$\binom{n}{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$ are equal and are the largest in the expansion.

nodes.label: Greatest Binomial Coefficient
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The binomial coefficients rise to the middle and then fall symmetrically, so the greatest is $$\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$$. For even $$n$$ this is the single central coefficient and for odd $$n$$ the two central coefficients are equal and greatest.

nodes.label: Term from the End
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The $$r$$-th term from the end of $$(a + b)^n$$ equals the $$r$$-th term from the beginning of $$(b + a)^n$$, that is $$T_r^{\text{end}} = T_{n-r+2}^{\text{beg}} = \binom{n}{r-1} a^{r-1} b^{n-r+1}$$. This reversal identity converts end-counting into the familiar beginning index.

nodes.label: Sum and Difference of Conjugate Expansions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Adding and subtracting the conjugate expansions gives $$(a + b)^n + (a - b)^n = 2\left[\binom{n}{0} a^n + \binom{n}{2} a^{n-2} b^2 + \dots\right]$$ and $$(a + b)^n - (a - b)^n = 2\left[\binom{n}{1} a^{n-1} b + \binom{n}{3} a^{n-3} b^3 + \dots\right]$$. The first isolates even-index terms and the second isolates odd-index terms.

nodes.label: Numerically Greatest Term
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The numerically greatest term of $$(a + b)^n$$ for given numerical values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ is found by a ratio test on consecutive terms. It differs from the greatest binomial coefficient because it depends on the actual magnitudes of $$a$$ and $$b$$.

nodes.label: Ratio Test on Consecutive Terms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The ratio of consecutive terms is $$\left| \frac{T_{r+1}}{T_r} \right| = \frac{n - r + 1}{r} \left| \frac{b}{a} \right|$$, and the terms increase while this ratio is at least one. Solving the inequality $$(n - r + 1)|b| \ge r|a|$$ localizes the peak term.

nodes.label: The NGT Parameter m
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The critical parameter is $$m = \frac{(n+1)|b|}{|a| + |b|} = \frac{n + 1}{1 + \left| \frac{a}{b} \right|}$$, and the terms increase up to $$r = m$$. Whether $$m$$ is an integer decides between two equal greatest terms and a single greatest term.

nodes.label: Integer m Gives Twin NGTs
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $$m$$ is an integer the ratio equals one at $$r = m$$, so $$|T_m| = |T_{m+1}|$$ and there are two numerically greatest terms, $$T_m$$ and $$T_{m+1}$$. The two terms have identical magnitude and both qualify as the NGT.

nodes.label: Non-Integer m Gives a Unique NGT
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $$m$$ is not an integer the terms increase strictly up to $$r = \lfloor m \rfloor$$ and decrease thereafter, giving a single numerically greatest term $$T_{\lfloor m \rfloor + 1}$$. The floor of $$m$$ therefore pins the unique peak term.

nodes.label: Greatest Coefficient versus NGT
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The greatest binomial coefficient depends only on $$n$$ and always sits at the middle term, whereas the numerically greatest term depends on the values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ through $$m = \frac{(n+1)|b|}{|a| + |b|}$$. Confusing the two is the classic JEE trap: one is purely combinatorial and the other is numerical.

nodes.label: Binomial Coefficient Series
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Substituting special values of $$x$$ into $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$, and differentiating or integrating it, yields a family of coefficient identities. These are the standard tools for summing series built from $$C_r = \binom{n}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Sum of Coefficients
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Setting $$x = 1$$ in the canonical expansion gives $$C_0 + C_1 + C_2 + \dots + C_n = 2^n$$, and setting $$x = -1$$ gives the alternating sum $$C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - \dots + (-1)^n C_n = 0$$. Adding and subtracting these two equations separates the even and odd indexed coefficients.

nodes.label: Even and Odd Indexed Sums
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: From the two substitutions one obtains $$C_0 + C_2 + C_4 + \dots = C_1 + C_3 + C_5 + \dots = 2^{n-1}$$, so the even-indexed and odd-indexed binomial coefficients each sum to half of $$2^n$$. This equal split is a favourite one-line JEE result.

nodes.label: Alternating Sum of Coefficients
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The alternating sum $$C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - C_3 + \dots + (-1)^n C_n = 0$$ follows directly from substituting $$x = -1$$ into $$(1 + x)^n$$. It shows the positive and negative binomial coefficients cancel exactly for every positive index $$n$$.

nodes.label: Differentiation Method
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Differentiating $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$ with respect to $$x$$ and then setting $$x = 1$$ gives $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r \binom{n}{r} = n \cdot 2^{n-1}$$. The method works whenever the coefficient is multiplied by an arithmetic factor like $$r$$ or $$r^2$$.

nodes.label: Second Derivative Identity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Multiplying the first derivative by $$x$$ and differentiating again, then setting $$x = 1$$, gives $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^2 \binom{n}{r} = n(n+1) \cdot 2^{n-2}$$. The same double-differentiation trick extends to any polynomial weight in $$r$$.

nodes.label: Alternating Weighted Sum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Setting $$x = -1$$ after the first differentiation gives the alternating weighted sum $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} (-1)^{r-1} r \binom{n}{r} = 0$$ for $$n > 1$$. The cancellation reflects the fact that the linear function $$nx(1+x)^{n-1}$$ vanishes at $$x = -1$$.

nodes.label: Integration Method
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Integrating $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$ from $$0$$ to $$x$$ and setting $$x = 1$$ gives $$\sum_{r=0}^{n} \frac{\binom{n}{r}}{r+1} = \frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1}$$. Integration is the dual of differentiation and handles coefficients divided by an arithmetic factor.

nodes.label: Product of Binomial Coefficients
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Multiplying $$(1 + x)^n$$ by $$(x + 1)^n$$ and equating the coefficient of $$x^n$$ gives the sum of squares $$C_0^2 + C_1^2 + \dots + C_n^2 = \binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{(n!)^2}$$. Equating other coefficients yields the shifted convolution identities.

nodes.label: Shifted Convolution Products
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Equating the coefficient of $$x^{n-k}$$ in the product $$(1+x)^n (x+1)^n = (1+x)^{2n}$$ gives $$\sum_{r=0}^{n-k} \binom{n}{r} \binom{n}{r+k} = \binom{2n}{n-k}$$. This convolution identity covers products of coefficients whose indices differ by a fixed shift $$k$$.

nodes.label: Pascal's Triangle Recursion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it, expressed as $$\binom{n}{r} + \binom{n}{r-1} = \binom{n+1}{r}$$. The symmetry $$\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$$ and the row sum $$\sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} = 2^n$$ are the other two structural facts.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Applications
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The binomial theorem converts large powers into a multiple of a modulus plus a small remainder, which is the backbone of divisibility, remainder, and last-digit problems. The trick is to write the base as $$M \pm 1$$ or $$Mk \pm R$$ for the modulus $$M$$.

nodes.label: Divisibility and Remainders
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: To find the remainder of a large power $$A^n$$ on division by $$M$$, one writes $$A$$ (or a power of $$A$$) as $$kM \pm 1$$ and expands, since $$(M + 1)^n \equiv 1 \pmod{M}$$. All terms except the last are multiples of $$M$$ and drop out.

nodes.label: Remainder Example
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: To find the remainder when $$7^{103}$$ is divided by $$25$$, note $$7^2 = 49 = 2(25) - 1$$, so $$7^{103} = 7(50 - 1)^{51} = 7(50k - 1) = 350k - 7 = 25(14k - 1) + 18$$. The remainder is therefore $$18$$.

nodes.label: Proving Divisibility
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: To prove an expression like $$a^n - b^n$$ is divisible by $$a - b$$, one writes $$a = (a - b) + b$$ and expands $$[(a - b) + b]^n$$; every term except $$b^n$$ carries the factor $$(a - b)$$. The binomial expansion thus exhibits the divisor explicitly.

nodes.label: Last Digits Determination
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The last digit of a number is its value modulo $$10$$, the last two digits are its value modulo $$100$$, and the last three are modulo $$1000$$. One expands the base as $$(10k \pm 1)^n$$ and retains only the terms that survive the chosen modulus.

nodes.label: Integral and Fractional Parts
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $$N = (A + \sqrt{B})^n = I + f$$ with $$A - 1 < \sqrt{B} < A$$, the conjugate bracket $$f' = (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ lies strictly between $$0$$ and $$1$$. Adding the two brackets eliminates the surds and yields an even integer, forcing the fractional parts to sum to one.

nodes.label: The Conjugate Bracket
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Defining $$f' = (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ gives $$0 < f' < 1$$ because $$0 < |A - \sqrt{B}| < 1$$, and the sum $$(A + \sqrt{B})^n + (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ is an even integer $$2K$$ since all odd surd powers cancel. As $$I + (f + f') = 2K$$ is an integer and $$0 < f + f' < 2$$, the fractional parts must satisfy $$f + f' = 1$$.

nodes.label: Integral Part Parity and Product
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Because $$f + f' = 1$$ and the total is the even integer $$2K$$, the integral part is $$I = 2K - 1$$, always an odd integer. The product of the number and its conjugate is $$(I + f)(1 - f) = (I + f)f' = (A + \sqrt{B})^n (A - \sqrt{B})^n = (A^2 - B)^n$$, a clean rational value.

nodes.label: Binomial Theorem for Any Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For a rational or negative index $$n$$ the expansion becomes an infinite series that converges only when the first term is unity and $$|x| < 1$$. The general term is $$T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$ and the series does not terminate.

nodes.label: Theorem for Rational Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For any real $$n$$ the series $$(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3 + \dots$$ converges if and only if $$|x| < 1$$. The base must first be normalized so that the leading term is exactly $$1$$, since $$(a + x)^n = a^n\left(1 + \frac{x}{a}\right)^n$$ needs $$\left|\frac{x}{a}\right| < 1$$.

nodes.label: General Term for Any Index
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The $$(r+1)$$-th term of the infinite series is $$T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$, a ratio of $$r$$ falling factors of $$n$$ over $$r!$$. Unlike the positive-index case there are infinitely many terms, and convergence requires $$|x| < 1$$.

nodes.label: Square Root and Fractional Expansions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For a fractional index such as $$n = \frac{1}{2}$$ the series gives $$\sqrt{1 + x} = 1 + \frac{x}{2} - \frac{x^2}{8} + \frac{x^3}{16} - \dots$$ valid for $$|x| < 1$$. Such expansions are the source of many limit and approximation problems in JEE calculus.

nodes.label: Canonical Infinite Expansions
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Four negative-power expansions recur constantly in JEE calculus and limits: $$(1 - x)^{-1}$$, $$(1 + x)^{-1}$$, $$(1 - x)^{-2}$$, and the general $$(1 - x)^{-n}$$. Each is an infinite series valid strictly for $$|x| < 1$$.

nodes.label: Expansion of (1 - x) to the -1
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The geometric series is $$(1 - x)^{-1} = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, and its alternating twin is $$(1 + x)^{-1} = 1 - x + x^2 - x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (-1)^r x^r$$. Both diverge at $$x = 1$$.

nodes.label: Expansion of (1 - x) to the -2
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Differentiating the geometric series gives $$(1 - x)^{-2} = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (r+1) x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, with the alternating version $$(1 + x)^{-2} = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (-1)^r (r+1) x^r$$. The coefficients are the natural numbers in arithmetic progression.

nodes.label: General Negative Power
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The general negative integer power expands as $$(1 - x)^{-n} = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \binom{n+r-1}{r} x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, so the coefficients are the diagonal binomial coefficients $$\binom{n+r-1}{r}$$. This unifies the $$-1$$ and $$-2$$ cases and connects to stars-and-bars counting.

nodes.label: Approximations for Small Quantities
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: When $$|x|$$ is very small the higher powers are negligible and $$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$$, with a second-order correction $$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} x^2$$. These linear and quadratic approximations are used throughout JEE for estimation and limits.

nodes.label: Multinomial Theorem
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The multinomial theorem generalizes the binomial to a sum of three or more terms raised to a power. The expansion of $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n$$ sums over all non-negative integer partitions of $$n$$ into $$k$$ parts.

nodes.label: Multinomial Expansion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The expansion is $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum \frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \cdots r_k!} x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \cdots x_k^{r_k}$$ summed over all $$r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n$$. Each term is weighted by the multinomial coefficient and the exponents of the variables add up to $$n$$.

nodes.label: Multinomial Coefficient
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The coefficient of the term $$x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \cdots x_k^{r_k}$$ is the multinomial coefficient $$\frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \cdots r_k!}$$, which counts the ways to partition $$n$$ objects into groups of sizes $$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_k$$. For $$k = 2$$ it reduces to the ordinary binomial coefficient $$\binom{n}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Total Number of Terms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Each distinct term corresponds to a non-negative integer solution of $$r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n$$, so by stars and bars the total number of terms is $$\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$$. This count depends only on $$n$$ and $$k$$, not on the variables themselves.

nodes.label: Trinomial Expansion
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For three terms the number of distinct terms in $$(x + y + z)^n$$ is $$\binom{n+2}{2} = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}$$, obtained by setting $$k = 3$$ in the general count $$\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$$. Before applying this one must simplify the base, since a perfect-square base collapses the effective number of terms.

nodes.label: Greatest Multinomial Coefficient
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The multinomial coefficient is maximized when the indices $$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_k$$ are as nearly equal as possible, i.e. as close to $$n/k$$ as integer partitions allow. Writing $$n = qk + r$$ with $$q = \lfloor n/k \rfloor$$, the maximum is $$\frac{n!}{(q!)^{k-r}\,[(q+1)!]^r}$$ with $$r$$ indices equal to $$q + 1$$ and the rest equal to $$q$$.

nodes.label: Term-Counting Caution
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A base that is secretly a perfect power must be condensed first: $$(1 + 2x + x^2)^{20} = [(1 + x)^2]^{20} = (1 + x)^{40}$$ has exactly $$40 + 1 = 41$$ dissimilar terms, not the $$\binom{22}{2} = 231$$ that a blind trinomial count would give. Always simplify the polynomial base before applying any term-counting formula.

nodes.label: Cartesian Foundations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Point geometry on the plane: distance, division, triangle centers, and area are the algebraic toolkit behind every curve. The distance formula is $$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$.

nodes.label: Distance and Section Formulas
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The section formula for internal division in ratio $$m:n$$ is $$P = \left( \frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n} \right)$$. External division simply flips the signs to $$\frac{mx_2 - nx_1}{m - n}$$.

nodes.label: Internal and External Division
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A positive ratio divides internally and a negative ratio divides externally. External division uses $$P = \left( \frac{mx_2 - nx_1}{m - n}, \frac{my_2 - ny_1}{m - n} \right)$$, and the midpoint is the special case $$m = n$$.

nodes.label: Triangle Centers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The centroid is the mean of the vertices, $$G = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3}, \frac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3} \right)$$. The incenter weights vertices by side lengths, $$I = \left( \frac{ax_1 + bx_2 + cx_3}{a + b + c}, \frac{ay_1 + by_2 + cy_3}{a + b + c} \right)$$.

nodes.label: Euler Line
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: In any non-equilateral triangle the orthocenter $$H$$, centroid $$G$$, and circumcenter $$O$$ are collinear. The centroid divides the segment in the fixed ratio $$\frac{HG}{GO} = \frac{2}{1}$$.

nodes.label: Area and Collinearity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The signed area of a triangle is a third-order determinant, $$\Delta = \frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$. Setting this determinant to zero is the collinearity test.

nodes.label: Collinearity Condition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Three points are collinear exactly when the area determinant vanishes, equivalently when $$\text{slope}(AB) = \text{slope}(BC)$$. The compact test is $$\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Straight Lines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A line is a first-degree equation $$ax + by + c = 0$$ whose slope is $$m = -a/b$$. All standard forms are reparametrizations of this single equation.

nodes.label: Slope and Inclination
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The slope is the tangent of the inclination $$\theta$$ measured from the positive $$x$$-axis, $$m = \tan\theta = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$. Vertical lines have undefined slope since $$\theta = \pi/2$$.

nodes.label: Standard Line Forms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Point-slope, two-point, slope-intercept, intercept, normal, and parametric forms all describe the same line. The intercept form is $$\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1$$ and the normal form is $$x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p$$.

nodes.label: Intercept Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The line cutting intercepts $$a$$ and $$b$$ on the axes is $$\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1$$. The area of the triangle it forms with the axes is $$\frac{1}{2}|ab|$$.

nodes.label: Parametric Distance Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A point at signed distance $$r$$ along a line of inclination $$\theta$$ through $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$\frac{x - x_1}{\cos\theta} = \frac{y - y_1}{\sin\theta} = r$$. Substituting into a curve gives a quadratic in $$r$$ whose roots are the distances to the intersection points.

nodes.label: Angle Between Lines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For slopes $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ the acute angle obeys $$\tan\theta = \left| \frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2} \right|$$. This ratio is the workhorse for angle-based locus problems.

nodes.label: Parallel and Perpendicular Criteria
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Two lines are parallel when their slopes match, which in general form is $$a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 = 0$$. They are perpendicular when $$a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 = 0$$, i.e. the product of slopes is $$-1$$.

nodes.label: Perpendicular Distance
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The distance from $$(x_1, y_1)$$ to the line $$ax + by + c = 0$$ is $$p = \frac{|ax_1 + by_1 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$$. From the origin this reduces to $$p = \frac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Distance Between Parallel Lines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For parallel lines with identical $$x$$ and $$y$$ coefficients the separation is $$d = \frac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$$. The coefficients of $$x$$ and $$y$$ must first be made equal before applying this formula.

nodes.label: Foot of Perpendicular and Reflection
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The foot of the perpendicular from $$(x_1, y_1)$$ to $$ax + by + c = 0$$ satisfies $$\frac{h - x_1}{a} = \frac{k - y_1}{b} = -\frac{ax_1 + by_1 + c}{a^2 + b^2}$$. The mirror image doubles this displacement.

nodes.label: Mirror Image of a Point
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The image of $$(x_1, y_1)$$ in the line mirror is given by $$\frac{h' - x_1}{a} = \frac{k' - y_1}{b} = -2\frac{ax_1 + by_1 + c}{a^2 + b^2}$$. The foot is the midpoint of the point and its image.

nodes.label: Family of Lines and Concurrency
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The family through the intersection of $$L_1 = 0$$ and $$L_2 = 0$$ is $$L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$$ for any real $$\lambda$$. Three lines are concurrent only when a determinant vanishes.

nodes.label: Concurrency Determinant
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Three lines $$a_i x + b_i y + c_i = 0$$ are concurrent if and only if $$\begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0$$. This is necessary but not sufficient when two lines are parallel.

nodes.label: Angle Bisectors
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Points equidistant from two lines give the bisectors $$\frac{a_1 x + b_1 y + c_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2}} = \pm \frac{a_2 x + b_2 y + c_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2}}$$. The two bisectors are always mutually perpendicular.

nodes.label: Pair of Straight Lines
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A homogeneous second-degree equation $$ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$$ represents two lines through the origin. The angle between them is $$\tan\theta = \frac{2\sqrt{h^2 - ab}}{|a + b|}$$ and they are perpendicular when $$a + b = 0$$.

nodes.label: Homogenization Technique
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: To find lines joining the origin to the intersection of a curve and a secant, write the line as $$\frac{lx + my}{-n} = 1$$ and multiply each term to make the curve degree-2. The resulting homogeneous equation represents the two rays $$OA$$ and $$OB$$.

nodes.label: Circles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A circle is the locus of a point at a fixed radius from a center, and its general equation is $$x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$$. The center is $$(-g, -f)$$ and the radius is $$r = \sqrt{g^2 + f^2 - c}$$.

nodes.label: Standard and General Forms
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The central form is $$(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$$, which expands to the general second-degree form. The radius is real, zero, or imaginary as $$g^2 + f^2 - c$$ is positive, zero, or negative.

nodes.label: Diametric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The circle on the segment joining $$A(x_1, y_1)$$ and $$B(x_2, y_2)$$ as diameter is $$(x - x_1)(x - x_2) + (y - y_1)(y - y_2) = 0$$. It is the smallest circle through the two points since the angle in a semicircle is $$90^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Parametric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A point on the circle with center $$(h, k)$$ and radius $$r$$ is $$x = h + r\cos\theta, y = k + r\sin\theta$$. The parameter $$\theta$$ is the eccentric angle measured from the horizontal through the center.

nodes.label: Intercepts on Coordinate Axes
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The general circle cuts the $$x$$-axis in an intercept of length $$2\sqrt{g^2 - c}$$ and the $$y$$-axis in $$2\sqrt{f^2 - c}$$. It touches an axis when the corresponding expression under the root is zero, i.e. $$g^2 = c$$ or $$f^2 = c$$.

nodes.label: Point Position and Power
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For a point $$P(x_1, y_1)$$ the expression $$S_1 = x_1^2 + y_1^2 + 2gx_1 + 2fy_1 + c$$ fixes its position: positive means outside, zero on, negative inside. The power of the point is $$PA \cdot PB = d^2 - r^2 = S_1$$.

nodes.label: Tangents to a Circle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A line $$y = mx + c$$ touches the circle $$x^2 + y^2 = r^2$$ when $$c^2 = r^2(1 + m^2)$$. The tangent at a point $$(x_1, y_1)$$ on the circle is obtained by the $$T = 0$$ substitution.

nodes.label: Slope Form of Tangent
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The tangent with slope $$m$$ to $$x^2 + y^2 = r^2$$ is $$y = mx \pm r\sqrt{1 + m^2}$$, touching at $$\left( \mp \frac{mr}{\sqrt{1 + m^2}}, \pm \frac{r}{\sqrt{1 + m^2}} \right)$$. The two signs give the two parallel tangents.

nodes.label: Point Form of Tangent
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For the circle $$x^2 + y^2 = r^2$$ the tangent at $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$xx_1 + yy_1 = r^2$$. For the general circle the $$T = 0$$ form is $$xx_1 + yy_1 + g(x + x_1) + f(y + y_1) + c = 0$$.

nodes.label: Pair of Tangents and Chord of Contact
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: From an external point the combined equation of the two tangents is $$SS_1 = T^2$$ and the tangent length is $$L = \sqrt{S_1}$$. The chord joining the contact points is the chord of contact $$T = 0$$.

nodes.label: Director Circle
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The locus of the intersection of perpendicular tangents is the director circle $$x^2 + y^2 = 2r^2$$. It is concentric with the original circle and has radius $$\sqrt{2}\,r$$.

nodes.label: Chord of Contact
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The chord of contact from an external point $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$T = 0$$, namely $$xx_1 + yy_1 + g(x + x_1) + f(y + y_1) + c = 0$$. Its length is $$\frac{2r\sqrt{S_1}}{\sqrt{r^2 + S_1}}$$.

nodes.label: Two Circles Configurations
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The number of common tangents depends on $$d$$ versus $$r_1 \pm r_2$$, giving five regimes from four tangents when disjoint down to zero when one circle lies inside the other. The direct and transverse common tangent lengths are $$L_{DCT} = \sqrt{d^2 - (r_1 - r_2)^2}$$ and $$L_{TCT} = \sqrt{d^2 - (r_1 + r_2)^2}$$.

nodes.label: Orthogonality of Circles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Two circles cut orthogonally when the radii at an intersection are perpendicular, so $$d^2 = r_1^2 + r_2^2$$. In general form the algebraic condition is $$2(g_1 g_2 + f_1 f_2) = c_1 + c_2$$, valid only for monic equations.

nodes.label: Radical Axis
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The radical axis is the locus of equal power with respect to two circles, found by subtracting the equations to get $$S_1 - S_2 = 0$$. It is always a straight line perpendicular to the line of centers, even when the circles do not intersect.

nodes.label: Family of Circles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Circles through the intersection of two circles form the family $$S_1 + \lambda S_2 = 0$$, and circles through a circle-line intersection form $$S + \lambda L = 0$$. Choosing $$\lambda$$ to cancel a term pins the member through a desired point.

nodes.label: Conic Sections
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Every conic is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed focus bears a constant ratio to its distance from a fixed directrix. The defining relation is $$SP = e \cdot PM$$ where $$e$$ is the eccentricity.

nodes.label: Focus-Directrix Definition
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A point $$P$$ lies on a conic when the ratio of its distance from the focus $$S$$ to its perpendicular distance $$PM$$ from the directrix is the constant eccentricity $$e$$, written $$\frac{SP}{PM} = e$$. Squaring $$SP = e \cdot PM$$ yields the second-degree equation of the curve.

nodes.label: Classification by Eccentricity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The value of $$e$$ selects the curve: $$e = 0$$ gives a circle, $$0 < e < 1$$ an ellipse, $$e = 1$$ a parabola, and $$e > 1$$ a hyperbola. This single parameter controls whether the conic is closed, open to one branch, or open to two.

nodes.label: Parabola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The parabola is the conic of eccentricity $$e = 1$$, with standard equation $$y^2 = 4ax$$, focus $$(a, 0)$$, and directrix $$x = -a$$. Its latus rectum has length $$4a$$ and endpoints $$(a, \pm 2a)$$.

nodes.label: Standard Equation
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $$y^2 = 4ax$$ the vertex is the origin, the axis is the $$x$$-axis, and the focus is $$(a, 0)$$. The distance of any point $$(x, y)$$ from the focus equals its distance from the directrix, giving the focal distance $$x + a$$.

nodes.label: Elements and Latus Rectum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis, of length $$4a$$ with endpoints $$(a, \pm 2a)$$. The four standard orientations are $$y^2 = \pm 4ax$$ and $$x^2 = \pm 4ay$$, each with the same latus rectum $$4a$$.

nodes.label: Parametric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: Every point on $$y^2 = 4ax$$ can be written as $$(at^2, 2at)$$ where $$t$$ is the parameter. The parameter is convenient because the slope of the tangent at that point is $$\frac{1}{t}$$ and the tangent is $$ty = x + at^2$$.

nodes.label: Tangents to the Parabola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The tangent at $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$yy_1 = 2a(x + x_1)$$, and in slope form the tangent is $$y = mx + \frac{a}{m}$$ touching at $$\left( \frac{a}{m^2}, \frac{2a}{m} \right)$$. From an external point the pair of tangents is $$SS_1 = T^2$$.

nodes.label: Slope Form of Tangent
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A line of slope $$m$$ touches $$y^2 = 4ax$$ when it is written as $$y = mx + \frac{a}{m}$$, valid for $$m \neq 0$$. The point of contact is $$\left( \frac{a}{m^2}, \frac{2a}{m} \right)$$, so each slope gives exactly one tangent.

nodes.label: Pair of Tangents
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: From an external point $$(x_1, y_1)$$ the combined equation of both tangents is $$SS_1 = T^2$$ where $$S \equiv y^2 - 4ax$$ and $$T \equiv yy_1 - 2a(x + x_1)$$. This second-degree equation represents the two straight tangents through the point.

nodes.label: Normals and Focal Chords
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The normal at parameter $$t$$ is $$y + tx = 2at + at^3$$, and a chord joining parameters $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$ has equation $$y(t_1 + t_2) = 2x + 2at_1 t_2$$. A chord through the focus is a focal chord, characterized by $$t_1 t_2 = -1$$.

nodes.label: Focal Chord Property
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: If the chord joining $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$ passes through the focus then $$t_1 t_2 = -1$$. Hence when one extremity of a focal chord is $$(at_1^2, 2at_1)$$ the other is $$\left( \frac{a}{t_1^2}, -\frac{2a}{t_1} \right)$$, and the latus rectum is the special case $$t = \pm 1$$.

nodes.label: Chord with Given Midpoint
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The chord of $$y^2 = 4ax$$ whose midpoint is $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is given by $$T = S_1$$, that is $$yy_1 - 2a(x + x_1) = y_1^2 - 4ax_1$$. This mirrors the circle result and is derived by equating the midpoint to the average of the intersection roots.

nodes.label: Ellipse
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The ellipse is the conic of eccentricity $$0 < e < 1$$ with standard equation $$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$ where $$b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$$. The sum of the focal distances of any point is the constant $$SP + S'P = 2a$$.

nodes.label: Standard Equation and Eccentricity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$ with $$a > b$$ the foci are $$(\pm ae, 0)$$ and the eccentricity is $$e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}}$$. The major axis has length $$2a$$ and the minor axis $$2b$$.

nodes.label: Eccentricity, Foci, and Latus Rectum
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The relation $$b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$$ ties the axes to the eccentricity, and the latus rectum has length $$\frac{2b^2}{a} = 2a(1 - e^2)$$ with endpoints $$(\pm ae, \pm b^2/a)$$. The directrices are $$x = \pm \frac{a}{e}$$ and the focal radii are $$SP = a - ex$$ and $$S'P = a + ex$$.

nodes.label: Parametric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A point on the ellipse is $$(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$$ where $$\theta$$ is the eccentric angle. Substitution verifies the equation instantly since $$\frac{a^2\cos^2\theta}{a^2} + \frac{b^2\sin^2\theta}{b^2} = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$$.

nodes.label: Tangents to the Ellipse
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The tangent at $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$\frac{xx_1}{a^2} + \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1$$, and the slope form is $$y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 + b^2}$$. The tangent at the parametric point is $$\frac{x\cos\theta}{a} + \frac{y\sin\theta}{b} = 1$$.

nodes.label: Slope Form of Tangent
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A line $$y = mx + c$$ touches the ellipse when $$c^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2$$, so the tangents are $$y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 + b^2}$$. The condition $$c^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2$$ is the tangency test and follows from setting the line-curve discriminant to zero.

nodes.label: Normal to the Ellipse
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The normal at the parametric point $$(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$$ is $$ax\sec\theta - by\csc\theta = a^2 - b^2$$. In point form it is $$\frac{a^2 x}{x_1} - \frac{b^2 y}{y_1} = a^2 - b^2$$, obtained from the gradient of the curve.

nodes.label: Auxiliary and Director Circles
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The auxiliary circle on the major axis is $$x^2 + y^2 = a^2$$ and supplies the eccentric angle via the perpendicular from a point on the ellipse. The director circle, the locus of perpendicular tangents, is $$x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2$$ and the area enclosed by the ellipse is $$\pi ab$$.

nodes.label: Hyperbola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The hyperbola is the conic of eccentricity $$e > 1$$ with standard equation $$\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$ where $$b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1)$$. The absolute difference of the focal distances is the constant $$|SP - S'P| = 2a$$.

nodes.label: Standard Equation and Eccentricity
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: For $$\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$ the foci are $$(\pm ae, 0)$$ with $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$$ and the eccentricity is $$e = \sqrt{1 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}}$$. The transverse axis has length $$2a$$ and the conjugate axis $$2b$$.

nodes.label: Eccentricity and Foci
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The identity $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$$ (note the plus sign, opposite to the ellipse) gives $$e = \frac{c}{a} > 1$$ and the foci $$(\pm ae, 0)$$. The directrices are $$x = \pm \frac{a}{e}$$ and the latus rectum is $$\frac{2b^2}{a} = 2a(e^2 - 1)$$.

nodes.label: Asymptotes
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{b}{a}x$$ and their combined equation is $$\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 0$$, differing from the hyperbola only in the constant term. The angle between them is $$2\tan^{-1}(b/a)$$ and the eccentricity satisfies $$e = \sec\theta$$ when the angle is $$2\theta$$.

nodes.label: Parametric Form
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A point on the hyperbola is $$(a\sec\theta, b\tan\theta)$$ since $$\frac{a^2\sec^2\theta}{a^2} - \frac{b^2\tan^2\theta}{b^2} = \sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$$. The parameter $$\theta$$ is used exactly as the eccentric angle is used for the ellipse.

nodes.label: Tangents to the Hyperbola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The tangent at $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$\frac{xx_1}{a^2} - \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1$$ and in slope form $$y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 - b^2}$$, which needs $$a^2 m^2 \ge b^2$$. The parametric tangent is $$\frac{x\sec\theta}{a} - \frac{y\tan\theta}{b} = 1$$.

nodes.label: Slope Form of Tangent
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: A line $$y = mx + c$$ touches the hyperbola when $$c^2 = a^2 m^2 - b^2$$, giving $$y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 - b^2}$$. Unlike the ellipse, slopes with $$|m| < b/a$$ yield no real tangent because the line would meet both branches.

nodes.label: Normal to the Hyperbola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The normal at $$(x_1, y_1)$$ is $$\frac{a^2 x}{x_1} + \frac{b^2 y}{y_1} = a^2 + b^2$$, again with a plus sign unlike the ellipse. It is derived from the gradient $$\left( \frac{x_1}{a^2}, -\frac{y_1}{b^2} \right)$$ and passes through the point of contact.

nodes.label: Conjugate and Rectangular Hyperbola
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.note: The conjugate hyperbola $$\frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1$$ shares the same asymptotes, and if $$e_1, e_2$$ are the two eccentricities then $$\frac{1}{e_1^2} + \frac{1}{e_2^2} = 1$$. A rectangular hyperbola has $$a = b$$, perpendicular asymptotes, eccentricity $$e = \sqrt{2}$$, and can be written as $$xy = c^2$$.
